Praise for Mark Forsyth’s previous books:

对马克·福赛斯之前作品的赞誉：

The Etymologicon

词源学

‘This year’s must-have stocking filler – the angel on the top of the tree, the satsuma in the sock, the threepenny bit in the plum pudding, the essential addition to the library in the smallest room is Mark Forsyth’s The Etymologicon ’

“今年圣诞袜里必备的礼物——圣诞树顶上的天使、袜子里的蜜柑、布丁里的三便士硬币，最小房间里图书馆的必备藏品是马克·福赛斯的《词源学》。”

Ian Sansom, Guardian

伊恩·桑索姆，《卫报》

‘I’m hooked on Forsyth’s book … Crikey, but this is addictive’

“我迷上了福赛斯的书……我的天，这本书太让人上瘾了。”

Matthew Parris, The Times

马修·帕里斯，《泰晤士报》

‘Kudos should go to Mark Forsyth, author of The Etymologicon … Clearly a man who knows his onions, Mr Forsyth must have worked 19 to the dozen, spotting red herrings and unravelling inkhorn terms, to bestow this boon … a work of the first water, to coin a phrase.’

“应该向《词源学》的作者马克·福赛斯致敬……显然，福赛斯先生是一位精通此道的人，他一定付出了无数心血，辨别了各种误导信息，破解了晦涩难懂的术语，才成就了这部杰作……用一句俗语来说，这是一部一流之作。”

William Leith, Evening Standard

Acknowledgements

致谢

I would like to bow down in thanks and prose to Jane Seeber for her indefatigable aid.

我谨以最诚挚的谢意和文字，向简·西伯致以最崇高的敬意，感谢她不懈的帮助。

For the last year, I have been unbearable company. My only question to friend or foe alike has been ‘Can you think of any famous phrases that follow this particular structure?’ Many people have helped, but I can’t exactly remember who. My thanks should probably go, in no particular order, to Jane Seeber, Andrea Coleman, Rob Colvile, Nick Popper, John Goldsmith, Michael Mellor, Hilary Scott, Adrian Hornsby, James Forsyth, Allegra Stratton, Alicia Roberts, Nick Roberts, my parents, Laura Humble, Simon Blake, Alister Whitford, Jeremy Large, Chris Mann, Claire Bodanis and anybody else whom I have rudely forgotten in my absence of mind.

过去一年，我简直是个令人难以忍受的家伙。我问朋友或敌人的唯一问题就是：“你能想到哪些符合这种结构的著名短语吗？” 很多人都帮过我，但我记不清是谁了。在此，我应该感谢以下几位（排名不分先后）：Jane Seeber、Andrea Coleman、Rob Colvile、Nick Popper、John Goldsmith、Michael Mellor、Hilary Scott、Adrian Hornsby、James Forsyth、Allegra Stratton、Alicia Roberts、Nick Roberts、我的父母、Laura Humble、Simon Blake、Alister Whitford、Jeremy Large、Chris Mann、Claire Bodanis，以及其他任何我因疏忽而遗漏的人。

About the author

关于作者

Mark Forsyth is a writer, journalist, proofreader, ghostwriter and pedant. He was given a copy of the Oxford English Dictionary as a christening present and has never looked back. In 2009 he started the Inky Fool blog, in order to share his heaps of useless information with a verbose world. He is also the author of the Sunday Times No. 1 bestseller The Etymologicon , and its successful sister volume, The Horologicon , both published by Icon Books.

马克·福赛斯是一位作家、记者、校对员、代笔作家，同时也是一位学究。他受洗时收到了一本《牛津英语词典》，从此便与它结下了不解之缘。2009年，他创办了“墨水傻瓜”（Inky Fool）博客，旨在与这个喋喋不休的世界分享他那堆积如山的无用信息。他还是《星期日泰晤士报》畅销书榜首作品《词源学》（The Etymologicon）及其姊妹篇《钟表学》（The Horologicon）的作者，这两本书均由Icon Books出版。

Preface

前言

On Cooking Blindfolded

蒙眼烹饪

Shakespeare was not a genius. He was, without the distant shadow of a doubt, the most wonderful writer who ever breathed. But not a genius. No angels handed him his lines, no fairies proofread for him. Instead, he learnt techniques, he learnt tricks, and he learnt them well.

莎士比亚并非天才。毫无疑问，他是史上最伟大的作家。但他并非天才。没有天使为他递上台词，也没有仙女为他校对。相反，他学习技巧，学习诀窍，并且将它们运用得炉火纯青。

Genius, as we tend to talk about it today, is some sort of mysterious and combustible substance that burns brightly and burns out. It’s the strange gift of poets and pop stars that allows them to produce one wonderful work in their early twenties and then nothing. It is mysterious. It is there. It is gone.

我们今天谈论的天才，就像某种神秘而易燃的物质，它光芒四射，却又转瞬即逝。诗人、流行歌星拥有这种奇特的天赋，让他们在二十出头时创作出一部杰作，之后便销声匿迹。它神秘莫测，时而存在，时而消逝。

This is, if you think about it, a rather odd idea. Nobody would talk about a doctor or an accountant or a taxi driver who burnt out too fast. Too brilliant to live long. Pretty much everyone in every profession outside of professional athletics gets better as they go along, for the rather obvious reason that they learn and they practise. Why should writers be different?

仔细想想，这确实是个相当奇怪的想法。没人会谈论医生、会计师或出租车司机过早陨落，因为他们才华横溢却英年早逝。除了职业运动员之外，几乎所有行业的人都会随着时间的推移而进步，原因显而易见：他们不断学习和练习。为什么作家就应该例外呢？

Shakespeare wasn’t different. Shakespeare got better and better and better, which was easy because he started badly, like most people starting a new job.

莎士比亚也不例外。他的水平越来越高，这很容易理解，因为他起步很差，就像大多数人开始一份新工作一样。

Nobody is quite sure which is Shakespeare’s first play, but the contenders are Love’s Labours Lost , Titus Andronicus , and Henry VI Part 1 . Do not, dear reader, worry if you have not read those plays. Almost nobody has, because, to be utterly frank, they’re not very good. To be precise about it, there isn’t a single memorable line in any of them.

没人能确切地说出莎士比亚的第一部剧作是哪一部，但《爱的徒劳》、《泰特斯·安德洛尼克斯》和《亨利六世（上）》都是有力的竞争者。亲爱的读者，如果您没读过这些剧作，也无需担心。几乎没人读过，因为坦白说，它们并不怎么样。确切地说，它们之中没有一句令人印象深刻的台词。

Now, for Shakespeare, that may seem rather astonishing. He was, after all, the master of the memorable line. But the first line of Shakespeare that almost anybody knows is in Henry VI Part 2 , when one revolting peasant says to another: ‘The first thing we do, let’s kill all the lawyers.’ In Part 3 there’s a couple more – ‘I can smile, and murder while I smile’. And each successive play has more and more and more great lines until you work up through Much Ado and Julius Caesar (1590s) to Hamlet and King Lear (1600s).

对于莎士比亚来说，这或许令人颇感意外。毕竟，他是创作经典台词的大师。但几乎人人都知道的第一句莎士比亚名言出自《亨利六世》第二部，一位反叛的农民对另一位农民说：“我们做的第一件事，就是杀光所有律师。”第三部里还有几句——“我可以微笑，然后一边微笑一边杀人”。此后，他的每一部剧作都涌现出越来越多的精彩台词，从《无事生非》和《尤利乌斯·凯撒》（16世纪90年代）一直到《哈姆雷特》和《李尔王》（17世纪初）。

Shakespeare got better because he learnt. Now some people will tell you that great writing cannot be learnt. Such people should be hit repeatedly on the nose until they promise not to talk nonsense any more. Shakespeare was taught how to write. He was taught it at school. Composition (in Latin) was the main part of an Elizabethan education. And, importantly, you had to learn the figures of rhetoric.

莎士比亚之所以能写得更好，是因为他不断学习。有些人会告诉你，伟大的写作是学不来的。这些人应该被狠狠地敲打鼻子，直到他们保证不再胡说八道为止。莎士比亚是被教导如何写作的。他在学校里学习写作。用拉丁语写作是伊丽莎白时代教育的重要组成部分。而且，更重要的是，你必须学习修辞手法。

Professionally, Shakespeare wrote in English. And for that he learnt and used the figures of rhetoric in English. This was easy, as Elizabethan London was crazy for rhetorical figures. A chap called George Puttenham had a bestseller in 1589 with his book on them (that’s about the year of Shakespeare’s first play). And that was just following on from Henry Peacham’s The Garden of Eloquence , which had come out a decade earlier. Book after book was published, all about the figures of rhetoric. So I should probably explain what the figures of rhetoric are.

莎士比亚的职业写作语言是英语。为此，他学习并运用了英语修辞手法。这并不难，因为伊丽莎白时代的伦敦对修辞手法趋之若鹜。一位名叫乔治·普特纳姆的作家在1589年出版了一本关于修辞手法的畅销书（那一年大约也是莎士比亚第一部戏剧问世的年份）。而在此之前，亨利·皮查姆的《雄辩花园》已经出版了十年。此后，一本又一本关于修辞手法的书籍相继问世。所以，我应该解释一下什么是修辞手法。

Rhetoric is a big subject. It consists of the whole art of persuasion. The lot. It includes logic (or the kind of sloppy logic most people understand, called enthymemes), it includes speaking loudly and clearly, and it includes working out what topics to talk about. Anything to do with persuasion is rhetoric, right down to the argumentum ad baculum , which means threatening somebody with a stick until they agree with you . One minuscule part of this massive subject is the figures of rhetoric, which are the techniques for making a single phrase striking and memorable just by altering the wording. Not by saying something different, but by saying something in a different way. They are the formulas for producing great lines.

修辞学是一门博大精深的学科，它涵盖了说服的方方面面，无所不包。它包括逻辑（或者说是大多数人都能理解的那种不太严谨的逻辑，称为省略推理），包括清晰响亮地表达，以及选择合适的谈话主题。任何与说服相关的都属于修辞的范畴，甚至包括诉诸武力的论证——也就是用棍棒威胁别人直到他们同意你的观点。修辞格只是这门庞大学科中微不足道的一部分，它指的是通过改变措辞，使一句话变得引人注目、令人难忘的技巧。并非改变内容，而是改变表达方式。它们是创作精彩语句的秘诀。

These formulas were thought up by the Ancient Greeks and then added to by the Romans. As Shakespeare set to work England was busy having the Renaissance (everybody else had had the Renaissance a century or so before, and we were running late). So the classical works on rhetoric were dug out, translated and adapted for use in English. But it wasn’t the enthymemes or the topics or even the baculums that the English liked. We loved the figures. The ‘flowers of rhetoric’ as they were called (hence The Garden of Eloquence ), because, as a nation, we were at the time rather obsessed with poetry.

这些修辞格公式由古希腊人构思，后经罗马人完善。莎士比亚开始创作时，英国正值文艺复兴时期（其他国家大约在一个世纪前就经历了文艺复兴，而我们却姗姗来迟）。于是，古典修辞学著作被挖掘出来，翻译并改编成英文版本。但英国人喜爱的并非省略句、论题，甚至也不是论证句。我们钟爱的是修辞格，也就是所谓的“修辞之花”（因此有了《雄辩花园》一书），因为当时的英国人对诗歌十分痴迷。

So Shakespeare learnt and learnt and got better and better, and his lines became more and more striking and more and more memorable. But most of his great and famous lines are simply examples of the ancient formulas. ‘I can smile, and murder while I smile’ was not handed to Shakespeare by God. It’s just an example of diacope.

于是莎士比亚不断学习，技艺日臻成熟，他的台词也变得越来越精彩，越来越令人难忘。但他那些伟大而著名的台词，大多只是古代公式的运用。“我可以微笑，也可以在微笑的同时杀人”并非上帝赐予莎士比亚的灵感，它只是双关语的一个例子。

So why, you may be asking, were you not taught the figures of rhetoric at school? If they make a chap write as well as Shakespeare, shouldn’t we be learning them instead of home economics and woodwork? There are three answers to that. First, we need woodworkers.

你可能会问，为什么学校里没有教过修辞手法？如果修辞手法能让一个人写出像莎士比亚一样的作品，我们难道不应该学习修辞手法，而不是学习家政和木工吗？对此，有三个答案。首先，我们需要木工。

Second, people have always been suspicious of rhetoric in general and the figures in particular. If somebody learns how to phrase things beautifully, they might be able to persuade you of something that isn’t true. Stern people dislike rhetoric, and unfortunately it’s usually stern people who are in charge: solemn fools who believe that truth is more important than beauty.

其次，人们历来对修辞，尤其是其中的数字，抱有怀疑态度。如果有人能把事情说得文采斐然，他们或许就能说服你相信一些不实之事。严肃的人厌恶修辞，而不幸的是，掌权的往往是严肃的人：这些一本正经的傻瓜认为真理比美更重要。

Third, the Romantic Movement came along at the end of the eighteenth century. The Romantics liked to believe that you could learn everything worth learning by gazing at a babbling mountain brook, or running barefoot through the fields, or contemplating a Grecian urn. They wanted to be natural, and the figures of rhetoric are not natural. They are formulas, formulas that you can learn from a book.

第三，浪漫主义运动兴起于十八世纪末。浪漫主义者喜欢相信，你可以通过凝视潺潺的山涧溪流、赤脚奔跑在田野间，或沉思古希腊瓮，来学习一切值得学习的东西。他们追求自然，而修辞格并非自然之物。它们是公式，是可以从书本上学到的公式。

So what with the dislike of beauty and books, the figures of rhetoric were largely forgotten. But that doesn’t mean that they ceased to be used. You see, when the Ancient Greeks were going around collecting their formulas, they weren’t plucking them out of thin air or growing them in a test tube. All that the Greeks were doing was noting down the best and most memorable phrases they heard, and working out what the structures were, in much the same way that when you or I eat a particularly delicious meal, we might ask for the recipe.

由于古人厌恶美和书籍，修辞格在很大程度上被遗忘了。但这并不意味着它们就此停止使用。要知道，古希腊人收集修辞格时，并非凭空捏造或人工培育。他们所做的，只是记录下听到的最精妙、最令人难忘的词句，并研究其结构，就像你我吃到美味佳肴后会向人索要食谱一样。

The figures are, to some extent, alive and well. We still use them. It’s just that we use them haphazardly. What Shakespeare had beaten into him at school, we might, occasionally, use by accident and without realising it. We just happen to say something beautiful, and don’t know how we did it. We are like blindfolded cooks throwing anything into the pot and occasionally, just occasionally, producing a delicious meal.

这些数字在某种程度上依然鲜活，我们仍然在使用它们。只不过，我们使用它们的方式变得随意。莎士比亚在学校里被灌输的那些东西，我们偶尔也会无意间、不自觉地用上。我们碰巧说出了一些优美的话语，却不知道自己是怎么做到的。我们就像蒙着眼睛的厨师，把任何东西都扔进锅里，偶尔，仅仅是偶尔，就能做出一顿美味佳肴。

Shakespeare had a big recipe book and his eyes wide open.

莎士比亚有一本厚厚的食谱，而且他的眼睛睁得大大的。

The figures are alive and thriving. The one line from that song or film that you remember and don’t know why you remember is almost certainly down to one of the figures, one of the flowers of rhetoric growing wild. They account for the songs you sing and the poems you love, although that is hidden from you at school.

这些修辞手法鲜活生动，生机勃勃。你记得某首歌或某部电影里的某句台词，却又不知为何记得，那几乎可以肯定出自其中一位修辞手法大师之手，他是修辞界的一颗璀璨明珠。你吟唱的歌曲和喜爱的诗歌，都源于此，尽管在学校里，这些都被隐藏了起来。

English teaching at school is, unfortunately, obsessed with what a poet thought, as though that were of any interest to anyone. Rather than being taught about how a poem is phrased, schoolchildren are asked to write essays on what William Blake thought about the Tiger; despite the fact that William Blake was a nutjob whose opinions, in a civilised society, would be of no interest to anybody apart from his parole officer. A poet is not somebody who has great thoughts. That is the menial duty of the philosopher. A poet is somebody who expresses his thoughts, however commonplace they may be, exquisitely. That is the one and only difference between the poet and everybody else.

遗憾的是，学校的英语教学似乎痴迷于诗人的思想，仿佛这真的会引起任何人的兴趣。学生们不去学习诗歌的句法，反而被要求写一篇关于威廉·布莱克对老虎的看法的文章；尽管威廉·布莱克是个疯子，在文明社会里，除了他的假释官，没人会关心他的观点。诗人并非拥有伟大思想的人，那是哲学家的琐碎职责。诗人是将自己的想法，无论多么平凡，以精妙的方式表达出来的人。这才是诗人与其他人之间唯一的区别。

So my aim in this book is to explain the figures of rhetoric, devoting one chapter to each. There are a couple of caveats that I should make clear before we begin. First of all, the study of rhetoric did not entirely disappear with the Romantics. There are still scholarly articles written. Unfortunately, almost all of these get tied in knots trying to define their terms. Rhetorical terminology, like anything kicked around for a couple of millennia, is a mess. So an article on syllepsis will start by defining the term, attacking other scholars for defining it differently, appealing to the authority of Quintilian or Susenbrotus, and then conclude without actually having said anything about syllepsis or what it is. I’ve written more on this subject in the Epilogue, but as I have no particular interest in such lexical squabbles I have simply adopted the rule of Humpty-Dumpty: When I use a rhetorical term, it means just what I choose it to mean – neither more nor less.

因此，本书旨在阐释修辞格的各种修辞手法，每一种修辞格都用一章的篇幅进行讲解。在正式开始之前，我需要先说明几点。首先，修辞学的研究并没有随着浪漫主义的消亡而彻底消失。至今仍有相关的学术论文发表。然而，遗憾的是，几乎所有这些论文都陷入了术语定义的泥潭。修辞术语，就像任何流传了几千年的东西一样，早已混乱不堪。所以，一篇关于“音节”（syllepsis）的文章，往往会先定义这个术语，然后抨击其他学者不同的定义，援引昆体良或苏森布罗图斯的权威，最后却对“音节”本身及其含义只字未提。我在后记中对此主题进行了更详细的阐述，但由于我对这种词汇上的争论没有特别的兴趣，所以我干脆采用了“矮胖子”的规则：当我使用一个修辞术语时，它的意思就是我选择的意思——不多也不少。

Second, some of you may think that I am trying to attack Shakespeare or whichever poet I’m quoting. You may consider this a cruel work of debunking, like the spoilsports who uncurtained the Wizard of Oz. Shakespeare is a god and it is sacrilege to unseal his star-y pointing pyramid. Little could be further from the truth. It doesn’t insult the Wright Brothers to explain the principles of aerodynamics, nor Neil Armstrong the spacesuit. Shakespeare was a craftsman, and if you told him that now people studied his attitudes to feminism more than his rhetorical figures he would chuckle.

其次，你们中有些人可能会认为我是在攻击莎士比亚，或者我引用的任何一位诗人。你们或许会觉得这是在残酷地揭开真相，就像那些破坏《绿野仙踪》神秘面纱的人一样。在你们看来，莎士比亚是神，揭开他那星光熠熠的金字塔的神秘面纱简直是亵渎神灵。然而，事实并非如此。解释空气动力学原理并不侮辱莱特兄弟，解释宇航服也一样。莎士比亚是一位匠人，如果你告诉他，现在人们研究他对女权主义的态度远胜于研究他的修辞手法，他一定会一笑置之。

Shakespeare did not consider himself sacred. He would often just steal content from other people. However, whatever he stole he improved, and he improved it using the formulas, flowers and figures of rhetoric.

莎士比亚并不认为自己是神圣不可侵犯的。他经常直接剽窃他人的作品。然而，无论剽窃的是什么，他都会加以改进，并运用修辞的公式、辞藻和比喻来加以完善。

# ↩

Chapter 1

第一章

Alliteration

头韵

Let us begin with something we know Shakespeare stole, simply so that we can see what a wonderful thief he was. When Shakespeare decided to write The Tragedie of Anthonie, and Cleopatra he of course needed a history book from which to work. The standard work on the subject was Plutarch’s Lives of the Noble Greeks and Romans , but Plutarch wrote in Greek, and, as Shakespeare’s friend Ben Jonson later pointed out, ‘thou hadst small Latin and less Greek’.

让我们先从莎士比亚剽窃的一件事说起，这样我们就能看出他是个多么高明的“窃贼”。莎士比亚决定创作《安东尼与克莉奥佩特拉》时，自然需要一本历史书作为参考。当时这方面的权威著作是普鲁塔克的《希腊罗马名人传》，但普鲁塔克是用希腊语写的，正如莎士比亚的朋友本·琼森后来指出的那样，“你懂一点拉丁语，希腊语就更不懂了”。

Despite years at Stratford Grammar School learning pretty much nothing but the classics, Shakespeare could never be bothered with foreign languages. He always used translations.

尽管莎士比亚在斯特拉特福文法学校学习多年，几乎只接触古典文学，但他始终对外国语言不感兴趣。他总是使用译本。

So he got hold of the standard English translation of Plutarch, which had been written by a chap called Thomas North and published in 1579. We know that this is the version Shakespeare used because you can sometimes see him using the same word that North used, and sometimes pairs of words. But when Shakespeare got to the big speech of the whole play, when he really needed some poetry, when he wanted true greatness, when he wanted to describe the moment that Antony saw Cleopatra on the barge and fell in love with her – he just found the relevant paragraph in North and copied it out almost word for word. Almost word for word.

于是他找到了普鲁塔克著作的标准英文译本，译者是一位名叫托马斯·诺斯的人，出版于1579年。我们知道莎士比亚使用的是这个版本，因为有时他使用的词语与诺斯使用的词语相同，有时甚至成对使用。但当莎士比亚写到全剧最重要的独白，当他真正需要一些诗意，当他想要展现真正的伟大，当他想要描绘安东尼在驳船上见到克莉奥佩特拉并爱上她的那一刻时——他只是在诺斯的译本中找到相关的段落，几乎一字不差地抄录了下来。几乎一字不差。

Here’s North:

这是北方：

… she disdained to set forward otherwise but to take her barge in the river Cydnus, the poop whereof was of gold, the sails of purple, and the oars of silver, which kept stroke in rowing after the sound of the music of flutes, howboys, cithernes, viols, and such other instruments as they played up in the barge.

她不屑于以其他方式出发，而是乘着她的驳船驶入西德努斯河。驳船的船尾是金色的，船帆是紫色的，船桨是银色的，随着船上笛子、小提琴、齐特琴、维奥尔琴和其他乐器的音乐声，船桨不停地划动。

And here’s Shakespeare:

接下来是莎士比亚：

The barge she sat in like a burnished throne,

她所坐的驳船宛如一座光洁的宝座，

Burned on the water: the poop was beaten gold;

在水上烧制：粪便被锤成了黄金；

Purple the sails and so perfumed that

紫色的帆，散发着浓郁的香气。

The winds were lovesick with them; the oars were silver,

风为他们而倾倒；船桨是银色的，

Which to the tune of flutes kept stroke, and made

伴着笛声，不断敲击，并发出

The water which they beat to follow faster,

他们拍打着水流，让水流更快涌来。

As amorous of their strokes.

如同他们爱抚一般。

The thing about this is that it’s definitely half stolen. There is no possible way that Shakespeare didn’t have North open on his desk when he was writing. But also, Shakespeare made little changes. That means that we can actually watch Shakespeare working. We can peep back 400 years and see the greatest genius who ever lived scribbling away. We can see how he did it, and it’s really pretty bloody simple. All he did was add some alliteration.

关键在于，这其中肯定有一半是抄袭的。莎士比亚写作时，桌上不可能没有《诺斯》这本书。但同时，莎士比亚也做了一些细微的改动。这意味着我们实际上可以窥见莎士比亚的创作过程。我们可以回溯400年前，看到这位史上最伟大的天才埋头写作。我们可以看到他是如何做到的，而这其实非常简单。他所做的只是添加了一些头韵。

Nobody knows why we love to hear words that begin with the same letter, but we do and Shakespeare knew it. So he picked the word barge and worked from there. Barge begins with a B, so Shakespeare sat back and said to himself: ‘The barge she sat in was like a …’ And then (though I can’t prove this) he said: ‘Ba … ba … ba … burnished throne.’ He jotted that down and then he decided to do another. ‘The barge she sat in like a burnished throne … ba … ba … burned? It burned on the water.’ And the poop was gold? Not any more: the poop was beaten gold. That’s four Bs in two lines. Enough to be getting on with. Shakespeare could have got carried away and written something like:

没人知道为什么我们喜欢听以相同字母开头的单词，但我们就是喜欢，莎士比亚也深谙此道。于是他选择了“barge”（驳船）这个词，并以此为基础展开创作。“barge”以字母B开头，莎士比亚便靠在椅背上，自言自语道：“她坐的驳船就像……”然后（虽然我无法证实），他又说：“Ba…ba…ba…闪亮的宝座。”他把这些记了下来，然后又决定再写一句。“她坐的驳船就像闪亮的宝座……ba…ba…燃烧？它在水面上燃烧。”船尾是金子吗？不，现在不是了：船尾是锤打过的金子。两行诗里就有四个B。够他继续创作了。莎士比亚本来可以继续写下去，写出类似这样的句子：

The barge she basked in, like a burnished boat

她沐浴在驳船上，就像一艘锃亮的船。

Burned by the banks, the back was beaten brass.

被银行烧毁，背部被敲打成黄铜。

But that would just be silly. Of course, Shakespeare did write like that sometimes. There’s a bit in A Midsummer Night’s Dream that goes:

但这未免太荒谬了。当然，莎士比亚有时确实会这样写作。《仲夏夜之梦》里就有一段是这样的：

Whereat, with blade, with bloody blameful blade,

然而，带着刀刃，带着血淋淋的罪孽之刃，

He bravely broached his boiling bloody breast;

他勇敢地袒露了自己滚烫流血的胸口；

But there he was taking the mickey out of poets who use alliteration but don’t know where to stop. No, Shakespeare wasn’t going to put any more Bs in, he was working on the Ps. North’s original had ‘the poop whereof was of gold, the sails of purple’. That’s two Ps already, so Shakespeare decided that the sails would be pa … pa … perfumed. Maybe he stopped to wonder how you would perfume a whole sail, or how you might be able to smell them from the river bank (the Cydnus is quite wide). Or maybe he didn’t. Accuracy is much less important than alliteration.

但他却在嘲讽那些滥用头韵却不知何时收手的诗人。不，莎士比亚并非打算再加一个“b”，他正在琢磨“p”的用法。诺斯的原句是“金色的粪便，紫色的帆”。这已经有两个“p”了，所以莎士比亚决定把帆写成“pa…pa…香水味的”。或许他曾想过如何给整张帆喷香水，或者如何从河岸上闻到香味（西德努斯河很宽阔）。又或许他根本没想过。对莎士比亚来说，准确性远不如头韵重要。

From there on in, Shakespeare was coasting. North had ‘After the sound’ so Shakespeare had ‘to the tune’. North had a whole orchestra of instruments – ‘flutes, howboys, cithernes, viols’ – Shakespeare cut that down to just flutes, because he liked the F. So flutes made the ‘ W ater W hich they beat to F ollow F aster, A s A morous of their strokes’.

从那以后，莎士比亚的创作就顺风顺水了。诺斯用了“顺着声音”，莎士比亚就用了“顺着旋律”。诺斯用了一整套管弦乐队的乐器——“长笛、管风琴、齐特琴、维奥尔琴”——莎士比亚把它简化成了只有长笛，因为他喜欢F音。于是，长笛奏出了“水声，他们吹奏着，加快了速度，如同爱抚着他们的吹奏”。

So Shakespeare stole; but he did wonderful things with his plunder. He’s like somebody who nicks your old socks and then darns them. Shakespeare simply knew that people are suckers for alliteration and that it’s pretty damned easy to make something alliterate (or that it’s surprisingly simple to add alliteration).

所以莎士比亚确实借鉴了其他作品；但他用这些“战利品”创作出了精彩的作品。他就像有人偷了你的旧袜子，然后又把它们补好。莎士比亚深知人们喜欢头韵，而且让句子押头韵非常容易（或者说，添加头韵其实出奇地简单）。

You can spend all day trying to think of some universal truth to set down on paper, and some poets try that. Shakespeare knew that it’s much easier to string together some words beginning with the same letter. It doesn’t matter what it’s about. It can be the exact depth in the sea to which a chap’s corpse has sunk; hardly a matter of universal interest, but if you say, ‘Full fathom five thy father lies’, you will be considered the greatest poet who ever lived. Express precisely the same thought any other way – e.g. ‘your father’s corpse is 9.144 metres below sea level’ – and you’re just a coastguard with some bad news.

你可以花一整天的时间试图构思一些普世真理并将其记录下来，有些诗人也确实这么做了。但莎士比亚深谙此道，他知道把一些以相同字母开头的单词串联起来要容易得多。内容是什么并不重要。它可以是某人的尸体沉入海底的确切深度；这并非什么人人关心的问题，但如果你说“你父亲的尸体沉入了五寻深的海底”，你就会被认为是史上最伟大的诗人。如果用其他方式表达同样的意思——例如“你父亲的尸体沉入了海平面以下9.144米”——那你只不过是一个带来坏消息的海岸警卫队员而已。

Any phrase, so long as it alliterates, is memorable and will be believed even if it’s a bunch of nonsense. Curiosity, for example, did not kill the cat. There are no widely reported cases of felines dying from being too inquisitive. In fact, the original proverb was not ‘curiosity killed the cat’ (which is recorded only from 1921), it was ‘ care killed the cat’. And even that one was changed. When the proverb was first recorded (in Shakespeare, actually, although he seems to be just referring to a well known bit of folk wisdom), care meant sorrow or unhappiness. But by the twentieth century it was care in the sense of too much kindness – something along the lines of a pet that is overfed and pampered. In a hundred years’ time it may be something else that does the pussy-killing, although you can be certain that whatever it is – kindness, consternation or corruption – will begin with a C or K.

任何短语，只要押头韵，就容易记住，即使全是胡说八道也会被人相信。比如，好奇害死猫的说法就站不住脚。并没有广泛报道的猫咪因过度好奇而丧命的案例。事实上，最初的谚语并非“好奇害死猫”（这个说法最早出现在1921年），而是“过度操心害死猫”。而且，就连这个说法也发生了变化。这句谚语最初被记录下来时（实际上出自莎士比亚的作品，尽管他似乎只是在引用一句广为人知的民间智慧），“操心”指的是悲伤或不幸。但到了20世纪，“操心”的含义变成了过度的关爱——类似于过度喂养和溺爱宠物。一百年后，或许会是其他原因导致猫咪死亡，但可以肯定的是，无论是什么——关爱、惊恐还是腐败——都将以字母C或K开头。

Similarly, there was once an old proverb, ‘An ynche in a misse is as good as an ell’, an ell being an old unit of measurement of 1.1 miles. So the ell was changed to a mile, and then the inch was dropped because it doesn’t begin with an M, and we were left with ‘A miss is as good as a mile’, which, if you think about it, doesn’t really make sense any more. But who needs sense when you have alliteration?

同样，以前有一句古老的谚语：“一英里中的一英寸相当于一英里”，其中“英里”是古老的长度单位，等于1.1英里。后来“英里”被改成了“英里”，然后又去掉了“英寸”，因为它不是以字母“M”开头的，于是就变成了“一英里的距离相当于一英里”。仔细想想，这其实已经没什么道理了。但是，有了头韵，谁还在乎逻辑呢？

Nobody has ever thrown a baby out with the bathwater, nor is there anything particularly right about rain. Even when something does make a bit of sense, it’s usually obvious why the comparison was picked. It takes two to tango, but it takes two to waltz as well. There are whole hogs, but why not pigs? Bright as a button. Cool as a cucumber. Dead as a doornail. In fact, Dickens made this point rather better than I at the opening of A Christmas Carol .

没人会把婴儿连同洗澡水一起倒掉，雨水本身也并非完美无缺。即便有些事听起来似乎有道理，通常也很容易理解为什么会选择这种比喻。跳探戈需要两个人，跳华尔兹也一样。有整头猪，但为什么不能是小猪呢？聪明绝顶。冷静沉着。死透了。事实上，狄更斯在《圣诞颂歌》的开头就比我更好地阐述了这一点。

Old Marley was as dead as a door-nail.

老马利死得透透的。

Mind! I don’t mean to say that I know, of my own knowledge, what there is particularly dead about a door-nail. I might have been inclined, myself, to regard a coffin-nail as the deadest piece of ironmongery in the trade. But the wisdom of our ancestors is in the simile; and my unhallowed hands shall not disturb it, or the Country’s done for. You will therefore permit me to repeat, emphatically, that Marley was as dead as a door-nail.

注意！我并非自以为是地认为，就我个人所知，门钉究竟有何特别之处。就我个人而言，我或许更倾向于认为棺材钉才是五金行业中最死气沉沉的物件。但我们先祖的智慧就蕴藏在这比喻之中；我这双不洁之手绝不会触碰它，否则国家就完了。因此，请允许我再次强调，马利死得就像门钉一样。

Except that Dickens knew full well why it is doornails that are dead. Dickens was a writer, and as a writer, he knew that alliteration is the simplest way to turn a memorable phrase. This was, after all, the guy who had written Nicholas Nickleby , The Pickwick Papers (full title: The Posthumous Papers of the Pickwick Club ) and, indeed, A Christmas Carol . He knew which side his bread was buttered, as had those who came before him, like Jane Austen ( Sense and Sensibility , Pride and Prejudice ), and those who came after him ( Where’s Wally? ).

然而，狄更斯非常清楚为什么门钉会死。狄更斯是一位作家，而作为一名作家，他深知头韵是创造令人难忘的短语的最简单方法。毕竟，他可是写出过《尼古拉斯·尼克尔贝》、《匹克威克外传》（全名：《匹克威克外传》）以及《圣诞颂歌》的作家。他深谙此道，就像他的前辈，如简·奥斯汀（《理智与情感》、《傲慢与偏见》），以及他的后辈（《威利在哪里？》）一样。

So popular is alliteration that in the 1960s it actually made a grab for political power. In the 1960s a vast radical youth movement began campaigning to do things for the sole reason that they began with the same letter. Ban the bomb. Burn your bra. Power to the people. For a moment there it seemed as though alliteration would change the world. But then the spirit of idealism faded and those who had manned the barricades went off and got jobs in marketing. They stopped telling people to ban the bomb and started telling them to put a tiger in your tank, chuck out the chintz and use Access – Your Flexible Friend, or perhaps PayPal. And all because the lady loves Milk Tray.

头韵如此流行，以至于在20世纪60年代，它竟然一度攫取了政治权力。在60年代，一场声势浩大的激进青年运动兴起，他们发起各种运动，仅仅因为这些运动的开头字母相同。比如“禁止核弹”、“烧掉你的胸罩”、“人民当家作主”。在那个时期，人们似乎真的相信头韵能够改变世界。但随后，理想主义的热情消退了，那些曾经在街头奋战的人们也纷纷转行，从事起了市场营销工作。他们不再呼吁人们禁止核弹，而是开始鼓吹“给你的油箱加点动力”、“扔掉印花棉布”、“使用Access——你的灵活朋友”，或者干脆用PayPal。而这一切，仅仅是因为那位女士喜欢牛奶巧克力。

It’s enough to get your goat. 1

真是让人火冒三丈。

Alliteration can be brief and obvious – a short, sharp, shock. Or it can be long and subtle. John Keats once wrote fourteen lines of Fs and Ss, and it was beautiful:

头韵可以简短而显眼——短促有力，令人震惊。也可以冗长而微妙。约翰·济慈曾写过十四行全是F和S的诗句，非常优美：

Deep in the shady sadness of a vale

在幽暗山谷的悲伤深处

Far sunken from the healthy breath of morn,

远离清晨清新的气息，

Far from the fiery noon, and eve’s one star,

远离炽热的正午，以及黄昏时分的一颗星，

Sat gray-hair’d Saturn, quiet as a stone,

灰白头发的土星静静地坐在那里，像石头一样纹丝不动。

Still as the silence round about his lair;

他巢穴周围一片寂静；

Forest on forest hung about his head

他头顶上挂满了层层叠叠的森林。

Like cloud on cloud. No stir of air was there,

就像云上叠云，一丝空气都没有。

Not so much life as on a summer’s day

与其说是生活，不如说是夏日里的生活。

Robs not one light seed from the feather’d grass,

它不会从羽状草丛中夺走一粒轻盈的种子。

But where the dead leaf fell, there did it rest.

但枯叶落下的地方，它就静静地躺在那里。

A stream went voiceless by, still deadened more

溪水无声流淌，依旧死寂。

By reason of his fallen divinity

由于他堕落的神性

Spreading a shade: the Naiad ’mid her reeds

芦苇丛中，水泽仙女撑起一片荫凉

Press’d her cold finger closer to her lips.

她将冰冷的手指更靠近嘴唇。

Whereas, at almost the same time, Thomas De Quincey, famous junkie and prose stylist, got himself all muddled up over this sentence:

然而，几乎在同一时间，著名瘾君子兼散文家托马斯·德·昆西却被这句话搞得一头雾水：

At present, after exchanging a few parting words, and a few final or farewell farewells with my faithful female agent …

目前，在与我忠诚的女特工互道了几句告别语，做了最后的道别之后……

So muddled was he that he decided to add a footnote apologising for his paroemion (that’s the technical name for excessive alliteration). The footnote went:

他当时脑子一片混乱，以至于决定加个脚注，为他过度使用头韵（这是过度使用头韵的专业术语）而道歉。脚注内容如下：

Some people are irritated, or even fancy themselves insulted, by overt acts of alliteration, as many people are by puns. On their account, let me say, that, although there are here eight separate f’s in less than half a sentence, this is to be held as pure accident. In fact, at one time there were nine f’s in the original cast of the sentence, until I, in pity of the affronted people, substituted female agent for female friend .

有些人对明显的头韵感到恼火，甚至觉得受到了侮辱，就像很多人对双关语感到恼火一样。对此，我想说，虽然这句话不到半句就出现了八个不同的“f”，但这纯属巧合。事实上，这句话最初有九个“f”，直到我出于对那些感到冒犯的人的同情，才把“female friend”替换成了“female agent”。

‘Agent’ seems a strange substitution for ‘friend’. But he probably had to do it as he couldn’t change ‘farewell farewells’. It’s much too clever to use a word as an adjective and then a noun. In fact, the trick has a name. It’s called polyptoton.

用“代理人”代替“朋友”似乎很奇怪。但他可能不得不这么做，因为他无法更改“再见再见”。先用一个词作形容词再作名词，这种手法确实很巧妙。事实上，这种技巧有个专门的名称，叫做多词性修辞法。

1 First recorded 1910 with no explanation at all.

1 最早记录于 1910 年，没有任何解释。

# ↩

Chapter 2

第二章

Polyptoton

多形性

Poor polyptoton is one of the lesser-known rhetorical tricks. It has no glamour. It isn’t taught to schoolchildren. It has a silly name which sounds a bit like polyp, a word for a nasal growth. In fact, it comes from the Greek for ‘many cases’, but that hardly makes up for it. Even once you’ve explained that that’s because it involves the repeated use of one word as different parts of speech or in different grammatical forms, polyptoton remains incorrigibly unsexy. This is a trifle unfair, especially as one of the best known examples of polyptoton is a song that is sometimes said to be about oral sex.

可怜的复述法（polyptoton）是鲜为人知的修辞技巧之一。它毫无魅力可言，也从未被教授给小学生。它的名字听起来有点傻，有点像“息肉”（polyp），一个指鼻息肉的词。事实上，它源自希腊语，意为“多种情况”，但这并不能弥补它的不足。即使你解释说这是因为它涉及将同一个词重复使用，使其具有不同的词性或语法形式，复述法仍然无可救药地缺乏吸引力。这有点不公平，尤其是考虑到复述法最著名的例子之一是一首有时被认为是关于口交的歌曲。

‘Please Please Me’ 1 is a classic case of polyptoton. The first please is please the interjection, as in ‘Please mind the gap’. The second please is a verb meaning to give pleasure, as in ‘This pleases me’. Same word: two different parts of speech. It’s easy, once you ponder it, to see how people could feel that the polyptoton was a little perverse. 2

“Please Please Me”¹ 是一个典型的多义词。第一个“please”是感叹词，例如“Please mind the gap”（请注意缝隙）。第二个“please”是动词，意思是使人愉悦，例如“This pleases me”（这让我很开心）。同一个词，两种不同的词性。仔细想想，很容易理解为什么人们会觉得这个多义词有点怪异。²

Whether the song is actually about matters carnal or emotional is beyond the scope of a book like this. All that we know about John Lennon’s motivations for writing it is that he had a specific interest in polyptoton (even if he may not have known the name). When Lennon was a child, his mother used to sing him a Bing Crosby song called ‘Please’. The lyrics went like this:

这首歌究竟是关于肉体还是情感方面的内容，超出了本书的讨论范围。我们只知道约翰·列侬创作这首歌的动机是他对多形性（即使他可能并不知道这个词）特别感兴趣。列侬小时候，他的母亲经常给他唱一首宾·克罗斯比的歌，叫做《请》（Please）。歌词是这样的：

Please,

请，

Lend your little ear to my pleas

请你侧耳倾听我的恳求。

Lend a ray of cheer to my pleas

请为我的请求带来一丝慰藉

And Lennon’s explanation of his own lyrics 3 was that in that song ‘I was always intrigued by the double use of the word “Please”’. Of course, in those lyrics the second please is spelled pleas, but that doesn’t matter. It’s still polyptoton if the words have a close etymological connection, or are just different parts of the same verb, which means that ‘All You Need is Love’ 4 is pretty much polyptoton beginning to end:

列侬对自己歌词的解释是，在那首歌里，“我一直对‘Please’这个词的双重用法很感兴趣”。当然，在那些歌词中，第二个“pleas”拼写成了“pleas”，但这并不重要。如果这两个词在词源上联系紧密，或者只是同一个动词的不同部分，那么它们仍然是多音词，这意味着《All You Need is Love》几乎从头到尾都是多音词：

Nothing you can do that can’t be done

没有什么事是你做不到的。

Nothing you can sing that can’t be sung

没有什么歌是唱不出来的。

Et cetera et cetera. Of course, John Lennon didn’t invent polyptoton. Shakespeare used it all the time. Some of his most famous lines go:

等等等等。当然，约翰·列侬并非多音节词的发明者。莎士比亚也经常使用它。他的一些最著名的台词是：

Let me not to the marriage of true minds

让我不要阻碍真心相爱者的结合

Admit impediments. Love is not love

承认障碍。爱并非只是爱。

Which alters when it alteration finds,

当发现变化时，它就会发生变化。

Or bends with the remover to remove.

或者用拆卸器弯曲将其移除。

Alters the verb, alteration the noun. Remover the noun, remove the verb. (‘Love is not love’ is merely a paradox, and we’ll come to that later.) He used it again in Macbeth with:

改变动词，改变名词。去掉名词，去掉动词。（“爱不是爱”仅仅是一个悖论，我们稍后再谈。）他在《麦克白》中再次使用了这种修辞手法：

Is this a dagger that I see before me,

我眼前看到的是一把匕首吗？

The handle towards my hand?

把手朝向我的手？

In fact, Shakespeare was so fond of polyptoton that he just repeated himself wholesale. He had a trick and he liked it and he used it again and again. So in Richard II Bolingbroke, busy revolting, says ‘My gracious uncle’, but his uncle, the Duke of York replies:

事实上，莎士比亚如此钟爱重复，以至于他经常原封不动地重复自己。他掌握了一种技巧，而且很喜欢，于是反复使用。例如在《理查二世》中，忙于叛乱的博林布鲁克说“我仁慈的叔叔”，但他的叔叔，约克公爵却回答说：

Tut, tut!

嘟嘟！

Grace me no grace, nor uncle me no uncle:

恩典不赐予我恩典，叔叔也不赐予我叔叔：

I am no traitor’s uncle; and that word ‘grace’

我不是叛徒的叔叔；而“恩典”这个词

In an ungracious mouth is but profane.

粗鲁无礼的言语只会显得亵渎神明。

Which is three counts of polyptoton and jolly clever. In fact, Shakespeare was so pleased with himself that when he got round to writing Romeo and Juliet he (hoping nobody would notice that he’s just reusing his old lines) has Juliet’s dad tell her:

这可是三个音节的谐音梗，而且非常巧妙。事实上，莎士比亚对自己非常满意，以至于当他着手创作《罗密欧与朱丽叶》时，他（希望没人会注意到他只是在重复使用自己以前的台词）让朱丽叶的父亲对她说：

Thank me no thankings, nor proud me no prouds.

谢我无需感谢，也无需骄傲。

It was just a trick that Shakespeare had in his bag, and a device like that can be devised anywhere you like. In fact, the most famous use of Shakespeare’s little trick wasn’t by Shakespeare. This makes sense really. Anybody can write ‘Hello me no hellos’ or ‘How are you old chap me no how are you old chaps’. It is a trick available to everyone and the best example was by a lady called Susanna Centlivre.

这只是莎士比亚惯用的小技巧，类似的技巧随处可得。事实上，莎士比亚这个小技巧最著名的运用并非出自莎士比亚之手。这其实也合情合理。任何人都能写出“Hello me no hellos”或“How are you old chap me no how are you old chaps”。这是人人都能掌握的技巧，而最好的例子是一位名叫苏珊娜·森特利弗的女士。

Susanna Centlivre had a strange life. She ran away from home, may have cross-dressed, may thus have been the first woman educated at Cambridge University, and was certainly the most successful female writer of the eighteenth century. But the only line of hers that has stood the test of time is from The Busybody . A son is arguing with his father about the usual father–son issues of money, marriage, and remarriage. The father says:

苏珊娜·森特利弗的一生颇为奇特。她离家出走，可能曾男扮女装，因此可能是剑桥大学第一位受过教育的女性，而且无疑是十八世纪最成功的女作家。但她唯一经受住时间考验的句子却出自《爱管闲事的人》。故事讲述的是一个儿子和父亲就金钱、婚姻和再婚等常见的父子话题争论不休。父亲说道：

Sir Francis : Out of my Doors, you Dog; you pretend to meddle with my Marriage, Sirrah.

弗朗西斯爵士：滚出我的门，你这条狗；你竟敢妄图干涉我的婚姻，先生。

Charles : Sir, I obey: But—

查尔斯：先生，我遵命：但是——

Sir Francis : But me no Buts— Be gone, Sir: Dare to ask me for Money agen— Refuse Forty Thousand Pound! Out of my Doors, I say, without Reply.

弗朗西斯爵士：但是，别跟我废话——滚开，先生：你竟敢再向我要钱——拒绝四万英镑！我毫不犹豫地让你滚出我的大门。

And poor old Shakespeare probably turned once in his grave and mumbled, ‘But! I should have used but.’

可怜的莎士比亚在坟墓里可能转过身来，喃喃自语道：“但是！我应该用‘但是’。”

Of course, these are the most obvious forms of polyptoton: but verb versus but viewed as a word itself. It’s almost too easy to do, but you’re bound to come up with a good line, so never say never. Much more subtle are Shakespeare’s ‘Speak the speech’ or ‘The rain it raineth every day’, both of which could be shortened to ‘Speak’ or ‘It raineth’, but they wouldn’t sound as good. The son of God tended to use subtler polyptotons. ‘Give us this day our daily bread and forgive us our trespasses as we forgive them that trespass against us’ is a pretty neat double.

当然，这些是最显而易见的多音句形式：比如“but”动词和“but”本身作为一个词来看。这种用法几乎太容易了，但你肯定能想出一句妙语，所以永远不要说“不可能”。莎士比亚的“Speak the speech”（说这句话）或“The rain it raineth every day”（雨，它每天都在下）则更为巧妙，这两句话都可以缩写成“Speak”或“It raineth”，但听起来就没那么好听了。上帝之子倾向于使用更微妙的多音句。“赐给我们今日的饮食，免我们的债，如同我们免了人的债”就是一个相当精妙的双关语。

So just as a little recap, polyptoton is a favourite of Jesus, Shakespeare and John Lennon. With a trio like that one can almost forget the smaller voices: Moses’ wife saying ‘I have been a stranger in a strange land’, or William Blake’s ‘Piper, pipe that song again’. Polyptoton, even though nobody has ever heard of it, succeeds, and nothing succeeds like success. Polyptoton is the sort of rhetorical trope you use when you’re the first man on the moon, unless cruelly messed up by the radio transmission. Neil Armstrong’s actual words were (beginning on the ladder of the Lunar Excursion Module): ‘I’m going to step off the LEM now.’ And then, as his boot touched the moon: ‘That’s one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind.’

简单回顾一下，多音节修辞法是耶稣、莎士比亚和约翰·列侬都钟爱的修辞手法。有了这三位大师的加持，人们几乎会忽略那些不太为人所知的声音：比如摩西的妻子说的“我曾是异乡的陌生人”，或是威廉·布莱克的“吹笛人，再吹一遍那首歌”。多音节修辞法，即便鲜为人知，却依然奏效，而成功本身就是最好的证明。多音节修辞法就像是你在成为第一个登上月球的人时会用到的那种修辞手法，除非无线电传输出了差错。尼尔·阿姆斯特朗当时的原话是（从登月舱的梯子上开始）：“我现在要离开登月舱了。”然后，当他的靴子触碰到月球时，他又说：“这是我个人的一小步，却是人类的一大步。”

Except that static on the radio cut in and the ‘a’ in ‘for a man’ got cut out. This was problematic as it meant that the phrase became utterly meaningless. Without an indefinite article to specify that the small step is being taken by one particular fellow, man is being used as a general noun meaning ‘mankind’. So the transmission to earth essentially says: ‘That’s one small step for mankind, one giant leap for mankind.’ Which rather ruins the point, not to mention the polyptoton. Of course, you have a bit of polyptoton left: there’s the ‘to step off’ verb against the ‘one small step’ noun. But nonetheless, it would have been good to begin our first extraterrestrial jaunt with a good, meaningful double-polyptoton.

然而，收音机里突然传来静电噪音，“for a man”中的“a”被屏蔽了。这造成了问题，因为这意味着这句话完全失去了意义。由于缺少不定冠词来指明这小步是由某个人迈出的，所以“man”被当作泛指名词，指代“人类”。因此，发回地球的信息实际上是：“这是人类的一小步，也是人类的一大步。”这完全破坏了原意，更不用说其中的双音节结构了。当然，这里还剩下一点双音节结构：动词“to step off”与名词“one small step”形成对比。但无论如何，如果我们的第一次外星之旅能以一个有意义、有意义的双音节结构开始，那就太好了。

I should point out that there is a theory that it wasn’t the static’s fault, and that Neil Armstrong simply fluffed his own lines, something that you could perhaps forgive him for considering the stressful circumstances. It is hard, polyptonically, to talk the talk when you’re also trying to moon-walk the moon-walk.

我应该指出，有一种理论认为，这并非静电干扰造成的，而是尼尔·阿姆斯特朗自己说错了话——考虑到当时紧张的气氛，或许可以原谅他。毕竟，一边要完成登月，一边还要说台词，这确实很难做到。

With the missing ‘a’ returned, the full phrase is also a great example of antithesis.

补回缺失的“a”后，完整的短语也是一个很好的对比例子。

1 Lennon/McCartney.

1 列侬/麦卡特尼。

2 Thus at least Robert Christgau, music editor of The Village Voice .

2 因此，至少《乡村之声》的音乐编辑罗伯特·克里斯特高是这样认为的。

3 Playboy interview, 1980.

3 1980 年《花花公子》采访。

# ↩

Chapter 3

第三章

Antithesis

对立

Polyptoton was complex. Antithesis is simple. Indeed, the only tricky thing about antithesis is how to punctuate it. Some insist that you should use a colon: others complain that you should use a full stop. But in essence antitheses are simple: first you mention one thing: then you mention another.

多音句很复杂，对立句则很简单。事实上，对立句唯一棘手的地方在于标点符号的使用。有人坚持应该用冒号，也有人抱怨应该用句号。但本质上，对立句很简单：先提及一件事，再提及另一件事。

Of course there are, occasionally, clever antitheses, antitheses that draw fine distinctions or tell you something that you did not know already. Oscar Wilde was the master of these, with lines like, ‘The well-bred contradict other people. The wise contradict themselves.’ But we can’t all be Oscar Wilde, and it would be interminably dull if we were. The world would degenerate into one permanent epigram.

当然，偶尔也会出现一些巧妙的对立句，它们能做出精妙的区分，或者揭示你原本不知道的道理。奥斯卡·王尔德就是这方面的个中高手，他曾说过：“有教养的人反驳别人，智者自相矛盾。” 但我们不可能都成为奥斯卡·王尔德，如果我们都成了王尔德，世界将会变得无比乏味。世界将会沦为一句永恒的格言。

Wildean antitheses are not too hard. You make a first statement that is relatively obvious, for example, ‘If a man is a gentleman he knows quite enough.’ The second half begins in an obvious way: ‘If he is not a gentleman’ … and then takes an odd turn: ‘whatever he knows is bad for him.’

王尔德式的对立并不难。你先提出一个相对显而易见的论点，例如，“如果一个人是绅士，他知道的就足够多了。” 后半部分也以显而易见的方式开头：“如果他不是绅士……”，然后笔锋一转，变得奇特起来：“他所知道的一切都对他有害。”

So ‘Wicked women bother one’ looks as though it will be followed by ‘Good women console one’, but instead it is followed by ‘Good women bore one.’ Or you have ‘Women represent the triumph of matter over mind; men represent the triumph of’ … and again the reader expects mind over matter, but instead gets ‘mind over morals’. Or ‘Journalism is unreadable, and literature is not read’, or ‘If one plays good music, people don’t listen, and if one plays bad music people don’t talk.’ And so on and so forth. So you start with a simple statement – Some men invent epigrams – and then you add unexpected inversion – others are invented by them .

所以，“恶妇烦扰人”这句话乍一看像是“善妇安慰人”，但实际上却是“善妇生子”。又比如，“女人代表物质战胜精神；男人代表……的胜利”，读者期待的是精神战胜物质，结果却是“精神战胜道德”。再比如，“新闻晦涩难懂，文学作品无人问津”，或者“好音乐无人欣赏，坏音乐无人问津”。诸如此类，不胜枚举。所以，你先是一个简单的陈述——有些人发明警句——然后又加上一个出人意料的反转——另一些人发明了警句。

But these are all just plays on the basic formula of antithesis: X is Y, and not X is not Y. Wilde did a few of these: ‘Fashion is what one wears oneself. What is unfashionable is what other people wear.’ This is the soul of antithesis, and this is what makes it so simple. Any statement, however basic, can grow into an antithesis. Why just say that life is sweet, when you can add that death is sour? Why point out that the sun rises in the morning without mentioning that it sets in the evening? Of course, anyone could have worked the second halves out for themselves, but what does that matter? United we stand, divided we fall, even though both statements imply the other.

但这些都只是对反义词基本公式的巧妙运用：X是Y，而非X不是Y。王尔德就曾使用过类似的修辞手法：“时尚是自己穿的衣服，不时尚的是别人穿的衣服。” 这就是反义词的精髓，也是它如此简洁的原因。任何陈述，无论多么简单，都可以发展成反义词。为什么只说生命是甜蜜的，而不说死亡是苦涩的呢？为什么只指出太阳早上升起，而不提它晚上落下呢？当然，任何人都可以自己推导出后半句，但这又有什么关系呢？团结则存，分裂则亡，即便这两个陈述都蕴含着另一个。

There is something final and certain about a good antithesis. If you said (as you have all right to do, dear reader) that those who can’t write themselves instead instruct other people on how to write, who would remember? But say ‘Those who can, do: those who can’t, teach’ and you sound as though you have sliced the world neatly into two and squeezed it out as an epigram.

好的对立句总给人一种确凿无疑的感觉。如果你说（亲爱的读者，你完全有权利这么说），那些自己不会写作的人反而去教别人写作，谁会记住这句话呢？但如果你说“能写的人写，不能写的人教”，听起来就像你把世界一分为二，然后浓缩成一句警句。

The Bible is chock-a-block with such unnecessary but beautiful antitheses. God, whatever his other failings, is a great rhetorician.

《圣经》中充满了这种不必要却又精妙绝伦的对立句。上帝，无论他其他方面有何不足，都是一位伟大的修辞家。

To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven: A time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted; A time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up; A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance; A time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing; A time to get, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away; A time to rend, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak; A time to love, and a time to hate; a time of war, and a time of peace.

凡事都有定期，天下万务都有定时：生有时，死有时；栽种有时，拔出所栽种的也有时；杀戮有时，医治有时；拆毁有时，建造有时；哭泣有时，欢笑有时；哀恸有时，跳舞有时；抛掷石头有时，堆聚石头有时；拥抱有时，不拥抱有时；得着有时，失落有时；保守有时，舍弃有时；撕裂有时，缝补有时；静默有时，言语有时；爱有时，恨有时；争战有时，和好有时。

If you stop and think about that little passage, you’ll notice that it consists mainly of the bleeding obvious, sprinkled with the thoroughly debatable (is there really a time for rending?). But to approach it like that is unfair, irreligious, and shows no appreciation for the beauties of prose. For though one antithesis is grand, a long list of antitheses is divine, and is technically known as a progressio. It was a favourite of God and Dickens:

如果你停下来仔细思考这段文字，你会发现它主要由显而易见的事实构成，其中夹杂着一些颇具争议的观点（真的有必要撕裂吗？）。但这样看待它是不公平的，有失偏颇，也丝毫没有欣赏散文之美。因为一个对立句固然精彩，但一系列对立句的并列才是精妙绝伦，这种修辞手法在文中被称为“渐进式对立”（progressio）。上帝和狄更斯都钟爱这种修辞手法。

It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness, it was the epoch of belief, it was the epoch of incredulity, it was the season of Light, it was the season of Darkness, it was the spring of hope, it was the winter of despair, we had everything before us, we had nothing before us, we were all going direct to Heaven, we were all going direct the other way …

这是最好的时代，也是最坏的时代；这是智慧的时代，也是愚昧的时代；这是信仰的时代，也是怀疑的时代；这是光明的季节，也是黑暗的季节；这是希望的春天，也是绝望的冬天；我们拥有一切，我们一无所有；我们都直奔天堂，我们也直奔地狱……

Or, if you want a more modern magnificence, there is this achingly beautiful disco song by a young lady called Katy Perry: 1

或者，如果你想要更现代的华丽感，可以听听凯蒂·佩里这位年轻女士演唱的这首美妙绝伦的迪斯科歌曲：1

You’re hot then you’re cold. You’re yes then you’re no. You’re in then you’re out. You’re up then you’re down.

你一会儿热情似火，一会儿又冷若冰霜；一会儿说“是”，一会儿又说“不”；一会儿加入，一会儿又退出；一会儿情绪高涨，一会儿又跌入谷底。

And so on, which is essentially just a reworking of Ecclesiastes. As T.S. Eliot put it: ‘Immature poets imitate. Mature poets steal.’ Songwriters love their antitheses and there are a million examples I could have used. Unfortunately I noticed that the lyrics ‘You say potato and I say potato. You say tomato and I say tomato’ don’t work that well when they’re written down.

诸如此类，本质上就是对《传道书》的改写。正如T·S·艾略特所说：“不成熟的诗人模仿，成熟的诗人窃取。” 词曲作者喜欢使用对立的表达方式，我本来可以举出无数个例子。可惜的是，我发现“你说土豆，我说土豆；你说番茄，我说番茄”这样的歌词写下来效果并不好。

However, for some reason the great subject of antithesis seems to be marriage. If I were a philosophical kind of chap I would probably say something about how marriage itself is an antithesis, a union of opposites into a pleasing whole, that man and woman is the ultimate antithesis (and perhaps love and marriage). As I am not a philosophical chap, I shall merely observe that ‘Marriage has many pains, but celibacy has no pleasures’ (Samuel Johnson), ‘Kissing don’t last, cookery do’ (George Meredith), and ‘For better for worse, for richer for poorer, in sickness and in health’ … except that, really, that’s an example of merism.

然而，不知为何，婚姻似乎成了对立关系的典型主题。如果我是个爱思考的人，我大概会说说婚姻本身就是一种对立，是将对立的两极融合成一个和谐的整体，男人和女人是终极的对立（或许爱情和婚姻也是如此）。但我并非哲学家，所以我只想简单地指出：“婚姻苦多，独身无乐”（塞缪尔·约翰逊），“亲吻转瞬即逝，烹饪却经久不衰”（乔治·梅瑞狄斯），以及“无论顺境逆境，无论贫穷富贵，无论健康疾病”……不过，说真的，这其实是“默契”的例子。

1 The song ‘Hot N Cold’ is credited to Katy Perry, Lukasz Gottwald, Max Martin. I have been unable to establish for certain which latter - day Dickens wrote the progressio.

1 歌曲《Hot N Cold》的词曲作者署名为 Katy Perry、Lukasz Gottwald 和 Max Martin。我一直无法确定这首组曲是由哪位狄更斯后期的作家创作的。

# ↩

Chapter 4

第四章

Merism

归类

Merism, ladies and gentlemen, often looks like antithesis, but it’s different. Merism is when you don’t say what you’re talking about, and instead name all of its parts. Ladies and gentlemen , for example, is a merism for people , because all people are either ladies or gentlemen. The beauty of merism is that it’s absolutely unnecessary. It’s words for words’ sake: a gushing torrent of invention filled with noun and noun and signifying nothing. Why a rhetorical figure that gabs on and on for no good reason should be central to the rite of marriage is beyond me.

各位，修辞格（或称“复数形式”）常常看起来像是反义词，但实际上并非如此。修辞格指的是不直接说出你谈论的内容，而是列举出它的所有组成部分。例如，“女士们先生们”就是一种指人的修辞格，因为所有人要么是女士，要么是先生。修辞格的妙处在于它完全没有必要。它纯粹是为了堆砌词语而堆砌词语：如同滔滔不绝的发明洪流，充斥着名词，却毫无意义。我实在无法理解，为什么这种喋喋不休、毫无意义的修辞手法会成为婚礼仪式的核心。

Then shall they give their troth to each other in this manner. The Minister, receiving the Woman at her father’s or friend’s hands, shall cause the Man with his right hand to take the Woman by her right hand, and to say after him as followeth.

然后他们要按此方式互许誓言。牧师从女子的父亲或朋友手中接过女子，让男子用右手牵起女子的右手，并按以下方式宣读誓词。

I N. take thee N. to be my wedded Wife, to have and to hold from this day forward, for better for worse, for richer for poorer, in sickness and in health, to love and to cherish, till death us do part, according to God’s holy ordinance; and thereto I plight thee my troth.

我愿娶你为妻，从今以后，无论顺境逆境、富裕贫穷、疾病健康，都将爱你、珍惜你，直到死亡将我们分开，这是上帝的神圣旨意；我向你许下我的誓言。

You’re either better or you’re worse, you’re either richer or you’re poorer, you’re either sick or you’re healthy. There are no other options. If you need some words there you could say ‘in any circumstances’. But really, you don’t need to say anything at all. ‘Till death us do part’ kind of has it sewn up. Anyway, it’s all terribly appropriate, as choosing to have two things form a single totality is exactly what marriage is. Even ‘loving and cherishing’ is a modern replacement for an ancient merism. In the medieval marriage service ‘sickness and health’ were followed by: ‘to be bonny and buxom, in bed and at board, till death do us part.’

要么更好，要么更糟；要么更富有，要么更贫穷；要么生病，要么健康。没有其他选择。如果你需要一些措辞，可以说“在任何情况下”。但实际上，你什么都不需要说。“至死不渝”已经把一切都说得很清楚了。总之，这一切都非常贴切，因为选择将两件事物融合为一体，正是婚姻的本质。甚至“爱与珍惜”也是对古代誓词的现代诠释。在中世纪的婚礼仪式中，“无论健康还是疾病”之后，紧接着是：“愿我们永远美丽丰满，无论在床上还是在餐桌旁，直到死亡将我们分开。”

Now, this seems to our modern eyes to be a strange sort of promise. How could a wife guarantee that she would be buxom? Were thin women unable to marry in church? However, the word buxom has changed in meaning over the years. The first citation in the Oxford English Dictionary comes from the twelfth century and is defined as: ‘Obedient; pliant; compliant, tractable.’ The sense then changed to happy, then to healthy, and thence to plump.

如今，在我们现代人看来，这似乎是一种奇怪的承诺。妻子如何能保证自己身材丰满呢？难道身材苗条的女性就不能在教堂结婚吗？然而，“丰满”（buxom）一词的含义随着时间的推移而发生了变化。《牛津英语词典》中最早的例证可以追溯到十二世纪，其定义为：“顺从的；柔顺的；温顺的，易于驾驭的。” 后来，其含义演变为“快乐的”，再后来是“健康的”，最终又演变为“丰满的”。

Meanwhile bonny comes from the French bon and the Latin bonus , both of which mean good . So a bonny and buxom wife was a good and obedient one. The phrasing was, I assume, deemed to be unreasonably optimistic.

“bonny”一词源于法语“bon”和拉丁语“bonus”，两者都表示“好”。因此，一位身材丰满、容貌姣好的妻子，也被认为是贤良顺从的妻子。我推测，这种说法后来被认为过于乐观。

Merism is also the most important feature in gay divorce, or, to be typographically precise about it, in Gay Divorce , the 1932 musical by Cole Porter. The hit song from that musical was an exercise in merisms, starting with one of the most common in the English language; ‘night and day’ is a merism for always . ‘Night and day you are the one’. It then moves on to the heavens: ‘Only you beneath the moon or under the sun’, which again means all the time (excluding moonless nights). The song even confesses how unnecessary merisms are: ‘Whether near to me or far / It’s no matter darling where you are’ (his emotions at middle distance are, again, unstated).

在同性离婚中，或者更准确地说，在科尔·波特1932年的音乐剧《同性离婚》中，多音韵也是最重要的特征。这部音乐剧的热门歌曲就是对多音韵的运用，开头就用了英语中最常见的多音韵之一：“night and day”（日夜），它表示“永远”。歌词唱道：“日夜你都是我的唯一”。接着，歌词又将意象延伸到天地：“Only you under the moon or under the sun”（只有你在月光下或阳光下），这同样表示“所有时间”（除了没有月光的夜晚）。这首歌甚至坦白了多音韵的不必要性：“Whether near to me or far / It’s no matter darling where you are”（无论你离我多远，亲爱的，你在哪里都无关紧要）（他身处中距离时的感受，依然没有明说）。

It would be tempting to construct an argument that merism is always about love, because love brings opposites together. If you wanted to argue this way (and who’s to stop you?), you could cite the song ‘Bless ’Em All’, which unnecessarily enlarges on the all being blessed:

人们很容易会想当然地认为，多元论总是与爱有关，因为爱能将对立的事物结合在一起。如果你想这样论证（谁又能阻止你呢？），你可以引用歌曲《祝福他们所有人》（Bless ’Em All），这首歌不必要地强调了“所有人”都得到了祝福：

Bless ’em all,

祝福他们所有人，

Bless ’em all.

祝福他们所有人。

The long and the short and the tall,

长的、短的、高的，

Bless all those Sergeants and WO1’s,

愿上帝保佑所有的士官和一级准尉们。

Bless all those Corporals and their bleedin’ sons …

愿上帝保佑所有那些下士和他们流血牺牲的儿子们……

It’s all rather lovely that thoughts like that could survive the miseries of war. Uplifts the human spirit, it does. The last two lines strike a strangely angry tone, or at least it’s strange until you go back to the original lyrics of 1917, where the word bless was replaced by fuck throughout. 1

令人欣慰的是，这样的思想竟然能在战争的苦难中幸存下来。它确实能鼓舞人心。最后两句歌词的语气略带愤怒，或者说，至少在你回溯到1917年的原版歌词之前，这种愤怒是难以言喻的，因为在原版歌词中，“bless”一词被“fuck”完全取代了。¹

In fact, merism works for love and hate and everything in between. Tennyson wrote up one of the most memorable in The Charge of the Light Brigade where the six hundred have:

事实上，这种比喻适用于爱、恨以及介于两者之间的一切情感。丁尼生在《轻骑兵的冲锋》中描写了最令人难忘的场景之一，其中六百名士兵：

Cannon to right of them,

他们右边是加农炮，

Cannon to left of them,

他们左边是加农炮，

Cannon in front of them …

他们面前的大炮……

The Oxford English Dictionary contains the word quaquaversally meaning in every direction . ‘Cannon quaquaversally’ would have saved time, but wouldn’t have been nearly as poetic, and almost everything in Tennyson’s most famous poem is there only for the sake of rhetoric. He even pointed out to the editor of the magazine that first published the poem that the charge of the Light Brigade had involved seven hundred men, not six, but ‘Six is much better than seven hundred (as I think) metrically so keep it.’

《牛津英语词典》收录了“quaquaversally”一词，意为“向各个方向”。“Cannon quaquaversally”虽然能节省时间，但远不如“Cannon quaquaversally”富有诗意，而丁尼生最著名的诗歌中几乎所有的一切都只是为了修辞。他甚至向首次发表这首诗的杂志编辑指出，轻骑兵的冲锋涉及七百人，而非六人，但他觉得“六比七百（依我之见）韵律更优美，所以就保留这个说法吧。”

But the true and natural home of merism is in legal documents. Lawyers are like Cole Porter and Alfred Lord Tennyson with a blender. A lawyer, for a reason or reasons known only to him or herself, cannot see a whole without dividing it into its parts and enumerating them in immense detail. This may be something to do with the billing system.

但这种繁琐的分类方式真正天然地存在于法律文件中。律师就像拿着搅拌机的科尔·波特和阿尔弗雷德·丁尼生。出于某种只有他们自己知道的原因，律师无法理解整体而不将其分解成各个部分并进行极其详细的列举。这或许与计费系统有关。

As we’ve dealt with marriage and divorce, the merism of modern love can be completed with a restraining order. These mirror marriage’s merisms with lines like: ‘The defendant is prohibited from communicating with the plaintiff, either personally or through other persons, by telephone, writing or any other means.’ The second half of that sentence is either utterly redundant, or a challenge. Perhaps there is a way through, perhaps there’s a loophole. After all, Cole Porter said that he loved her night and day, but what did he do at twilight? The marriage service promises fidelity in sickness and in health, but might a mild cold bring on a furious bout of adultery? ‘Ladies and gentlemen’ gets one into all sorts of trouble with those people of no specific gender, although to be fair such ambiguous creatures usually count as both.

既然我们已经探讨了婚姻和离婚，那么现代爱情的种种限制或许可以用限制令来补充。这些限制令与婚姻的限制如出一辙，例如：“被告被禁止以任何方式与原告联系，无论是亲自联系还是通过他人，无论是电话、书面联系还是其他任何方式。”这句话的后半部分要么完全多余，要么就是在挑衅。或许有办法可以绕过限制，或许存在漏洞。毕竟，科尔·波特曾说过他日夜爱她，但他在黄昏时分又做了什么呢？婚姻仪式承诺无论健康还是疾病都要忠贞不渝，但一场小感冒会不会引发一场疯狂的婚外情呢？“女士们先生们”这种说法在与性别模糊的人群交往时会让人惹上各种麻烦，不过公平地说，这种性别模糊的人群通常既可以被视为男性也可以被视为女性。

The lawyer’s lucky phrase is ‘including but not limited to’, which gets you out of the utterly unnecessary trouble that the utterly unnecessary merism got you into in the first place. Unfortunately, it’s hard to slip that weaselish phrase into the lyrics of ‘Night and Day’, as they wouldn’t scan any more. They might also give a rather bureaucratic feel to a wedding.

律师的幸运短语是“包括但不限于”，它能让你摆脱最初因一句毫无必要的玩笑而陷入的完全不必要的麻烦。可惜的是，很难把这句狡猾的短语塞进《日夜》的歌词里，因为那样就押韵了。而且，用在婚礼上可能会显得过于官僚主义。

Merism searches for wholes, and leaves holes. Thus the most awkward and derided poetic figure is the extended merism, the dismemberment of the loved one: the blazon.

分句诗寻找的是整体，却留下的是空洞。因此，最尴尬、最受嘲讽的诗歌修辞手法就是延伸的分句诗，即对所爱之人的肢解：纹章。

1 Fred Godfrey explained the composition of the song in a 1941 letter to the Daily Mirror : ‘I wrote “Bless ’Em All” while serving in the old R.N.A.S. in France in 1916. And, furthermore, it wasn’t “Bless”.’

1 弗雷德·戈弗雷在 1941 年写给《每日镜报》的一封信中解释了这首歌的创作过程：“我在 1916 年在法国皇家海军航空兵服役期间创作了《祝福他们所有人》。而且，它原本并不是《祝福》。”

Chapter 5

第五章

The Blazon (A Merism Too Far)

纹章（一种过于夸张的拼写错误）

Then in the blazon of sweet beauty’s best

然后，在甜美之美的绝妙颂歌中

Of hand, of foot, of lip, of eye, of brow …

手、脚、嘴唇、眼睛、眉毛……

When healthy people fall in love, they buy a bunch of flowers or an engagement ring and go and Do Something About It. When poets fall in love, they make a list of their loved one’s body parts and attach similes to them. Your lips are like cherries, your hair is like gold, and your eyes are like traffic lights that make my heart stop and go. These lists are almost universally awkward. Even the Bible starts to sound like the ravings of a lunatic.

健康的人坠入爱河时，会买束鲜花或一枚订婚戒指，然后付诸行动。而诗人坠入爱河时，却会列出爱人身体的各个部位，并赋予它们各种比喻。你的嘴唇像樱桃，你的头发像黄金，你的眼睛像交通信号灯，让我的心跳时而停止，时而加速。这些清单几乎无一例外地显得尴尬无比。就连《圣经》听起来都像是疯子的呓语。

Behold, thou art fair, my love; behold, thou art fair; thou hast doves’ eyes within thy locks: thy hair is as a flock of goats, that appear from mount Gilead. Thy teeth are like a flock of sheep that are even shorn, which came up from the washing; whereof every one bear twins, and none is barren among them. Thy lips are like a thread of scarlet, and thy speech is comely: thy temples are like a piece of a pomegranate within thy locks. Thy neck is like the tower of David builded for an armoury, whereon there hang a thousand bucklers, all shields of mighty men. Thy two breasts are like two young roes that are twins, which feed among the lilies.

看哪，我的佳偶，你真美；看哪，你真美；你的秀发里有鸽子的眼睛；你的头发如同基列山上出来的一群山羊。你的牙齿如同刚剪过毛、刚从洗礼中出来的一群羊，其中每一只都生双胞胎，没有一只不生育。你的嘴唇如同朱红色的线，你的言语优美动听；你的太阳穴如同秀发里一颗石榴。你的颈项如同大卫的塔，为要塞而建，上面悬挂着千面盾牌，都是勇士的盾牌。你的双乳如同两只双胞胎小鹿，在百合花丛中吃草。

I suppose that goats had a better reputation back then. And sheep. But nobody’s forehead looks like a pomegranate; if it does, they should be rushed to a dermatologist. However, it’s not just the choice of similes that makes these lists odd, it’s that there are similes at all. If I were to ask you to draw a picture based on that blazon, you’d end up with someone (or something) rather peculiar, and not in the slightest bit attractive.

我猜想，那时候山羊的名声应该更好一些。绵羊也是。但没人会长得像石榴；如果真长得像，那应该赶紧去看皮肤科医生。不过，这些列表的奇怪之处不仅在于比喻的选择，还在于它们本身就带有比喻的意味。如果我让你根据这些纹章画一幅画，你画出来的肯定会是相当古怪的人（或物），而且一点也不好看。

This hasn’t stopped poets going on like surrealist anatomy textbooks for millennia. Take out your sketch-pad again and attempt this lady from Thomas Watson’s Hekatompathia (1582):

但这并没有阻止诗人像超现实主义解剖学教科书一样创作诗歌数千年。再次拿出你的素描本，尝试描绘一下托马斯·沃森的《百人诗》（1582）中的这位女士：

Hark you that list to hear what saint I serve:

仔细听听这份名单，看看我侍奉的是哪位圣人：

Her yellow locks exceed the beaten gold;

她金色的头发比锤打的金子还要亮丽；

Her sparkling eyes in heav’n a place deserve;

她闪亮的双眸在天堂里应该占有一席之地；

Her forehead high and fair of comely mold;

她额头高耸白皙，容貌秀丽；

Her words are music all of silver sound;

她的话语如同银铃般悦耳动听；

Her wit so sharp as like can scarce be found;

她的机智如此敏锐，世间罕见；

Each eyebrow hangs like Iris in the skies;

每条眉毛都像天空中的鸢尾花一样垂着；

Her Eagle’s nose is straight of stately frame;

她的鹰鼻笔直挺拔，姿态高贵；

On either cheek a Rose and Lily lies;

两颊各绘一朵玫瑰和一朵百合；

Her breath is sweet perfume, or holy flame;

她的呼吸如同甜美的香水，或是神圣的火焰；

Her lips more red than any Coral stone;

她的嘴唇比任何珊瑚石都红；

Her neck more white than aged Swans that moan;

她的脖子比哀鸣的老天鹅还要白皙；

Her breast transparent is, like Crystal rock;

她的乳房透明如水晶般晶莹剔透；

Her fingers long, fit for Apollo’s Lute;

她的手指修长，适合弹奏阿波罗的鲁特琴；

Her slipper such as Momus dare not mock;

她的拖鞋，连摩摩斯都不敢嘲笑；

Her virtues all so great as make me mute:

她的美德如此伟大，令我哑口无言：

What other parts she hath I need not say,

她身上其他部位我无需赘述。

Whose face alone is cause of my decay.

仅仅是他的脸，就足以让我堕落。

One can pretty much guarantee that Mr Watson never got to see her other parts after that effort, and if that poem seems somehow familiar, it’s probably because of Shakespeare’s parody:

几乎可以肯定，在那次努力之后，沃森先生再也没有机会看到她的其他部分，如果这首诗让你觉得似曾相识，那很可能是因为莎士比亚的戏仿：

My mistress’ eyes are nothing like the sun

我女主人的眼睛与太阳截然不同。

Coral is far more red than her lips’ red;

珊瑚的颜色比她嘴唇的颜色要红得多；

If snow be white, why then her breasts are dun;

如果雪是白色的，那么她的乳房为什么是灰褐色的呢？

If hairs be wires, black wires grow on her head.

如果头发是电线，那么她头上长出来的就是黑色的电线。

I have seen roses damask’d, red and white,

我见过红白相间的锦缎玫瑰，

But no such roses see I in her cheeks;

但我却在她脸颊上看不到一丝玫瑰色的红晕；

And in some perfumes is there more delight

有些香水更令人愉悦。

Than in the breath that from my mistress reeks.

比我情妇身上散发的恶臭气息还要难闻。

I love to hear her speak, yet well I know

我喜欢听她说话，但我很清楚

That music hath a far more pleasing sound;

那种音乐听起来悦耳得多；

I grant I never saw a goddess go;

我承认我从未见过女神离去；

My mistress, when she walks, treads on the ground:

我的女主人走路时，脚踩在地上：

And yet, by heaven, I think my love as rare

然而，老天作证，我认为我的爱是如此罕见。

As any she belied with false compare.

她用虚假的比较来掩盖自己的谎言。

Mind you, I can’t imagine that Shakespeare’s mistress was terribly charmed with that description either. There’s something basically and horribly wrong with cutting somebody up and replacing them with a bunch of inanimate objects; doing it symbolically in verse is also slightly disturbing. If you took them at all seriously you’d be talking about something that was no longer recognisable as a living human being, which is where Shakespeare ended up. The final and finest blazon is an epitaph for a drowned man:

不过，我猜莎士比亚的情妇对这种描述也未必十分满意。把人肢解，换成一堆无生命物体，这本身就存在着某种根本性的、可怕的错误；用诗歌来象征性地表达这种错误，也略显诡异。如果你认真对待这些诗句，你会发现它们描绘的是一个已无法辨认的活人，而这正是莎士比亚最终的结局。最后，也是最精彩的一首诗，其实是为一个溺亡者所作的墓志铭：

Full fathom five thy father lies;

你父亲的遗体躺在五寻深处；

Of his bones are coral made;

他的骨头变成了珊瑚；

Those are pearls that were his eyes;

他的眼睛就像珍珠一样；

Nothing of him that doth fade,

他的一切永不消逝，

But doth suffer a sea-change

但确实发生了翻天覆地的变化

Into something rich and strange.

变成某种丰富而奇特的东西。

The idea that an oyster has eaten and then excreted your eyeballs is about as romantic as the blazon gets, yet it continues. People are never people, they’re scrapbooks, from Petrarch’s Laura to Dolly Parton’s Jolene. Jolene is composed of ivory, emeralds and unseasonable rain (skin, eyes and voice). But her smile is like a breath of spring, which is an example of synaesthesia.

牡蛎吞食并吐出你的眼球这种说法，浪漫程度简直无与伦比，然而这种比喻却屡见不鲜。人永远不是人，他们更像是剪贴簿，从彼特拉克的劳拉到多莉·帕顿的乔琳，莫不如此。乔琳由象牙、祖母绿和反常的雨水（皮肤、眼睛和声音）构成。但她的笑容却如同春风拂面，这正是联觉的体现。

Chapter 6

第六章

Synaesthesia

联觉

She smelled the way the Taj Mahal looks by moonlight.

她身上散发着泰姬陵在月光下的那种气息。

The Little Sister by Raymond Chandler

雷蒙德·钱德勒的《小妹妹》

Synaesthesia is either a mental condition whereby colours are perceived as smells, smells as sounds, sounds as tastes etc., or it is a rhetorical device whereby one sense is described in terms of another. If colours are harmonious or a voice is silky, that is synaesthesia (or some other spelling).

联觉要么是一种心理状态，在这种状态下，颜色会被感知为气味，气味会被感知为声音，声音会被感知为味道等等；要么它是一种修辞手法，用一种感官来描述另一种感官。如果色彩和谐，或者声音如丝般柔滑，那就是联觉（或其他拼写方式）。

It is a common enough device, except that there seem to be rules or norms governing which senses can be coupled. Sight and sound are interchangeable. Quite aside from John Lennon’s request to George Martin that the orchestration of ‘Strawberry Fields’ should be ‘orange’, colours can be loud or discordant while melodies can be bright and rumblings dark. Tone is even an ambiguous word that can be applied to either sense. (I omit colours that are purely symbolic: blues music is no more blue than blue movies are.)

这是一种相当常见的手法，只不过似乎存在一些规则或规范，规定了哪些感官可以结合起来。视觉和听觉是可以互换的。暂且不谈约翰·列侬要求乔治·马丁将《草莓园》的管弦乐编曲改为“橙色”，色彩本身可以是响亮的或不和谐的，而旋律可以是明快的，隆隆声可以是阴暗的。“音调”甚至是一个含义模糊的词，可以用来指代任何一种感官。（我省略了纯粹象征性的颜色：布鲁斯音乐并不比蓝色电影更“蓝”。）

Touch can be applied to sound – a gravelly voice – and to sight – the warm colours of a painting. But rarely is the favour returned; indeed, I can’t think of a single example.

触觉可以应用于听觉——比如沙哑的嗓音——也可以应用于视觉——比如画作中温暖的色彩。但这种作用却很少得到回报；事实上，我想不出一个例子。

Taste gives you a couple of terms of approbation – delicious and tasty – and of deprecation – bland or disgusting. But again it receives no thanks from its fellow senses.

味觉会给出褒义词——美味可口——以及贬义词——平淡无味或令人作呕。但它却得不到其他感官的认可。

And smell. Smell sits apart on his own, blowing his nose. Odious , before you ask, means hateful and has nothing to do with odour . Rank and pungent have, over the centuries, been sent as emissaries to the other senses, but that is all and it is possible to forget that those words were ever native to a nostril. And smells are never described as being like anything else at all.

还有气味。气味仿佛置身事外，独自擤着鼻子。在你问之前，我要解释一下，“可憎的”指的是令人厌恶的，与气味无关。几个世纪以来，“刺鼻的”和“浓烈的”被当作使者传递给其他感官，但也仅此而已，人们很容易忘记这些词原本就源于鼻孔。而且，气味从来不会被描述成像其他任何东西。

And that is why the Raymond Chandler line is so striking. Though the sense is quite discernible, the expression of it pulls you up short. The phrase is memorable in a way that it would never have been if it were, ‘She sounded the way the Taj Mahal looks by moonlight’.

这就是雷蒙德·钱德勒那句话如此引人注目的原因。虽然意思很容易理解，但它的表达方式却能让人猝不及防。如果换成“她的声音就像月光下的泰姬陵”，这句话就不会如此令人难忘了。

Synaesthesias of smell are jarring and effective, and are probably an easy shortcut to a memorable line. However, caution, dear reader, should be observed. You may not want your line to be remembered. Many critics have been wrong, some amazingly so, but few will be remembered as Eduard Hanslick is; he wrote of Tchaikovsky’s First Violin Concerto that it showed there could be ‘music that stinks to the ear’.

嗅觉联觉令人震惊却又效果显著，或许是创作令人难忘的台词的捷径。然而，亲爱的读者，务必谨慎。你或许并不希望自己的台词被人记住。许多评论家都犯过错，有些错得离谱，但很少有人能像爱德华·汉斯立克那样名垂青史；他曾评价柴可夫斯基的第一小提琴协奏曲，说它证明了“音乐也可以是听起来难闻的”。

Synaesthesia reaches its purest form, though, when, rather than shuffling the senses, a sense is given to something completely abstract. Victory does not look like anything visible or sound like anything audible or taste like anything edible, but it has a smell, a smell memorably described in Apocalypse Now .

然而，联觉最纯粹的形式并非感官的混杂，而是将某种感觉赋予完全抽象的事物。胜利既不像任何可见之物，也不像任何可听之物，更不像任何可食用之物，但它却有一种气味，一种在《现代启示录》中被令人难忘地描绘过的气味。

I love the smell of napalm in the morning. You know, one time we had a hill bombed, for twelve hours. […] The smell, you know that gasoline smell, the whole hill. Smelled like … victory. Someday this war’s gonna end …

我喜欢清晨凝固汽油弹的味道。你知道吗，有一次我们轰炸了一座山，整整十二个小时。[…] 那味道，你知道的，汽油味，整座山都弥漫着。闻起来就像……胜利的味道。总有一天，这场战争会结束……

Which is an example of aposiopesis.

这是省略的一个例子。

Chapter 7

第七章

Aposiopesis

省略

Aposiopesis is when …

省略是指……

Aposiopesis is …

省略是……

Aposiopesis …

省略……

All of the above is technically true, as aposiopesis is signalled in English punctuation by three dots. Like … like this … Aposiopesis is Greek for becoming silent and it’s the reason that we do not live in Paradise.

以上说法在技术上都是正确的，因为英语标点符号中省略号（aposiopesis）是用三个点表示的。就像……像这样……省略号（aposiopesis）在希腊语中是“沉默”的意思，这也是我们无法生活在天堂的原因。

There were two important trees in the Garden of Eden: the Tree of Knowledge and the Tree of Life. We chose the wrong one. The fruit of the Tree of Life would have given us immortality. The fruit of the Tree of Knowledge informed us that we were nude, which, as knowledge goes, is pretty low down the list of amazing facts. If my greatest grandmother had picked differently I would be able to expose myself for eternity without anybody realising. If only …

伊甸园里有两棵重要的树：知识树和生命树。我们选错了。生命树的果实能让我们永生。知识树的果实却告诉我们，我们赤身裸体——就知识而言，这算不上什么了不起的事实。如果我的曾祖母当初选了别的树，我就能永远赤身裸体而不被人察觉。要是……

But to return to aposiopesis. God didn’t want anybody to notice they were naked. Why God didn’t want this is unexplained, but I have my theories … Once the game was up, He cursed Adam, Eve and the talking snake, and then He said:

但回到省略的话题。上帝不想让任何人注意到他们赤身裸体。上帝为何如此不愿如此，至今仍是个谜，但我有一些猜想……游戏结束后，祂诅咒了亚当、夏娃和那条会说话的蛇，然后祂说：

And now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever … Therefore the Lord God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken.

现在，恐怕他伸手又摘生命树的果子吃，就永远活着……因此，耶和华神打发他出伊甸园去，耕种他所自出之土。

You will notice that God did not finish His sentence. Mankind left paradise without a main verb. Theologically, this presents some odd questions. First, God appears to have been talking to Himself. Second, why did he not finish His sentence? He must have been capable of it. He’s omnipotent and does not suffer from sore throats and forgetfulness. This does not fit either of the three usual reasons for aposiopesis: that you can’t go on, that you don’t need to go on, or that you want to leave the audience hanging.

你会注意到，上帝并没有说完祂的句子。人类离开伊甸园时，祂的句子中并没有一个完整的动词。从神学的角度来看，这引出了一些奇怪的问题。首先，上帝似乎是在自言自语。其次，祂为什么没有说完？祂肯定有能力说完。祂是全能的，不会嗓子疼，也不会健忘。这与通常的三种省略句解释都不符：无法继续、无需继续，或者故意留下悬念。

The simplest reason for aposiopesis is death. In fact, the Tree of Life would have robbed us of all those whodunit scenes where a chap stumbles in with a knife between his shoulder blades and just enough breath in his body to tell the detective ‘It was … It was …’ before giving up the ghost and returning to the ground from whence he came, usually with his finger pointing towards a Vital Clue. Shakespeare does it a little better in Henry IV Part 1 with the death of Henry Percy. Percy has just enough breath in his body for a good bit of anadiplosis (q.v.) and a final aposiopesis:

最简单的省略理由就是死亡。事实上，如果生命之树存在，我们就看不到那些侦探小说里常见的场景了：一个家伙踉跄着走进来，肩胛骨之间夹着一把刀，奄奄一息地告诉侦探“是……是……”，然后就断气回天，通常手指还指向某个关键线索。莎士比亚在《亨利四世》第一部中对亨利·珀西之死的处理更胜一筹。珀西临死前还有足够的气息，可以进行一段精彩的重复（参见相关条目），最后以省略结尾：

But thought’s the slave of life, and life time’s fool;

但思想是生命的奴隶，是生命的傻瓜；

And time, that takes survey of all the world,

而时间，则对整个世界进行了考察。

Must have a stop. O, I could prophesy,

必须停下来。哦，我可以预言，

But that the earthy and cold hand of death

但那冰冷而尘世的死亡之手

Lies on my tongue: no, Percy, thou art dust

谎言在我舌尖：不，珀西，你已化为尘埃

And food for …

以及食物……

And just in case the audience was wondering what creature would have had gastronomic designs on the dying hero, Prince Hal explains, ‘For worms, brave Percy’. It’s rude to finish other people’s sentences, unless you killed them first.

为了避免观众好奇究竟是什么生物对垂死的英雄垂涎三尺，哈尔王子解释道：“是蠕虫，勇敢的珀西。” 除非你先杀了别人，否则打断别人说话是很不礼貌的。

Sometimes, though, aposiopesis is because you simply don’t know what to say. This can leave you looking rather foolish, like a parent trying to get children to do something but not being able to think, offhand, of an appropriate threat. Thus poor King Lear with his naughty daughters:

然而，有时候，省略句的出现仅仅是因为你不知道该说什么。这会让你显得相当愚蠢，就像父母想让孩子做某事，却一时想不出合适的威胁的话一样。可怜的李尔王和他的淘气女儿们就是如此：

No, you unnatural hags,

不，你们这些不自然的巫婆！

I will have such revenges on you both,

我一定会报复你们俩！

That all the world shall … I will do such things …

愿全世界都……我将做这样的事……

What they are, yet I know not: but they shall be

它们是什么，我尚不知晓；但它们终将存在。

The terrors of the earth.

地球上的恐怖。

Which is a much more verbose version of the common or garden aposiopesis: ‘Tidy your room, or else …’ Sometimes an aposiopesis can make a threat more impressive, as the threatee will write all his or her worst fears on the dotted line. So Samuel Beckett in the novel Murphy has:

这其实是常见省略句的冗长版本：“收拾你的房间，否则……” 有时，省略句能让威胁更具威慑力，因为被威胁者会把所有最可怕的事情都写在虚线上。例如，塞缪尔·贝克特在小说《墨菲》中就使用了省略句：

‘Have fire in this garret before night or—’

“晚上之前，一定要在这个阁楼里生火，否则——”

He stopped because he could not go on. It was an aposiopesis of the purest kind. Ticklepenny supplied the missing consequences in various versions, each one more painful than any that Murphy could have specified, terrifying taken all together.

他停了下来，因为他再也坚持不下去了。这是一种最纯粹的否定。蒂克尔佩尼用各种版本补充了缺失的后果，每一个版本都比墨菲所能设想的任何版本都更加痛苦，所有版本加起来更是令人毛骨悚然。

But King Lear is just too tired and emotional to work out exactly what he plans to do. He can’t finish his sentence. This is, of course, an easy and effective thing to fake. If you’re too overcome to even finish your sentence then you must be sincere, you must really mean what you’re not saying, you must … I’m sorry. I cannot type. My fingers are crying.

但李尔王实在太累太激动了，根本没法好好想想自己到底该怎么做。他一句话也说不出来。当然，这很容易伪装。如果你激动得连话都说不完，那你一定很真诚，你一定真的把没说出口的话都说了，你一定……对不起，我打字打不开了。我的手指都快哭了。

In Julius Caesar , Antony, while doing a very calculated job of stirring up the people of Rome to rebellion, pretends that he’s too sad to speak:

在《尤利乌斯·凯撒》中，安东尼精心策划煽动罗马人民叛乱，却假装悲伤得说不出话来：

You all did love him once, not without cause:

你们都曾爱过他，这并非没有原因：

What cause withholds you then, to mourn for him?

那么，是什么原因阻止你为他哀悼呢？

O judgment! thou art fled to brutish beasts,

审判啊！你已逃往野兽之手！

And men have lost their reason. Bear with me;

人们已经丧失了理智。请容我解释一下；

My heart is in the coffin there with Caesar,

我的心和凯撒一起躺在棺材里了。

And I must pause till it come back to me.

我必须停下来，直到我想起来为止。

But God, as we have said, should have more self-control than that. 1 The natural conclusion is that God is using the other form of aposiopesis, the form where the second half of the sentence is so bleeding obvious that it’s not even worth saying.

但正如我们所说，上帝应该比这更有自制力。1 自然的结论是，上帝使用了另一种省略形式，即句子的后半部分如此显而易见，以至于根本不值得一提。

When in Rome …

入乡随俗……

Speak of the Devil …

说曹操曹操到……

Out of the mouths of babes …

童言无忌……

Such lines are so familiar that the writer need shed no ink in their conclusion. When in Rome, do as the Romans do. But as God was engaged in the first recorded conversation, he probably wasn’t using this sort of aposiopesis at all. Rome wasn’t built, there were as yet no babes, and the Devil, in snake form, had already appeared. No, God seems to have used aposiopesis for the sheer joy of it. He wanted to be the first being to break off mid …

这样的句子如此耳熟能详，以至于作者无需在结尾处多加赘述。入乡随俗。但当上帝进行有记载的第一次对话时，他很可能根本没有使用这种省略句。罗马城尚未建成，世上还没有婴孩，而魔鬼以蛇的形态已经出现。不，上帝似乎只是为了享受省略句的乐趣而使用它。他想成为第一个在对话进行到一半时突然中断的人……

Perhaps God’s silence is as mysterious as that of the advertisers, who never tell you what would happen ‘If only everything in life was as reliable as a Volkswagen’. God moves in a mysterious way, his wonders to perform, which is an example of hyperbaton.

或许上帝的沉默如同广告商的沉默一样神秘莫测，他们从不告诉你“如果生活中的一切都像大众汽车一样可靠就好了”会发生什么。上帝的行事方式神秘莫测，祂的奇迹总能以某种方式展现，这正是一种夸张手法。

1 Raising the theological question of whether an omnipotent being can control himself.

1 提出了一个神学问题：全能的存在能否控制自己。

# ↩

Chapter 8

第八章

Hyperbaton

超级棒

Hyperbaton is when you put words in an odd order, which is very, very difficult to do in English. Given that almost everything else in the English language is slapdash, happy-go-lucky, care-may-the-Devil, word order is surprisingly strict. John Ronald Reuel Tolkien wrote his first story aged seven. It was about a ‘green great dragon’. He showed it to his mother who told him that you absolutely couldn’t have a green great dragon, and that it had to be a great green one instead. Tolkien was so disheartened that he never wrote another story for years.

倒装是指将单词以奇数顺序排列，这在英语中非常非常难做到。考虑到英语中几乎所有其他方面都显得随意、轻松、漫不经心，词序的严格程度就显得格外令人惊讶。约翰·罗纳德·鲁埃尔·托尔金七岁时写了他的第一个故事，讲的是一条“绿色巨龙”。他把故事拿给母亲看，母亲告诉他，绝对不能写一条绿色的巨龙，必须是一条绿色的巨龙才行。托尔金非常沮丧，以至于好几年都没再写过故事。

The reason for Tolkien’s mistake, since you ask, is that adjectives in English absolutely have to be in this order: opinion-size-age-shape-colour-origin-material-purpose Noun. So you can have a lovely little old rectangular green French silver whittling knife. But if you mess with that word order in the slightest you’ll sound like a maniac. It’s an odd thing that every English speaker uses that list, but almost none of us could write it out. And as size comes before colour, green great dragons can’t exist.

既然你问了，托尔金犯错的原因在于，英语中形容词的顺序必须严格遵循：观点-大小-年龄-形状-颜色-来源-材质-用途-名词。所以你可以说一把可爱的小巧的、古老的、长方形的、绿色的法国银质削木刀。但如果你稍微打乱了这个顺序，听起来就像个疯子。奇怪的是，每个说英语的人都遵循这个顺序，但几乎没有人能把它写出来。而且由于大小在前，绿色的巨龙是不存在的。

There are other rules that everybody obeys without noticing. Have you ever heard that patter-pitter of tiny feet? Or the dong-ding of a bell? Or hop-hip music? That’s because, when you repeat a word with a different vowel, the order is always I A O. Bish bash bosh. So politicians may flip-flop, but they can never flop-flip. It’s tit-for-tat, never tat-for-tit. 1 This is called ablaut reduplication, and if you do things any other way, they sound very, very odd indeed.

还有一些规则，大家都在不知不觉中遵守。你听过小脚丫的轻快脚步声吗？或是铃铛的叮咚声？又或是嘻哈音乐的节奏？那是因为，当你重复一个元音不同的单词时，顺序永远是 I A O。就像 Bish bash bosh 一样。所以政客们可能会反复无常，但他们永远不会反复无常。是以牙还牙，而不是以牙还牙。¹ 这叫做元音重复，如果你用其他方式处理，听起来会非常非常奇怪。

The importance of English word order is also the reason that the idea that you can’t end a sentence with a preposition is utter hogwash. In fact, it would be utter hogwash anyway, and anyone who claims that you can’t end a sentence with up , should be told up to shut. It is, as Shakespeare put it, such stuff as dreams are made on, but it’s one of those silly English beliefs that flesh is heir to.

英语词序的重要性也正是“句子不能以介词结尾”这种说法纯属无稽之谈的原因。事实上，即便没有介词，这种说法也纯属无稽之谈。任何声称句子不能以“up”结尾的人都应该被骂闭嘴。正如莎士比亚所说，这种说法不过是“梦想的产物”，但却是英国人与生俱来的愚蠢观念之一。

Still, it’s a favourite line of English teachers who Haven’t Thought It Through. The rule is often unfairly blamed on a chap called Robert Lowth who wrote a book called A Short Introduction to English Grammar (1762). But all that book actually says is this:

然而，这却是那些没经过深思熟虑的英语老师最爱用的一句话。这条规则常常被不公平地归咎于一位名叫罗伯特·洛斯的人，他写了一本名为《英语语法简明入门》（1762年）的书。但这本书实际上只说了这些：

PREPOSITIONS have Government of Cases; and in English they always require the Objective Case after them: as, ‘ with him; from her, to me .’

介词有格的支配；在英语中，介词后面总是需要宾格：例如，“与他在一起；从她那里，到我那里”。

The Preposition is often separated from the Relative which it governs and joined to the Verb at the end of the Sentence, or of some member of it: as, ‘Horace is an author, whom I am much delighted with .’ ‘The world is too well bred to shock authors with a truth, which generally their booksellers are the first that inform them of .’ This is an Idiom which our language is strongly inclined to; it prevails in common conversation, and suits very well with the familiar style in writing; but the placing of the Preposition before the Relative is more graceful as well as more perspicuous; and agrees much better with the solemn and elevated Style … But in English the Preposition is more frequently placed after the Verb, and separate from it like an Adverb; in which Situation it is no less apt to affect the Sense of it, and to give it a new Meaning; and may still be considered as belonging to the Verb, and a part of it. As to cast is to throw; but to cast up , or to compute, an account, is quite a different thing: thus to fall on , to bear out , to give over &c. So that the Meaning of the Verb, and the Propriety of the Phrase, depend upon the Preposition subjoined.

介词通常与它所支配的关系词分开，并与句末的动词或句子成分连接，例如：“贺拉斯是一位我非常欣赏的作家。”“世人太有教养，不会用真理来震惊作家，而真理通常是他们的书商最先告知他们的。”这是我们语言中一种常见的用法；它在日常对话中很普遍，也与写作中常见的风格非常契合；但是，将介词放在关系词之前则更加优雅清晰，也更符合庄重高雅的文风……但在英语中，介词更常放在动词之后，像副词一样与动词分开；在这种情况下，它同样会影响动词的含义，赋予其新的含义；并且仍然可以被视为动词的一部分。正如“cast”的意思是“throw”一样。但是，计算或整理账目则完全是另一回事：例如，证实、交出等等。因此，动词的含义和短语的恰当性取决于所附加的介词。

Any phrasal verb in the imperative has to end with a preposition. Otherwise, you’d shout ‘Out look! Down get! On we are being fired!’ Referees would say ‘On play’. Off would take planes. And nobody would be allowed to sleep in.

任何祈使句中的短语动词都必须以介词结尾。否则，你会喊出“快看！快趴下！我们被解雇了！”裁判会说“比赛开始”。“下场”会变成坐飞机。而且谁也不许睡懒觉。

In fact, the most famous example of hyperbaton in English comes from a civil servant twisting a sentence round to get the preposition away from the end. Nobody actually knows what the sentence was. All that history records is that Winston Churchill underlined it and wrote in the margin: ‘This is the kind of English up with which I will not put.’

事实上，英语中最著名的倒装句例子是一位公务员为了把介词从句末移开而故意扭曲句子结构。没人知道这句话原本是什么。历史记载的只是温斯顿·丘吉尔在这句话下面划了线，并在旁边写道：“这种英语我绝不容忍。”

Hyperbaton is a slap in the face to any English speaker, and when it works it goes straight into the language. In 1642 a chap called Richard Lovelace was stuck in prison, pining for his girlfriend. He wrote her a poem about how he wasn’t really in prison, and proved it with metaphor. The last verse began:

倒装句对任何英语使用者来说都是一种侮辱，但一旦运用得当，便会直接融入语言之中。1642年，一位名叫理查德·洛夫莱斯的男子身陷囹圄，思念着他的女友。他写了一首诗，讲述自己其实并未身陷囹圄，并用比喻加以证明。诗的最后一节以这样的方式开头：

Stone walls do not a prison make,

石墙并不能构成监狱。

Nor iron bars a cage …

铁栏杆也不是牢笼……

Which is a) hyperbaton because make should come between not and a , b) technically untrue and c) quoted so much that it has become part of the language.
