And not just that exact line, any variant can be used: adjective noun does not a noun make. So, 333 years after the original was written, in the American television series Moonlighting , 2 the Cybill Shepherd character says: ‘Well, let me remind you, Mr Addison, that one case does not a detective make.’ To which the Bruce Willis character replies: ‘Well, let me remind you, Ms Hayes, that I hate it when you talk backwards.’

a) 这句是倒装句，因为“make”应该放在“not”和“a”之间；b) 从技术上讲是不成立的；c) 被引用太多以至于成了语言的一部分。而且不仅仅是这句话，任何变体都可以用：形容词名词不能构成名词。所以，在原句写成333年后，在美剧《蓝色月光》（Moonlighting）中，西比尔·谢泼德饰演的角色说：“好吧，让我提醒你，艾迪森先生，一个案子并不能让你成为一名侦探。”布鲁斯·威利斯饰演的角色回答说：“好吧，让我提醒你，海耶斯女士，我讨厌你倒着说话。”

And all because Mr Lovelace had to make his poem scan.

这一切都是因为洛夫莱斯先生必须让他的诗符合韵律。

Uneasy lies the head that wears the crown is one hell of a lot more memorable than The head that wears the crown lies uneasily . But when hyperbaton doesn’t work it can just be odd. Milton had a bit of a weakness for hyperbaton. Sometimes it worked, as in pastures new , and sometimes it really didn’t, as in this bit from Paradise Lost :

“戴王冠的头颅安然入睡”比“戴王冠的头颅安然入睡”要令人印象深刻得多。但当倒装句运用不当时，就会显得怪异。弥尔顿似乎对倒装句情有独钟。有时它运用得当，例如“新的牧场”，有时却适得其反，例如《失乐园》中的这一段：

Him who disobeys, me disobeys.

凡不服从我的，就是不服从我。

It’s a sentence that’s liable to make you cock your head on one side and frown. A translation into something approaching English would be ‘Whoever disobeys him, disobeys me’, but that takes some working out. To be fair to Milton, it would make perfect sense in Latin, but Latin died a long, long time ago. Mind you, the only being who’s ever really been able to carry off consistent hyperbaton in English lived a long, long time ago in a galaxy far, far away. In Dagobah, to be precise. And even Yoda dropped hyperbaton when he could get in a good bit of anadiplosis.

这句话很容易让人歪着头皱眉。如果要把它翻译成接近英语的表达，应该是“凡违抗他的，就是违抗我”，但这需要一番琢磨。平心而论，这句话用拉丁语说得通，但拉丁语早已消亡。话说回来，唯一一个真正能把倒叙手法运用得炉火纯青的人，也生活在很久很久以前一个遥远的星系。确切地说，是在达戈巴星球。就连尤达大师在能用上叠句的时候，也会放弃倒叙。

1 Except in extremely cheap brothels.

1 除了极其廉价的妓院。

2 Created by Glenn Gordon Caron.

2 由 Glenn Gordon Caron 创建。

# ↩

Chapter 9

第九章

Anadiplosis

复读

Yoda 1 is known for wrong his word order getting, but his most quoted line, from Star Wars, Episode 1: The Phantom Menace , uses a different figure entirely. Yoda announces that fear leads to anger. He then takes the last word of that sentence and repeats it as the first word of the next: anger leads to hatred. He then takes the last word of that sentence and repeats it as the first word of the next: hatred leads to suffering. This is a case of anadiplosis. It links him directly to a previous spiritual teacher: St Paul.

尤达大师（Yoda1）以语序混乱而闻名，但他最广为人知的一句台词，出自《星球大战：第一集——魅影危机》，却运用了截然不同的修辞手法。尤达大师先说恐惧导致愤怒，然后把这句话的最后一个词作为下一句的开头：愤怒导致仇恨。接着，他又把这句话的最后一个词作为下一句的开头：仇恨导致痛苦。这是一种重复修辞法，它将尤达大师与他之前的一位精神导师——圣保罗——直接联系起来。

We glory in tribulations also, knowing that tribulation worketh patience, and patience, experience, and experience, hope, and hope maketh man not ashamed.

我们也因患难而欢喜，因为知道患难生忍耐，忍耐生经验，经验生盼望，盼望使人不至于羞愧。

It is the anadiplosis, the repetition of the last word of one clause as the first word of the next, that gives both lines their power, whether they’re written by a saint or uttered by a small green alien.

正是叠句（anadiplosis），即一个分句的最后一个词重复作为下一个分句的第一个词，赋予了这两行诗以力量，无论它们是圣人所写还是绿色小外星人所说。

The content doesn’t matter much. In fact, anadiplosis doesn’t care what you say and will give its gravitas to a diametrically opposed opinion. Yoda seems to think suffering a bad thing, but there’s another semi-fictional American character called Jesse Jackson who observed that:

内容本身并不重要。事实上，重复现象并不在意你说什么，反而会赋予截然相反的观点以分量。尤达似乎认为受苦是件坏事，但另一位名叫杰西·杰克逊的半虚构美国人物却观察到：

Suffering breeds character; character breeds faith; in the end faith will not disappoint.

苦难造就品格；品格造就信仰；最终，信仰不会让人失望。

And anyway, Yoda’s lines look similar to those of Richard II (as set down by one William Shakespeare):

而且，尤达的台词看起来和理查二世（由威廉·莎士比亚创作）的台词很相似：

The love of wicked men converts to fear;

恶人的爱会转化为恐惧；

That fear to hate, and hate turns one or both

恐惧会转化为仇恨，而仇恨会使一方或双方都发生改变。

To worthy danger and deserved death

值得冒的危险和应得的死亡

So between Yoda, Jesse Jackson and Shakespeare we may have a change in philosophy. This isn’t necessarily a bad thing. Malcolm X observed that:

所以，尤达、杰西·杰克逊和莎士比亚或许会给我们的哲学带来变革。这未必是件坏事。马尔科姆·X曾指出：

Once you change your philosophy, you change your thought pattern. Once you change your thought pattern, you change your attitude. Once you change your attitude, it changes your behavior pattern and then you go on into some action.

一旦你改变了你的哲学理念，你的思维模式就会改变。一旦你改变了思维模式，你的态度就会改变。一旦你改变了态度，你的行为模式就会改变，然后你就会付诸行动。

And action, in my experience, ends in tiredness and the need for a drink. Drink leads to drunkenness. Drunkenness leads to a hangover. Hangovers cause suffering. Suffering leads to …

而就我的经验而言，行动最终只会带来疲惫和对酒精的渴望。饮酒会导致醉酒。醉酒会导致宿醉。宿醉会带来痛苦。痛苦会导致……

But anyway, this chain has gone on for long enough and one cannot be quite sure where it starts and ends, only that it sounds lovely because of anadiplosis. Anadiplosis gives the illusion of logic. Like a conquering general it arrives at a word, plants a flag there, and then moves on. By doubling down it makes everything seem strong, structured and certain.

不过，无论如何，这个句式已经持续了足够长的时间，人们很难确定它的起点和终点，只知道它听起来悦耳动听是因为使用了叠句。叠句给人一种逻辑的错觉。它就像一位凯旋的将军，来到一个词前，插上旗帜，然后继续前进。通过反复强调，它使一切看起来都强有力、结构严谨且确定无疑。

Of course, that doesn’t mean that things are strong, structured and certain. There’s a logical fallacy called the quaternio terminorum , or fallacy of the four terms, that goes something like this:

当然，这并不意味着事物就稳固、结构严谨且确定无疑。有一种逻辑谬误叫做“四项谬误”（quaternio terminorum），或者说“四项谬误”，其大致内容如下：

A ham sandwich is better than nothing. Nothing is better than eternal happiness. So eternal happiness is beaten by a ham sandwich.

火腿三明治总比没有强。没有什么比得上永恒的幸福。所以，永恒的幸福也比不上一个火腿三明治。

The trick there is that the specific meaning of nothing has been changed from ‘lack of food’ to ‘impossibility’. Yoda could have said that fear leads to running away, and running away leads to safety. If the line had simply been ‘Fear leads to anger, which leads to hate, which leads to suffering’ it wouldn’t have sounded half as good, or half as convincing. But with the doubling of anadiplosis, it feels like an inevitable progress.

妙处在于，“无”的具体含义从“缺乏食物”变成了“不可能”。尤达本可以说，恐惧导致逃跑，逃跑带来安全。如果这句话只是“恐惧导致愤怒，愤怒导致仇恨，仇恨导致痛苦”，听起来就逊色不少，也缺乏说服力。但通过重复使用叠句，这感觉就像是水到渠成。

Of course, anadiplosis doesn’t have to be used for logic. It can simply add a harmony, in the same way that a repeated musical phrase binds two sections together. So Milton, mourning his dead friend in Lycidas , wrote:

当然，叠句并不一定用于逻辑推理。它也可以仅仅起到和声的作用，就像重复的乐句将两个乐段连接起来一样。例如，弥尔顿在《利西达斯》中悼念亡友时写道：

For Lycidas is dead, dead ere his prime;

利西达斯死了，他的鼎盛时期也结束了；

And later:

后来：

But O the heavy change now thou art gone,

但哦，如今你已离去，这沉重的变故啊。

Now thou art gone and never must return.

你已离去，永不再来。

Anadiplosis gives the glue and connection to the Lennon and McCartney song ‘Here, There and Everywhere’:

叠置手法为列侬和麦卡特尼的歌曲《Here, There and Everywhere》提供了粘合剂和联系：

To lead a better life, I need my love to be here.

为了过上更好的生活，我需要我的爱人在这里。

Here, making each day of the year,

在这里，让一年中的每一天都变得有意义。

Changing my life with the wave of her hand,

她挥了挥手，就改变了我的人生。

Nobody can deny that there’s something there.

谁都不能否认那里确实有东西。

There, running my hands through her hair,

我双手轻轻抚摸着她的头发

Both of us thinking how good it can be,

我们俩都在想这该有多好，

Someone is speaking but she doesn’t know he’s there.

有人在说话，但她不知道他在那里。

There’s simply a satisfaction, half logical and half beautiful, in seeing the same word ending one phrase and coming back to life at the start of the next. It is progression. Progression is a story. A story leads to a climax, just as here leads there and there leads everywhere. As the Emperor Commodus (didn’t actually) put it when chatting to the (utterly fictional) Maximus Decimus Meridius Russellus Crowus in the film Gladiator :

看到同一个词出现在一个短语的结尾，又出现在下一个短语的开头，这其中蕴含着一种满足感，一半合乎逻辑，一半令人愉悦。这就是进步。进步本身就是一个故事。故事会走向高潮，正如此地通往彼地，彼地通往万处。正如电影《角斗士》中，皇帝康茂德（实际上并没有）与（完全虚构的）马克西姆斯·狄西姆斯·梅里迪乌斯·罗素·克劳斯交谈时所说：

The general who became a slave. The slave who became a gladiator. The gladiator who defied an emperor. Striking story.

将军沦为奴隶，奴隶成为角斗士，角斗士挑战皇帝。引人入胜的故事。

And it is, but only when anadiplosis is on hand. The general who became a slave who became a gladiator who defied an emperor would sound like a rather incoherent nursery rhyme. But perhaps the greatest anadiplosis is not biblical or Shakespearian, it’s simply a description of a dismal dinner, and nobody knows who wrote it:

的确如此，但前提是运用了首尾呼应的修辞手法。一个将军沦为奴隶，又成为角斗士，最终反抗皇帝，这样的故事听起来就像一首语无伦次的童谣。但或许最精彩的首尾呼应并非出自圣经或莎士比亚之手，而仅仅是对一顿糟糕晚餐的描述，而且无人知晓其作者是谁：

If the soup had been as warm as the wine, and the wine as old as the fish, and the fish as young as the maid, and the maid as willing as the hostess, it would have been a very good meal.

如果汤像酒一样温暖，酒像鱼一样陈年，鱼像女仆一样年轻，女仆像女主人一样热情，那这将是一顿非常美味的晚餐。

Which is an example of a periodic sentence.

这是一个周期句的例子。

1 Yoda is a fictional character created by George Lucas.

1 尤达是乔治·卢卡斯创作的虚构人物。

# ↩

Chapter 10

第十章

Periodic Sentences

周期句

The little dot at the end of a sentence is either called a full stop or, if you’re of the American persuasion, a period. In fact, Americans rather like saying the word period aloud in order to add emphasis, as in, ‘You can’t do that, period!’, or, ‘We’ll wait a certain amount of time, period!’ This all goes back to the notion of a period as a complete cycle of time, and thus a complete, or periodic, sentence.

句子末尾的小点要么叫做句号，要么，如果你是美国人，就叫它句点。事实上，美国人很喜欢把“句点”这个词大声说出来以示强调，比如，“你不能那样做，句点！”或者，“我们会等一段时间，句点！”这一切都源于句点代表一个完整的时间周期，因此也代表一个完整的、周期性的句子。

The period is one of the most complicated and convoluted concepts of classical rhetoric. Nobody in the ancient world could quite decide what it meant, but they were united in the belief that it was terribly, terribly important. Fortunately, in English we tend to take a much more limited view and the periodic sentence is simply a very big sentence that is not complete until the end.

句号是古典修辞学中最复杂、最晦涩的概念之一。古代世界无人能确切定义它的含义，但他们一致认为它极其重要。幸运的是，在英语中，我们对句号的理解往往更为简洁，我们通常将句号理解为一个很长的句子，直到结尾才算完整。

Now you might think that no sentence is complete until the end, but you’d be wrong. That last sentence could have finished at the comma, the but you’d be wrong was not grammatically necessary. In fact, if you’d got bored halfway through, you could have put this book down and gone off to make a cup of tea with no syntactic shadow hanging over you. The same cannot be said of Rudyard Kipling’s poem ‘If’.

你或许会认为句子不到结尾都不算完整，但你错了。上一句其实在逗号处就结束了，但“你错了”在语法上并非必要。事实上，如果你读到一半觉得无聊，完全可以放下这本书，去泡杯茶，完全不用担心语法问题。但鲁德亚德·吉卜林的诗作《如果》却并非如此。

‘If’ is one long, 294-word sentence, 273 of which are conditional clauses. If you can keep your head, trust yourself, dream, think etc., then you can finally get to the main verb on the 31st line, and then ‘Yours is the Earth and everything that’s in it / And – which is more – you’ll be a Man, my son!’

“如果”是一个长达294个单词的句子，其中273个是条件从句。如果你能保持冷静，相信自己，敢于梦想，敢于思考等等，那么你最终就能读到第31行的主要动词，然后是“地球和地球上的一切都是你的/而且——更重要的是——我的儿子，你将成为真正的男子汉！”

The trick of the periodic sentence is that, until you’ve got to the end, until you’ve found that clause or verb that completes the syntax, until you’ve finally got to the period of the period, you can’t stop. Kipling forces you along to the climax. Read the first line of ‘If’ and you have to read on until line 31 before you’re grammatically satisfied. And by that time you might as well read line 32, just so you can say you have.

周期句的诀窍在于，在你读到句末，找到完成句法的那个从句或动词，最终到达句末的句点之前，你根本停不下来。吉卜林强迫你一路读到高潮。读完《如果》的第一行，你必须一直读到第31行才能在语法上感到满意。而到了那时，你或许干脆把第32行也读完，好让自己可以说已经读完了。

Shakespeare used the same trick, but usually by piling nouns one on top of the other. In The Tempest Prospero says:

莎士比亚也用过同样的技巧，但通常是通过将名词一个接一个地堆叠起来。在《暴风雨》中，普洛斯彼罗说道：

And, like the baseless fabric of this vision,

就像这种毫无根据的愿景一样，

The cloud-capp’d towers, the gorgeous palaces,

云雾缭绕的塔楼，华丽的宫殿，

The solemn temples, the great globe itself,

庄严的庙宇，巨大的地球仪本身，

Yea, all which it inherit, shall dissolve …

是的，它所继承的一切，都将消亡……

He knew the reader can’t stop until they get to that main verb. The Tempest example is actually remarkably restrained for Shakespeare. In John of Gaunt’s death scene in Richard II , the old man is meant to be so ill he can barely speak. One wonders, therefore, how he managed to take a breath deep enough for this periodic parade:

他知道读者不读到那个主要动词就停不下来。《暴风雨》的例子对莎士比亚来说其实相当克制。在《理查二世》中，约翰·冈特的临终场景里，这位老人被设定为病重到几乎说不出话来。因此，人们不禁要问，他究竟是如何在这种反复出现的场景中深吸一口气的：

This royal throne of kings, this scepter’d isle,

这国王的宝座，这权杖之岛，

This earth of majesty, this seat of Mars,

这片充满威严的土地，这火星的居所，

This other Eden, demi-paradise,

这另一个伊甸园，半个天堂，

This fortress built by Nature for herself

大自然为自己建造的这座堡垒

Against infection and the hand of war,

抵御感染和战争之手

This happy breed of men, this little world,

这群幸福的人，这个小世界，

This precious stone set in the silver sea,

这颗镶嵌在银色海洋中的宝石，

Which serves it in the office of a wall,

它就像一面墙，为办公室服务。

Or as a moat defensive to a house,

或者作为房屋的护城河防御工事

Against the envy of less happier lands,

面对来自那些生活条件较差地区的嫉妒，

This blessed plot, this earth, this realm, this England,

这片福地，这片土地，这片王国，这片英格兰，

This nurse, this teeming womb of royal kings,

这位护士，这孕育着无数王室成员的子宫，

Fear’d by their breed and famous by their birth,

因其种族而令人畏惧，因其出身而闻名遐迩

Renowned for their deeds as far from home,

他们因远离家乡的英勇事迹而闻名，

For Christian service and true chivalry,

为了基督教的服侍和真正的骑士精神，

As is the sepulchre in stubborn Jewry,

就像顽固的犹太人的坟墓一样，

Of the world’s ransom, blessed Mary’s Son,

蒙福的玛利亚之子，世人的赎价，

This land of such dear souls, this dear dear land,

这片土地上居住着如此善良的人们，这片我亲爱的土地，

Dear for her reputation through the world,

她因享誉全球的声誉而备受爱戴。

Is now leased out, I die pronouncing it,

现在已经租出去了，我念到死都念不完。

Like to a tenement or pelting farm …

就像去贫民窟或剥皮农场一样……

The substance of that sentence is ‘England is now leased out’. Everything else is, from the point of view of content, irrelevant. But ‘England is now leased out’ is much too tedious, and Shakespeare knew that content was not nearly as important as form. If you want to know what actually happened to Richard II, read a history book. Shakespeare is in it for the periods.

这句话的实质是“英格兰现在被租出去了”。从内容上看，其他一切都无关紧要。但是“英格兰现在被租出去了”这句话太过冗长乏味，而莎士比亚深知形式远比内容重要。如果你想了解理查二世的真实遭遇，那就去读历史书。莎士比亚创作这部作品是为了展现历史时期。

So long as you remember not to blurt out your main verb too early, so long as you begin clause after clause with when or if or though or while or so long , so long as you have very large lungs that can keep you going through fourteen apposite clauses for England (despite the fact that you’re on your death bed), so long as you don’t mind being a tad artificial, periodic sentences are a doddle.

只要你记得不要过早地脱口而出主要动词，只要你用 when、if、though、while 或 so long 来开始一个又一个从句，只要你肺活量很大，即使你病入膏肓也能写出十四个与英格兰相关的恰当从句，只要你不介意稍微有点矫揉造作，那么周期句就很容易写。

In the song ‘Every Breath You Take’, even in the midst of a jealous rage, Sting still maintained the self-control to save his main verb for the end of the verse:

在歌曲《Every Breath You Take》中，即使在嫉妒的怒火中，Sting 仍然保持着自制力，将主要动词留到歌词的结尾：

Every breath you take,

你的每一次呼吸，

Every move you make,

你的每一个举动，

Every bond you break,

你打破的每一段关系，

Every step you take,

你走的每一步，

I’ll be watching you.

我会盯着你的。

Likewise, in the Four Tops’ ‘Reach Out I’ll Be There’ you have a long series of temporal clauses introduced by the word ‘when’ before you get your reassurance.

同样，在 Four Tops 的歌曲《伸出援手，我会在那里》中，在你得到保证之前，你会看到一长串由“when”一词引入的时间状语从句。

However, you don’t need to keep using exactly the same structures to stop the sentence finishing. Kipling had his conditional clauses, Shakespeare and Sting their nouns, but Milton managed to hold off the first verb of Paradise Lost by digging a huge grammatical hole and setting up camp in it. Like this:

然而，你并不需要一直使用完全相同的结构来阻止句子结束。吉卜林用条件从句，莎士比亚和斯汀用名词，但弥尔顿却通过挖一个巨大的语法坑并在其中安营扎寨，成功地拖延了《失乐园》中第一个动词的出现。就像这样：

Of man’s first disobedience and the fruit

人类第一次违抗命令及其果实

Of that forbidden tree, whose mortal taste

那棵禁树，它那凡人的品味

Brought death into the world, and all our woe,

祂将死亡带到世间，带来了我们所有的苦难。

With loss of Eden, till one greater Man

伊甸园的消逝，直到一位更伟大的人出现

Restore us, and regain the blissful seat,

恢复我们的荣光，让我们重获幸福的宝座。

Sing Heav’nly Muse …

歌唱天籁缪斯……

Which is an example of hypotaxis.

这是下渗的一个例子。

# ↩

Chapter 11

第十一章

Hypotaxis and Parataxis (and Polysyndeton and Asyndeton)

下位句和并列句（以及多连接子句和无连接子句）

Before we get to hypotaxis, we’ve got to go through parataxis. Parataxis is like this. It’s good, plain English. It’s one sentence. Then it’s another sentence. It’s direct. It’s farmer’s English. You don’t want to buy my cattle. They’re good cattle. You don’t know cattle. I’m going to have a drink. Then I’m going to break your jaw. I’m a paratactic farmer. My cattle are the best in England.

在学习主句之前，我们得先了解并列句。并列句是这样的：它简洁明了，用词朴实无华，一句话接着一句话，直截了当，就像农民的英语一样。比如，“你不想买我的牛。我的牛很好。你不懂牛。我要喝一杯。然后我要打断你的下巴。” 我是个讲并列句的农民。我的牛是全英国最好的。

Parataxis is the natural way of speaking English. It’s the way English wants to be spoken. English is a basically uninflected language. Everything depends on the word order. It’s all subject verb object. The man kicked the dog. The cat sat on the mat. The angels have the phone box. In Latin and German it’s different. Words can be moved around, but you still understand the sentence because of the endings. ‘Nauta amat puellam’ and ‘Puellam nauta amat’ both mean ‘The sailor loves the girl’. English isn’t like that. It’s paratactic. It’s linear. It’s one sentence. Then it’s another.

并列句是英语自然的表达方式，也是英语表达的本能。英语基本上是一种非屈折语，一切都取决于词序，遵循主语-谓语-宾语的模式。例如：男人踢了狗。猫坐在垫子上。天使们拥有电话亭。拉丁语和德语则不同，词序可以改变，但由于词尾变化，句子仍然能够理解。“Nauta amat puellam”和“Puellam nauta amat”都表示“水手爱上了那个女孩”。英语并非如此，它是并列句，结构线性，一个句子接着一个句子。

They don’t have to be sentences, they could be divided by commas, they could be divided by semi-colons; there’s a class of people who get very worked up about such things – they’re lonely people – they tend to have stains down the fronts of their shirts – they’ll tell you that dashes should be used only to subordinate complete sentences. You must forgive them.

它们不必是完整的句子，可以用逗号分隔，也可以用分号分隔；有一类人对这种事特别较真——他们是孤独的人——他们衬衫前面往往沾着污渍——他们会告诉你破折号只能用来连接完整的句子。你应该原谅他们。

But you can get round the punctuation problem by using conjunctions and just keep your sentence going and going for ever and then chuck in a few buts but not too many then a couple of thens so listen carefully to people telling a story and you’ll find that usually there are no full stops and it’s just conjunctions and they go on and on for ever.

但是你可以通过使用连词来绕过标点符号的问题，让你的句子一直往前延伸，然后插入一些“但是”，但不要太多“然后”，几个“然后”就行了。仔细听人们讲故事，你会发现通常没有句号，只有连词，而且它们会一直往前延伸，永无止境。

Using lots of conjunctions is called polysyndeton. No conjunctions is called asyndeton.

使用大量连接词的句法称为多连接词句法。不使用连接词的句法称为无连接词句法。

And Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to his disciples saying ‘Take, eat, this is my body’

耶稣拿起饼来，祝福了，掰开，递给门徒，说：“你们拿着吃，这是我的身体。”

So St Mark was very fond of polysyndeton and Jesus was more of an asyndeton chap. There’s nothing wrong with parataxis. It’s good, simple, clean, plain-living, hard-working, up-bright-and-early English. Wham. Bam. Thank you, ma’am. Orwell liked it. Hemingway liked it. Almost no English writer between about 1650 and 1850 liked it.

所以圣马可很喜欢多连接词，而耶稣则更喜欢无连接词。并列句没什么不好。它简洁明了，干净利落，体现了朴素、勤劳、早起的英国人特有的风格。铿锵有力，妙不可言。奥威尔喜欢它，海明威也喜欢它。但在1650年到1850年间，几乎没有哪个英国作家喜欢它。

The alternative, should you, or any writer of English, choose to employ it (and who is to stop you?) is, by use of subordinate clause upon subordinate clause, which itself may be subordinated to those clauses that have gone before or after, to construct a sentence of such labyrinthine grammatical complexity that, like Theseus before you when he searched the dark Minoan mazes for that monstrous monster, half bull and half man, or rather half woman for it had been conceived from, or in, Pasiphae, herself within a Daedalian contraption of perverted intention, you must unravel a ball of grammatical yarn lest you wander for ever, amazed in the maze, searching through dark eternity for a full stop.

如果你或任何英语写作者选择采用这种方法（谁又能阻止你呢？），那就是使用层层嵌套的从句，这些从句本身又可以隶属于前面或后面的从句，从而构建出一个语法极其复杂的句子，就像忒修斯在你之前在黑暗的米诺斯迷宫中寻找那个半人半牛的怪物一样，或者更确切地说，是半人半牛的怪物，因为它是由帕西法厄在她体内孕育而生，而帕西法厄本身又被置于一个扭曲意图的代达罗斯式装置之中，你必须解开一团语法线团，否则你将永远在迷宫中徘徊，惊奇地在黑暗的永恒中寻找一个句号。

That’s hypotaxis, and it used to be everywhere. It’s hard to say who started it, but the best candidate was a chap called Sir Thomas Browne.

这就是下移现象，以前非常普遍。很难说是谁发明了这种现象，但最有可能的候选人是一位名叫托马斯·布朗爵士的人。

In 1671, King Charles II visited Norwich and decided he’d like to give someone a knighthood. It didn’t matter who. Charles just enjoyed knighting people. The trouble was that there weren’t many people in Norwich who seemed to need knighting. Somebody suggested the mayor, but the mayor, apparently, was not really knight material. They settled instead on a doctor called Thomas Browne. Thomas Browne was nothing special as a doctor; but he was the first ever English prose writer, and that’s got to be worth a good knighting.

1671年，查理二世国王访问诺里奇，决定册封某人为骑士。至于人选，查理二世并不在意，他只是喜欢册封骑士。问题是，诺里奇似乎并没有多少人需要被册封。有人提议册封市长，但市长显然并不符合骑士的条件。最终，他们决定册封一位名叫托马斯·布朗的医生。托马斯·布朗作为医生并无过人之处，但他却是英国历史上第一位散文作家，这足以让他获得一枚令人艳羡的骑士勋章。

Some people (foolish, deranged and sinister people) will tell you that Sir Thomas Browne was not the first English prose writer. They will point out (quite unhelpfully) that people had been writing English prose for nearly a thousand years before Browne was born. They’ll tell you all about Aelfric, Bacon and the King James Bible – Shakespeare, they’ll point out, sometimes wrote prose. They’ll demonstrate, using mere fact, that I’m talking nonsense. But facts obscure the truth, which is that writing prose doesn’t make you a prose writer any more than philosophising makes you a philosopher or fooling around makes you a fool. Or to put it another way:

有些人（愚蠢、疯狂、阴险的人）会告诉你，托马斯·布朗爵士并非第一位英国散文作家。他们会指出（毫无帮助地），在布朗出生前近千年，人们就已经开始创作英国散文了。他们会跟你滔滔不绝地讲述埃尔弗里克、培根和《詹姆斯国王钦定版圣经》——他们还会指出，莎士比亚有时也写散文。他们会用事实来证明我的说法纯属无稽之谈。但事实掩盖了真相，那就是：写散文并不能让你成为散文作家，就像思考哲学并不能让你成为哲学家，胡闹也不能让你成为傻瓜一样。或者换句话说：

Many from the ignorance of these Maxims, and an inconsiderate zeal unto Truth, have too rashly charged the troops of error, and remain as Trophies unto the enemies of Truth: A man may be in as just possession of Truth as of a City, and yet be forced to surrender.

许多人由于不了解这些格言，又出于对真理的盲目热情，贸然向谬误大军发起冲锋，最终沦为真理敌人的战利品：一个人即便拥有真理如同拥有一座城市，也仍然可能被迫投降。

You see, up until Browne, people wrote prose for three reasons: 1) They couldn’t be bothered to write poetry (Aelfric). 2) They were translating something and had to make it precise (the Bible). 3) They were trying to write in the way that normal people speak (Shakespeare). Sir Thomas Browne was the first person to write prose because he was damn well writing prose. He wasn’t translating anything. He wasn’t imitating the man on the street, because no man on any street ever spoke sentences like his. Browne’s prose was an awful lot more complicated than poetry. He used hypotaxis, with sentences hidden inside sentences like Russian dolls, clauses hidden in clauses, prepositions referring this way and that, until the bemused reader needs a diagram just to find out where the main verb is. Browne adored hypotaxis, and built huge rococo sentences filled with trap-doors and secret passages and little subordinate clauses dancing around. Here he is on the subject of whether the Bible is literally true:

你看，在布朗之前，人们写散文的原因有三个：1）他们懒得写诗（比如艾尔弗里克）。2）他们在翻译，必须做到精准（比如《圣经》）。3）他们试图用普通人说话的方式写作（比如莎士比亚）。托马斯·布朗爵士是第一个写散文的人，因为他就是在写散文。他不是在翻译什么，也不是在模仿普通人，因为任何普通人都不会像他那样说话。布朗的散文比诗歌复杂得多。他运用了层层嵌套的结构，句子像俄罗斯套娃一样层层嵌套，从句又嵌套在从句中，介词指代不明，以至于读者需要借助图表才能找到主要动词的位置。布朗酷爱这种结构，他构建了庞大而华丽的句子，里面充满了陷阱、秘密通道和翩翩起舞的小从句。以下是他对《圣经》是否字面意义上的真实性的论述：

… thus is man that great and true Amphibium, whose nature is disposed to live not onely like other creatures in divers elements, but in divided and distinguished worlds; for though there bee not one to sense, there are two to reason; the one visible, the other invisible, whereof Moses seemes to have left description, and of the other so obscurely, that some parts thereof are yet in controversie; and truely for the first chapters of Genesis, I must confesse a great deale of obscurity, though Divines have to the power of humane reason endeavoured to make all goe in a literall meaning, yet those allegoricall interpretations are also probable, and perhaps the mysticall method of Moses bred up in the Hieroglyphicall Schooles of the Egyptians.

……因此，人类是伟大而真实的两栖动物，其本性不仅倾向于像其他生物一样生活在不同的元素中，而且倾向于生活在分离且不同的世界中；因为虽然没有一个感官世界，但有两个理性世界：一个是可见的，另一个是不可见的，摩西似乎没有描述后者，而后者又如此晦涩难懂，以至于其中的一些部分至今仍存在争议；的确，对于《创世记》的前几章，我必须承认其中有很多晦涩之处，尽管神学家们努力运用人类理性来解释一切，但那些寓意性的解释也是可能的，或许摩西的神秘方法源于埃及象形文字学校的教育。

Browne gave to the English language the glory of the preposterously long sentence: sentences that nobody in their right minds would ever say aloud, sentences that are intricate games, filled with fine flourishes and curious convolutions. Such sentences have a remarkable quality: civilisation.

布朗赋予英语一种荒诞长句的荣耀：这种句子，正常人绝不会大声说出口；它如同精巧的游戏，充满了华丽的辞藻和奇特的转折。这样的句子有一种非凡的特质：文明。

Hypotaxis is unnatural in English; nobody would ever say a sentence like the one above. You have to think calmly for a long time to come up with a good hypotactic sentence, and so a good hypotactic sentence tells the reader that you have been thinking calmly for long time. An angry drunk might shout paratactically; only a just and gentle mind can be hypotactic.

在英语中，从句是不自然的；没有人会说出像上面那样的句子。你需要冷静思考很长时间才能写出一个好的从句，因此，一个好的从句能告诉读者你已经冷静思考了很久。一个愤怒的醉汉可能会大声喊叫，使用并列结构；只有公正温和的人才能使用从句。

If someone was furious about a sycophantic lawyer they might say: ‘Lawyers are only interested in money. Sure, lawyers pay you compliments. Compliments are free.’ But when Charles Dickens said exactly the same thing, he phrased it like this:

如果有人对一个阿谀奉承的律师感到愤怒，他们可能会说：“律师只对钱感兴趣。没错，律师会赞美你。赞美是免费的。”但当查尔斯·狄更斯表达同样的观点时，他是这样说的：

It was a maxim with Mr Brass that the habit of paying compliments kept a man’s tongue oiled without any expense; and that, as that useful member ought never to grow rusty or creak in turning on its hinges in the case of a practitioner of the law, in whom it should be always glib and easy, he lost few opportunities of improving himself by the utterance of handsome speeches and eulogistic expressions.

布拉斯先生奉行一条格言：善于恭维人，就能让舌头保持灵活，而且无需花费任何代价；对于律师来说，舌头这件有用的器官绝不能生锈或转动时发出吱吱声，而应该始终灵活自如，因此他很少错过通过发表优美的演讲和赞美之词来提升自己的机会。

Seventy-three words of hypotactic fun that somehow never seems rude, even though it definitely is. Indeed, if Mr Brass were allowed to read his creator’s description of him, he would probably have chuckled. But hypotaxis doesn’t just stop you being rude, it stops you being too enthusiastic as well. You can’t gush with hypotaxis. If I told you: ‘She’s beautiful and clever and rich. She’s got a lovely house. She’s always friendly. She has all the best things that a person can have. She’s 21. Nothing bad ever happens to her’, you’d think that I was afflicted with the most tedious variety of love, and you probably wouldn’t believe me. But Jane Austen wrote exactly the same thing as the first line of Emma :

七十三个字的句式修辞，妙趣横生，却又丝毫不显粗鲁，尽管它确实很粗鲁。事实上，如果布拉斯先生能读到他创造者对他的描述，他大概会忍不住笑出声来。但句式修辞不仅能避免粗鲁，还能避免过于热情。你不能用句式修辞来滔滔不绝。如果我告诉你：“她美丽、聪明、富有。她有一栋漂亮的房子。她总是很友善。她拥有一个人所能拥有的一切美好事物。她21岁。她从没遇到过任何坏事”，你会觉得我患上了最乏味的爱情，而且你可能不会相信我。但简·奥斯汀在《爱玛》的第一句话里就写了同样的话：

Emma Woodhouse, handsome, clever, and rich, with a comfortable home and happy disposition, seemed to unite some of the best blessings of existence; and had lived nearly twenty-one years in the world with very little to distress or vex her.

艾玛·伍德豪斯，美丽、聪明、富有，拥有舒适的家和快乐的性情，似乎集世间最美好的事物于一身；她在世上生活了近二十一年，几乎没有什么事情让她感到痛苦或烦恼。

You can almost see Miss Austen winking at you over a cup of tea.

你仿佛能看到简·奥斯汀小姐一边喝茶一边向你眨眼。

Absolutely anything sounds civilised and well-thought-out, provided that it’s expressed in the most syntactically complicated, hyper-hypotactic manner. And so from 1650 to 1850 everybody sounded civilised and wise. Even pornography had an air of considered calm to it, now lost for ever to the discerning pervert. Fanny Hill (1748) is generally thought the greatest mucky novel in English literature. Its content is, of course, much like the content of any dirty story, human nature being what it is, and the human body having only so many viable entrances and exits; but when such coarsely eternal activities are laced into a mad grammarian’s fantasy, the result is superb.

只要用最复杂、最繁复的句法表达，任何话听起来都显得文明而深思熟虑。因此，从1650年到1850年，每个人听起来都彬彬有礼、智慧过人。就连色情作品也带着一种深思熟虑的平静，而这种平静如今已永远地被有识之士所遗忘。《芬妮·希尔》（1748）通常被认为是英国文学中最伟大的低俗小说。当然，它的内容与任何色情故事的内容并无二致，毕竟人性如此，人体的入口和出口也终究有限；但当这些粗俗永恒的活动被融入一个疯狂语法学家的幻想之中时，其结果却堪称绝妙。

Coming then into my chamber, and seeing me lie alone, with my face turned from the light towards the inside of the bed, he, without more ado, just slipped off his breeches, for the greater ease and enjoyment of the naked touch; and softly turning up my petticoats and shift behind, opened the prospect of the back avenue to the genial seat of pleasure; where, as I lay at my side length, inclining rather face downward, I appeared full fair, and liable to be entered. Laying himself gently down by me, he invested me behind, and giving me to feel the warmth of his body, as he applied his thighs and belly close to me, and the endeavours of that machine, whose touch has something so exquisitely singular in it, to make its way good into me.

他走进我的房间，见我独自躺着，脸背对着光线，面向床内，便毫不犹豫地脱下裤子，以便更方便地享受赤裸的触碰；他轻轻撩起我的衬裙和睡袍，露出通往那幽静之所的后门；我侧身躺着，脸略微向下倾斜，显得格外诱人，仿佛随时准备被他进入。他轻轻地躺在我身边，从后面环抱着我，让我感受到他身体的温暖，他的大腿和腹部紧贴着我，那触感如此奇妙的机器，正努力地想要进入我的身体。

If one attempts to rewrite that in the paratactic style, it loses all its charm and might indeed be considered almost smutty, almost vulgar.

如果尝试用并列句式重写这句话，它就会失去所有的魅力，甚至可能被认为近乎下流，近乎粗俗。

Hypotaxis was what made English prose so terribly, terribly civilised. It still works. Angry letters of complaint, redundancy notices and ransom notes will, if written in careful hypotaxis, sound as reasonable, measured and genial as a good dose of rough Enlightenment pornography.

正是句式结构（hypotaxis）造就了英语散文的优雅和文明。时至今日，它依然有效。即使是愤怒的投诉信、裁员通知和勒索信，如果运用严谨的句式结构，听起来也如同粗俗的启蒙时代色情作品一般，合情合理、克制温和。

Yet hypotaxis (along with reason) has been declining for a century or more. Gone are those heady and incomprehensible sentences of Johnson, Dickens and Austen, replaced with the cruel, brutalist parataxes of writers whose aim is to agitate and distress. The long sentence is now a ridiculed rarity, usually hidden away in the Terms and Conditions, its commas and colons, clauses and caveats languishing unread and unloved.

然而，长句（以及理性）在一个世纪或更久的时间里一直在衰落。约翰逊、狄更斯和奥斯汀那些令人陶醉、晦涩难懂的句子已不复存在，取而代之的是那些旨在煽动和扰乱读者情绪的作家们所使用的残酷、粗暴的并列句。长句如今已成为一种被嘲笑的稀罕物，通常隐藏在条款和条件中，其逗号、冒号、从句和附加条件无人问津，无人问津。

The long sentence did have one last hurrah, though, one farewell bash before it was retired to exhausted obscurity. The last sentence of James Joyce’s Ulysses is 4,391 words long and has no punctuation at all, not a dash or a semi-colon from its opening to its last words: ‘yes I said yes I will Yes.’

不过，这句长句在彻底消失于历史的尘埃中之前，还有最后一次辉煌，最后一次告别演出。詹姆斯·乔伊斯《尤利西斯》的最后一句长达4391个单词，从头到尾没有任何标点符号，既没有破折号也没有分号：“是的，我说是的，我会的，是的。”

Which is an example of diacope.

这是双关语的一个例子。

# ↩

Chapter 12

第十二章

Diacope

迪亚科普

In 1962 cinema-goers were introduced to a new hero and a new Great Line. They met him for the first time in Le Cercle casino, but they weren’t allowed to see his face. Instead, the camera concentrated on a pretty woman in a red dress who is losing at baccarat. She loses and loses and loses until, finally, she says that she needs to borrow another thousand pounds. And now we hear the hero’s voice, off camera. He says, rather sarcastically, ‘I admire your courage, Miss …’

1962年，影迷们迎来了一位新英雄和一句新的经典台词。他们在勒塞尔克赌场第一次见到他，但却无法看清他的真容。取而代之的是，镜头聚焦在一位身着红裙的漂亮女子身上，她正在百家乐游戏中节节败退。她输个不停，直到最后，她说她还需要再借一千英镑。这时，我们听到了英雄的声音，从镜头外传来。他略带讽刺地说：“我佩服你的勇气，小姐……”

‘Trench,’ the lady replies tetchily. And then, seeing who’s asked the question and clearly finding him attractive, she adds her first name: ‘Sylvia Trench.’

“特伦奇，”那位女士不耐烦地回答道。然后，看到是谁问了这个问题，显然觉得他很有魅力，她又加上了自己的名字：“西尔维娅·特伦奇。”

Then she, clearly miffed, adds: ‘I admire your luck, Mr …’

然后她显然有些恼火，补充道：“我佩服你的运气，先生……”

The camera turns to the mysterious man; and he, still making fun of her and mimicking her rather silly introduction, says: ‘Bond. James Bond.’ 1

镜头转向那位神秘男子；他仍在取笑她，模仿她略显愚蠢的自我介绍，说道：“邦德。詹姆斯·邦德。”¹

It’s a tit-for-tat flirtation. The each imitate the other’s sentences, until inevitably she goes back to Bond’s flat, undresses and plays golf. It wasn’t meant to be a great line. Nonetheless, the American Film Institute rates it as the 22nd greatest line in all cinema (how they can be so precise, I don’t precisely know). Another poll had it as the best-loved one-liner in the history of film. This is, if you think about it, peculiar. The content of the line, for what it’s worth is … well … that he’s called James Bond. And James Bond is a boring, boring name. It was deliberately chosen to be tedious. Ian Fleming explained:

这是一场你来我往的调情。两人互相模仿对方的台词，最终，她不可避免地回到了邦德的公寓，脱掉衣服，开始打高尔夫。这句台词原本并不出彩。然而，美国电影学会却将其评为影史上第22佳台词（他们是如何做到如此精准的，我实在不得而知）。另一项民意调查则将其评为电影史上最受欢迎的经典台词。仔细想想，这确实很奇怪。这句台词的内容，说到底……就是他叫詹姆斯·邦德。而詹姆斯·邦德，一个极其乏味的名字。这个名字显然是故意取的，就是为了让人感到无聊。伊恩·弗莱明解释道：

I wanted the simplest, dullest, plainest-sounding name I could find, James Bond was much better than something more interesting, like ‘Peregrine Carruthers.’ Exotic things would happen to and around him, but he would be a neutral figure – an anonymous, blunt instrument wielded by a government department. 2

我想要一个最简单、最乏味、最平淡的名字，詹姆斯·邦德比“佩雷格林·卡拉瑟斯”之类的更有趣的名字要好得多。奇特的事情会发生在他身上和他周围，但他将是一个中立的人物——一个政府部门使用的匿名、冷酷的工具。

So just to recap, one of the greatest lines in the history of cinema is a man saying a name deliberately designed to be dull. The only possible explanation for the line’s popularity is the way it is phrased. Would the line have been remembered if he had said ‘My name is Mr James Bond’, or ‘Bond, first name James’, or ‘Bond, but you can call me James’, or ‘James Bond’?

简单回顾一下，电影史上最经典的台词之一，竟然是一个男人念出了一个故意设计得平淡无奇的名字。这句台词之所以如此受欢迎，唯一的解释就是它的措辞方式。如果他说的是“我的名字是詹姆斯·邦德先生”、“邦德，我的名字是詹姆斯”、“邦德，不过你可以叫我詹姆斯”或者“詹姆斯·邦德”，这句台词还会被人记住吗？

Wording, pure wording.

措辞，纯粹的措辞。

Diacope (pronounced die-ACK-oh-pee) is a verbal sandwich: a word or phrase is repeated after a brief interruption. You take two Bonds and stuff James in the middle. Bingo. You have a great line. Or if you like you can take two burns and stuff a baby in the middle, and you’ve got a political slogan and disco hit: burn, baby, burn (‘Disco Inferno’).

Diacope（发音为 die-ACK-oh-pee）是一种语言上的“三明治”：一个词或短语在短暂的停顿后重复出现。比如，你可以把两个 Bonds 和 James 夹在中间，妙哉！一句精彩的台词就诞生了。或者，如果你愿意，也可以把两个 Burns 和 Baby 夹在中间，这样就成了一句政治口号和一首迪斯科金曲：Burn, Baby, Burn（《迪斯科地狱》）。

If you want to write the greatest line in The Godfather Part II , all you need is two It was you s with a Fredo, I know as the stuffing. In fact, you don’t even need to use diacope at all. Diacope has a life of its own and flits, like a winged monkey, into places it was never meant to be. Every child remembers how, in The Wizard of Oz , the Wicked Witch of the West 3 cries: ‘Fly, my pretties, fly!’

如果你想写出《教父2》里最精彩的台词，你只需要两个“It was yous”加上一个弗雷多（Fredo），我知道那是填充物。事实上，你甚至根本不需要用到双关语。双关语有它自己的生命，像一只长着翅膀的猴子一样，飞到它原本不该去的地方。每个孩子都记得，在《绿野仙踪》里，西方女巫喊道：“飞吧，我的宝贝们，飞吧！”

Except that she doesn’t.

但她并没有。

In the film the flying monkeys are instructed to ‘Fly! Fly! Fly! Fly!’ and there is no vocative my pretties to be heard. So why does everybody remember it incorrectly? There is plenty of diacope around in the film. There’s ‘Run, Toto – run!’ and ‘I’m frightened, Auntie Em – I’m frightened!’ 4 And diacope is powerful, so powerful that it somehow spread in our memories and the witch’s my pretties slid into every repetition.

电影里，飞猴们被指示“飞！飞！飞！飞！”，并没有听到呼格“my pretties”。那么，为什么大家都记错了呢？电影里有很多长音，比如“快跑，托托——快跑！”和“我害怕，艾姆阿姨——我害怕！”⁴。长音的力量非常强大，它不知怎么地就融入了我们的记忆，女巫的“my pretties”也悄然渗入了每一次重复。

British Prime Ministers are always having diacope thrust upon them by the popular imagination. There’s a well-known story of a journalist asking Harold Macmillan what the biggest problem was for a government. Harold Macmillan replied, ‘Events, dear boy, events.’ Except that there is no written record of his ever saying this. He did once talk about the ‘opposition of events’, but that’s it. His best known line is probably not even his, but it is diacope.

英国首相总是被大众想象强加一些双关语。有个广为流传的故事：一位记者问哈罗德·麦克米伦，政府面临的最大问题是什么。麦克米伦回答说：“是事件，亲爱的孩子，是事件。”然而，没有任何书面记录表明他曾说过这句话。他确实曾谈到过“事件的对立面”，但也仅此而已。他最著名的名言或许并非出自他之口，但它确实带有双关语的意味。

In 1979, Britain was in a wintry and discontented state. Inflation was running at 10 per cent and everybody, even the rubbish collectors and grave-diggers, was on strike. James Callaghan, the Prime Minister, on the other hand, was at a trade conference in the Caribbean. When he returned, looking decidedly tanned and healthy, journalists at the airport asked him what he was going to do about the mounting chaos. He replied that ‘I don’t think other people in the world would share the view that there is mounting chaos.’ It is the line for which he is remembered, though not in that phrasing. Diacope had again slithered in and the headline in The Sun the next day was ‘Crisis? What Crisis?’

1979年，英国正处于寒冬腊月，民怨沸腾。通货膨胀率高达10%，就连垃圾工和掘墓人也加入了罢工行列。而当时的首相詹姆斯·卡拉汉却正在加勒比海参加贸易会议。他返回英国时，看起来容光焕发，气色极佳。机场的记者们问他打算如何应对日益严重的混乱局面。他回答说：“我不认为世界上其他人会认同‘日益严重的混乱’这种说法。” 这句话虽然并非卡拉汉原话，却成了他最广为人知的名言。迪亚科普再次趁虚而入，第二天《太阳报》的头条标题是“危机？什么危机？”

It’s a shame when your most famous line isn’t yours. Several dictionaries of quotations have it under his name, but point out that the line is actually by a Sun journalist. They’re wrong too. Crisis? What Crisis? was the title of a Supertramp album released in 1975, and they appear to have got it from The Day of the Jackal .

最令人遗憾的是，你最著名的台词并非出自你之手。一些名言词典将其列在他名下，但同时指出这句台词实际上出自《太阳报》的一位记者之口。他们的说法也是错误的。《危机？什么危机？》是超级流浪汉乐队（Supertramp）1975年发行的一张专辑的名称，他们似乎是从《豺狼之日》（The Day of the Jackal）一书中借用了这个名字。

It doesn’t matter whether you intended to deploy diacope. It’s rather like the story of James Whistler and Oscar Wilde. Whistler had just made a particularly witty witticism and Wilde ruefully commented, ‘I wish I’d said that.’ Whistler, who liked to imply that all Wilde’s best lines were stolen from him, replied, ‘You will, Oscar. You will.’ You may not mean to diacopise, but you will, dear reader, you will.

无论你是否刻意使用双关语，都无关紧要。这有点像詹姆斯·惠斯勒和奥斯卡·王尔德的故事。惠斯勒刚刚说了一句特别妙语，王尔德懊恼地说：“我真希望这话是我说的。”惠斯勒喜欢暗示王尔德所有最精彩的台词都是偷来的，他回答说：“你会的，奥斯卡。你会的。”亲爱的读者，你或许并非有意使用双关语，但你终究会用到，你终究会用到。

Diacope comes in a number of forms. The simplest is the vocative diacope: Live, baby, live . Yeah, baby, yeah . I am dying, Egypt, dying . Game over, man, game over . Zed’s dead, baby, Zed’s dead . 5 All you do is chuck in somebody’s name or their title and repeat. The effect is to put a bit of emphasis, a certain finality, on the second word. Somehow it ceases to be a joke or an off-the-cuff remark and becomes a rhadamantine judgement.

重复句有多种形式。最简单的是呼格重复句：活下去，宝贝，活下去。耶，宝贝，耶。我要死了，埃及，我要死了。游戏结束了，伙计，游戏结束了。泽德死了，宝贝，泽德死了。⁵ 你只需要把某人的名字或头衔加进去，然后重复一遍。这样做的效果是强调第二个词，赋予它某种终结感。不知何故，它不再是一个玩笑或随口说说的话，而变成了一种不容置疑的判断。

You can even deploy this with phrases ( They told me, Heraclitus, they told me you were dead ), or whole sentences ( Do you remember an inn, Miranda, do you remember an inn? ).

你甚至可以用短语（他们告诉我，赫拉克利特，他们告诉我你死了）或整个句子（你还记得一家旅馆吗，米兰达，你还记得一家旅馆吗？）来运用这个技巧。

The other main form of diacope is the elaboration, where you chuck in an adjective. From sea to shining sea . Sunday bloody Sunday . O Captain! My Captain! Human, all too human . From harmony, from heavenly harmony … or Beauty, real beauty, ends where intellectual expression begins . This form gives you a feeling both of precision (we’re not talking about fake beauty) and crescendo (it’s not merely a sea, it’s a shining sea).

另一种主要的修饰形式是附加形容词，即插入形容词。例如：从大海到闪耀的大海。血腥的星期天。哦，船长！我的船长！人啊，太人性化了。从和谐，从天上的和谐……或者，真正的美，止于理性表达的起点。这种形式既给人以精准之感（我们说的不是虚假的美），又给人以渐强之感（它不仅仅是一片大海，它是一片闪耀的大海）。

Or you can combine the two. Dr Johnson once met a lady who was very keen on horses. She asked him why, in his dictionary, he had defined pastern as the knee of a horse when in fact, as she helpfully explained, it was the portion below the fetlock. Johnson replied: ‘Ignorance, Madam. Pure ignorance.’

或者你可以将两者结合起来。约翰逊博士曾遇到一位非常喜爱马的女士。她问他，为什么在他的字典里，他把系部定义为马的膝盖，而实际上，正如她热心地解释的那样，系部是球节以下的部分。约翰逊回答说：“夫人，那是无知。纯粹的无知。”

Finally there’s extended diacope. All the previous examples have had the structure ABA. But you can extend that to AABA. When Richard III is dying he shouts, ‘A horse! A horse! My kingdom for a horse!’ Shakespeare knew a show-stopping line when he wrote one, which is probably why he stole his own formula for Juliet on her balcony asking, ‘Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?’

最后，还有扩展的音节结构。之前所有的例子都采用了ABA结构，但你可以将其扩展为AABA。理查三世临终前高喊：“一匹马！一匹马！我的王国换一匹马！”莎士比亚深谙如何写出令人叹为观止的台词，这或许也是为什么他借鉴了自己的创作手法，让朱丽叶在阳台上发出“罗密欧，罗密欧，你为什么是罗密欧？”的疑问。

(While we’re on the subject of this line, I’d like to point out that she’s not asking where Romeo is. Wherefore doesn’t mean where , it means why . Juliet is upset because she’s fallen in love with a chap without asking his name, and then found out that he’s called Romeo and Romeo is the one chap in Verona that she really shouldn’t be getting soppy over.)

（既然说到这句台词，我想指出，她并不是在问罗密欧在哪里。“Wherefore”的意思不是“在哪里”，而是“为什么”。朱丽叶生气是因为她爱上了一个男人，却没问他的名字，然后才发现他叫罗密欧，而罗密欧正是维罗纳城里她最不应该动情的人。）

Since then the trick has been used again, again and once again. Compare these:

此后，这种伎俩被反复使用。请比较以下几点：

‘O villain, villain, smiling, damned villain!’
– Shakespeare, Hamlet

“哦，恶棍，恶棍，笑着的，该死的恶棍！”——莎士比亚，《哈姆雷特》

‘Alone, alone, all all alone’
– Coleridge, The Rime of the Ancient Mariner

“孤身一人，孤身一人，全然孤身一人”——柯勒律治，《古舟子咏》

‘Dead, dead, long dead, / And my heart is a handful of dust.’
– Tennyson, Maud

“死了，死了，早已死去，/我的心也化作了一把尘埃。”——莫德·丁尼生

‘Mud! Mud! Glorious mud!’
“泥！泥！光荣的泥！”
– Flanders and Swann, ‘The Hippopotamus Song’
——弗兰德斯和斯旺，《河马之歌》

Free at last. Free at last. Thank God almighty we are free at last.
– Martin Luther King’s epitaph, taken from an old spiritual

终于自由了。终于自由了。感谢全能的上帝，我们终于自由了。——马丁·路德·金的墓志铭，取自一首古老的灵歌

‘Love me. Love me. Say that you love me.’
“爱我。爱我。说你爱我。”
– Cardigans, ‘Lovefool’
– Cardigans，《Lovefool》

But the greatest example of this extended diacope is the immortal line of Julius Caesar in Carry on Cleo : ‘Infamy! Infamy! They’ve all got it in for me.’ 6

但这种扩展的双关语最杰出的例子，莫过于《凯撒大帝》中尤利乌斯·凯撒那句不朽的台词：“耻辱！耻辱！他们都想害我。”<sup>6</sup>

Diacope, diacope. They all used diacope. It works. Nobody would have cared if Hamlet had asked ‘Whether or not to be?’, or ‘To be or not?’, or ‘To be or to die?’ No. The most famous line in English literature is famous not for the content, but for the wording. To be or not to be .

长短句，长短句。他们都用了长短句。这招管用。如果哈姆雷特问的是“生存还是毁灭？”，或者“生存还是毁灭？”，或者“生存还是死亡？”，恐怕没人会在意。不，英国文学中最著名的台词并非因其内容而闻名，而是因其措辞。“生存还是毁灭。”

That is the rhetorical question.

这是一个反问句。

1 Dr No (1962), written by Richard Maibaum, Johanna Harwood, Berkely Mather from the novel by Ian Fleming.

1 《诺博士》（1962 年），由理查德·迈鲍姆、乔安娜·哈伍德、伯克利·马瑟根据伊恩·弗莱明的小说改编。

2 Interview with the Manchester Guardian (1958).

2 接受《曼彻斯特卫报》采访（1958 年）。

3 See chapter on alliteration .

3 参见关于头韵的章节。

4 Screenplay by Noel Langley, Florence Ryerson and Edgar Allan Woolf, adapted from the novel by L. Frank Baum. All excerpts from The Wizard of Oz granted courtesy of Warner Bros. Entertainment Inc. All Rights Reserved, © 1939.

4 剧本由诺埃尔·兰利、弗洛伦斯·赖尔森和埃德加·爱伦·伍尔夫改编自L·弗兰克·鲍姆的小说。所有摘自《绿野仙踪》的片段均经华纳兄弟娱乐公司授权使用。版权所有，© 1939。

5 In case you were wondering, that’s INXS, Austin Powers, Antony and Cleopatra , Aliens and Pulp Fiction .

5 如果你想知道的话，它们分别是 INXS 乐队、《王牌大贱谍》、《安东尼与克莉奥佩特拉》、《异形》和《低俗小说》。

6 Actually, this line was first used on the radio series Take It From Here and was recycled for Carry On Cleo .

6 事实上，这句台词最初出现在广播剧《听我说》中，后来又被用在了《继续克莱奥》中。

# ↩

Chapter 13

第十三章

Rhetorical Questions

反问句

What, O what is a rhetorical question? Is it merely a question that requires no answer? No. Is it a question where the answer is too obvious to need stating? Or one where there is no answer? Or just a cold-blooded thing to say to a chap before you pop a cap in his ass?

什么，什么，是反问句？它仅仅是一个不需要答案的问题吗？不。它是答案显而易见、无需赘述的问题吗？还是根本没有答案的问题？又或者只是在爆头之前冷酷无情地对某人说的一句话？

Most of us, to be frank, don’t know. Including me. The Greeks and Romans had a jolly good shot at it, but they certainly didn’t use a term as vague and nebulous as ‘rhetorical question’. They distinguished between every different sort of rhetorical question. And then they gave them names. They had erotesis, hypophora, epiplexis, anthypophora, antiphora, apocrisis, interrogatio, rogatio, subjectio, ratiocinatio, dianoea, erotema, epitemesis, percontatio, aporia, and pysma. Isn’t that a lot? And each term had a slightly different and very specific meaning. Unfortunately they could never agree what those meanings were, and how one differed from the others, and just when they were getting close they declined, fell, and were overrun by barbarians.

坦白说，我们大多数人都不知道。包括我。希腊人和罗马人曾经很想解决这个问题，但他们肯定不会使用像“反问句”这样模糊不清的术语。他们区分了各种不同的反问句，并给它们起了名字。他们有：erotesis、hypophora、epiplexis、anthypophora、antiphora、apocrisis、interrogatio、rogatio、subjectio、ratiocinatio、dianoea、erotema、epitemesis、percontatio、aporia 和 pysma。是不是很多？而且每个术语都有略微不同且非常具体的含义。可惜的是，他们始终无法就这些含义达成一致，也无法明确它们之间的区别。就在他们即将达成共识的时候，他们衰落了，最终被蛮族征服。

Just to give you an idea of how complicated this all is, the same rhetorical question can be completely different depending on where it’s asked. Take the question, ‘Which party cares about what’s best for Britain?’ This might be asked by a Labour leader at a rally of Labour supporters and get the answer ‘Labour!’ Or it might be asked by the Conservative leader at a rally of Conservative supporters and get the answer ‘Conservative!’ (Both of these would be anacoenosis.) Or it might be asked by a solemn and reasonable chap on the telly, who would proceed to weigh up the pros and cons (anthypophora), or it might be asked by a confused chap in the tearful privacy of the polling booth (aporia). And then everything gets more confused if you write the question down in a book, because that way the author doesn’t know who’s answering.

为了让你们明白这有多复杂，同一个反问句在不同的场合可能会产生截然不同的结果。比如，“哪个政党真正关心英国的利益？”这个问题，可能是工党领袖在工党支持者的集会上提出的，得到的答案是“工党！”。也可能是保守党领袖在保守党支持者的集会上提出的，得到的答案是“保守党！”（这两种情况都属于反问）。或者，这个问题也可能是由一位严肃理性的电视主持人提出的，他会权衡利弊（反问），或者是由一位困惑的选民在投票站里泪流满面地提出的（困惑）。如果把这个问题写在书里，情况就更复杂了，因为这样作者就不知道是谁在回答了。

Shall we begin with erotesis? That’s the sort of question that really isn’t a question at all. ‘Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?’ asked Shakespeare, and did not wait for a reply. Fun as it may be to imagine him sending the first line of that sonnet off to his beloved and, a couple of days later, getting the answer, ‘Go ahead’, I don’t think that’s what happened. The line could just as easily be: ‘I shall compare thee to a summer’s day. / Thou art more lovely and more temperate …’ but it wouldn’t sound as good. The same thing pretty much holds for William Blake’s poem about the ancient and preposterous belief that Jesus, before starting his ministry, took a gap year in England.

我们先从情色描写说起吧？这其实根本算不上一个问题。“我能否将你比作夏日？”莎士比亚问道，并未等待回复。想象一下他把这首十四行诗的第一句寄给心爱之人，几天后收到“请便”的回信，或许很有趣，但我并不认为事情就是这样发生的。这句诗完全可以写成：“我将你比作夏日。/你比夏日更可爱，更温和……”，但听起来就没那么妙了。威廉·布莱克那首关于耶稣在开始传道之前曾在英国度过间隔年的诗歌，也同样如此。

And did those feet in ancient time

那些脚在古代也曾存在过吗？

Walk upon England’s mountains green?

漫步在英格兰翠绿的山峦间？

Again, we might be tempted to say no. But that would be to miss the point. ‘And did those feet’ simply sounds better than ‘And those feet did’.

我们或许会忍不住说不。但这就忽略了重点。“And did those feet”听起来比“And those feet did”要好得多。

This is the purest form of the rhetorical question, where a couple of words have been switched around and a question mark slapped on the end. It’s also a form much loved by Australians. When asked in the Antipodes, ‘How bright is the sun?’, ‘How cute is that koala?’ or ‘How close is that great white shark?’, no answer is required. A question is just their upside-down way of making a statement.

这是最纯粹的反问句形式，只需将几个词顺序颠倒，最后加上一个问号即可。澳大利亚人也特别喜欢这种形式。在南半球，如果你问“太阳有多亮？”、“那只考拉有多可爱？”或者“那条大白鲨离我有多近？”，他们不需要回答。对他们来说，问句只是表达观点的一种颠倒方式。

Epiplexis is a more specific form of this where a lament or an insult is asked as a question. What’s the point? Why go on? What’s a girl to do? How could you? What makes your heart so hard? When, in the Bible, Job asks: ‘Why died I not from the womb? why did I not give up the ghost when I came out of the belly?’, it’s not a real question. It’s epiplexis. Epiplexis is the puzzled grief of ‘Why, God? Why?’ in Miss Saigon ; or it is the bemused disdain in the film Heathers that prompts the question: ‘Did you have a brain tumour for breakfast?’

情绪崩溃（Epiplexis）是一种更特殊的表现形式，它将哀叹或侮辱以疑问句的形式提出。这有什么意义？为什么还要继续？一个女孩该怎么办？你怎么能这样？是什么让你的心如此冷酷无情？当《圣经》中的约伯问道：“我为何没有在母胎中死去？我为何没有在出母胎时就断气？”时，这并非一个真正的问题，而是情绪崩溃。情绪崩溃体现在《西贡小姐》中那句困惑的悲痛：“为什么，上帝？为什么？”；又体现在电影《希瑟斯》中那句令人困惑的轻蔑，引出“你早餐是不是吃了脑瘤？”这样的质问。

Though epiplexis doesn’t have a real answer, it does at least have a meaning and a purpose.

虽然上脉络丛没有真正的答案，但它至少具有意义和目的。

Anacoenosis, as we saw above, is the sort of question where a particular audience will answer in a particular way. The Beatles did a song called ‘Why Don’t We Do It In The Road?’ 1 in which fifteen of the eighteen lines are all ‘Why don’t we do it in the road?’

正如我们前面看到的，共生关系（Anacoenosis）这类问题，特定的受众会以特定的方式作答。披头士乐队有一首歌叫《为什么不在路上做？》（Why Don't We Do It In The Road?）¹，其中十八句歌词中有十五句都是“为什么不在路上做？”

Now if Paul McCartney were to ask me that question, I would have a stack of answers. But we must assume that he’s not asking me. He’s asking her (whoever she may be). And she can’t think of one good reason. Well … maybe one. She may have planned to object that somebody might be watching them. Luckily Mr McCartney has foreseen this objection and the remaining three lines assure her that nobody will be observing (foreseeing and answering a possible objection is a rhetorical device called procatalepsis).

如果保罗·麦卡特尼问我这个问题，我肯定能给出一大堆答案。但我们必须假设他问的不是我，而是她（不管她是谁）。而她想不出一个合理的理由。嗯……或许有一个。她可能原本打算反驳说有人在监视他们。幸运的是，麦卡特尼先生预料到了这种反驳，接下来的三行歌词向她保证不会有人监视他们（预见并回应可能的反驳是一种修辞手法，称为“预先回答”）。

The thing about anacoenosis is that it makes us realise how much we have in common. We both want to do it in the road. We can both see no serious practical obstacles to doing it in the road. I don’t need to tell you how close we are. I can simply ask you questions and we will both know that we have the same answer. 2

共生关系的奇妙之处在于，它让我们意识到彼此有多少共同之处。我们都想在路上实现这个目标。我们都看不到在路上实现这个目标在实际操作上有什么重大障碍。我无需赘述我们之间的距离有多近。我只需问你一些问题，我们就能知道答案是一致的。

This appeal to shared interests makes politicians particularly fond of anacoenosis. The voter hears the question and automatically gets to the answer that the politician wants. Who do you trust to run the economy? Would you buy a used car from this man? Why don’t we pass a law to stop libidinous Liverpudlians from obstructing traffic? All these are anacoenosis because all these questions bring out our shared values. Or they’re supposed to. Monty Python 3 had great fun in Life of Brian with the failed anacoenosis of ‘What have the Romans ever done for us?’ The question is intended as a binding anacoenosis, but unfortunately the audience keep answering until the question has to be restated as: ‘All right, apart from the sanitation, medicine, education, wine, public order, irrigation, roads, the fresh water system and public health, what have the Romans ever done for us?’ They could have got round this with a good bit of hypophora.

这种诉诸共同利益的策略使得政客们格外钟爱“利益冲突论证”（anacoenosis）。选民一听到问题，就会不假思索地给出政客想要的答案。你信任谁来管理经济？你会从这个人手里买二手车吗？为什么我们不立法禁止利物浦那些好色之徒阻碍交通？所有这些都是利益冲突论证，因为这些问题旨在揭示我们的共同价值观。或者说，它们本应如此。在《布莱恩的一生》中，蒙提·派森三部曲就曾用“罗马人究竟为我们做过什么？”这个失败的利益冲突论证玩得不亦乐乎。这个问题原本意在引发一场具有约束力的利益冲突，但不幸的是，观众们不断地回答，直到问题不得不被重新表述为：“好吧，除了卫生、医疗、教育、葡萄酒、公共秩序、灌溉、道路、淡水系统和公共卫生之外，罗马人究竟为我们做过什么？”他们本可以用一些巧妙的“反问”（hypophora）来解决这个问题。

Hypophora is a rhetorical question that is immediately answered aloud, usually by the person who asked. When A Tribe Called Quest recorded the song ‘Can I Kick It?’, they did not wait for an answer. Instead, the chorus immediately comes back with the reassuring words Yes, you can . No suspicion is allowed to slip into the listener’s mind concerning the capabilities of the asker’s legs, or the kickability of It (whatever It is). They are, at least, a little more succinct than Elizabeth Barrett Browning, who asked, ‘How do I love thee? Let me count the ways’, and then spent thirteen lines on her reply.

反问句是一种会立即大声回答的反问句，通常由提问者本人回答。例如，当A Tribe Called Quest录制歌曲《Can I Kick It?》时，他们并没有等待答案。相反，副歌部分立刻用令人安心的歌词回应：“是的，你可以。” 听众不会对提问者的腿力或“它”（无论它是什么）是否能踢产生任何怀疑。至少，他们比伊丽莎白·巴雷特·勃朗宁要简洁得多。勃朗宁曾问道：“我该如何爱你？让我细数”，然后用了十三行诗句来回答这个问题。

Can you go beyond hypophora? You can. What’s that called? Anthypophora. Where is it used? In the nursery rhyme ‘Who Killed Cock Robin?’ Where else? Well, Winston Churchill rather liked it at times of crisis. When he addressed Parliament on 13 May 1940, with the British army nearly defeated in France and the question of whether to surrender to Germany still being asked, he dodged everything by asking his own questions.

你能超越隐喻吗？当然可以。那叫什么？反喻。它用在哪里？童谣《谁杀了知更鸟？》里。还有哪里？嗯，温斯顿·丘吉尔在危机时刻很喜欢用这招。1940年5月13日，英国军队在法国几乎战败，是否向德国投降的问题仍然悬而未决。丘吉尔在议会发表讲话时，通过提出自己的问题巧妙地回避了所有问题。

You ask, what is our policy? I will say it is to wage war, by sea, land, and air, with all our might and all the strength that God can give us; to wage war against a monstrous tyranny, never surpassed in the dark, lamentable catalogue of human crime. That is our policy.

你问，我们的政策是什么？我会说，我们的政策就是用尽全力，动用上帝赐予我们的一切力量，从海、陆、空三个方向发动战争；向一个残暴的暴政宣战，这个暴政在人类罪恶的黑暗篇章中前所未有，令人发指。这就是我们的政策。

You ask, what is our aim? I can answer in one word: Victory. Victory at all costs, victory in spite of all terror; victory, however long and hard the road may be, for without victory, there is no survival.

你问，我们的目标是什么？我可以用一个词来回答：胜利。不惜一切代价取得胜利，克服一切恐惧取得胜利；无论道路多么漫长艰难，都要取得胜利，因为没有胜利，就没有生存。

Falstaff has a rather more cowardly go at it in Henry IV Part 1 . He’s wondering whether it’s worthwhile to die in battle and his reasoning goes thus:

在《亨利四世》第一部中，福斯塔夫的思考方式则显得更加懦弱。他犹豫着是否值得战死沙场，他的理由如下：

Well, ’tis no matter; honour pricks [spurs] me on. Yea, but how if honour prick me off when I come on? how then? Can honour set to a leg? no: or an arm? no: or take away the grief of a wound? no. Honour hath no skill in surgery, then? no. What is honour? a word. What is in that word honour? What is that honour? air. A trim reckoning! Who hath it? he that died o’ Wednesday. Doth he feel it? no. Doth he hear it? no. ’Tis insensible, then. Yea, to the dead. But will it not live with the living? no. Why? detraction will not suffer it. Therefore I’ll none of it. Honour is a mere scutcheon: and so ends my catechism.

好吧，这无关紧要；荣誉激励我前行。是啊，但如果荣誉在我前进时反而让我退缩呢？那该怎么办？荣誉能接好腿吗？不能。能接好胳膊吗？不能。能消除伤痛吗？不能。那么，荣誉没有医术吗？没有。荣誉是什么？一个词。荣誉这个词里有什么？荣誉是什么？空气。一针见血！谁拥有它？星期三死去的那个人。他能感觉到它吗？不能。他能听到它吗？不能。那么，它是无知的。是的，对死人来说是这样。但它难道不能与生者同在吗？不能。为什么？因为诽谤容不下它。因此，我什么也不要。荣誉不过是一块盾牌：我的教义问答到此结束。

A catechism is a series of questions and answers about religion that you have to memorise. Once you’ve got the whole thing by rote, a stern and solemn priest will test you on your catechism. He reads out the questions and you recite the responses. Of course, the priest knows the answers already, he just wants to hear you say them.

教理问答是一系列关于宗教的问答，需要背诵。当你把所有内容都背得滚瓜烂熟之后，一位严肃的牧师会考查你的教理问答。他会读出问题，你需要复述答案。当然，牧师其实早就知道答案，他只是想听你背诵而已。

This is partly because you should really know about the true nature of God and all that sort of stuff. It would be terrible to end up a heretic by mistake. But there’s also something immensely powerful, something satisfying in a megalomaniacal, egocentric way, about forcing somebody to answer a question when you both know the answer already. Teachers do it. Policemen do it. Traffic policemen always bloody do it. ‘Is there any particular reason that you were doing 123mph … sir?’

部分原因是，你确实应该了解上帝的真谛以及诸如此类的事情。万一误打误撞成了异端，那就太糟糕了。但强迫别人回答一个你们都心知肚明的问题，也会带来一种极其强大的快感，一种自大狂式的满足感。老师会这么做。警察会这么做。交警总是会这么做。“先生，您当时的车速是123英里/小时，请问有什么特别的原因吗？”

And then they wait for an answer.

然后他们等待答复。

‘Did you think that the speed limit didn’t apply to you?’

“你以为限速规定对你无效吗？”

And so on and so forth. The point of all this is not so that the copper in question can learn more about your motivations and beliefs. They lack such psychoanalytic curiosity. That’s why they’re traffic policemen. By making you answer a question to which they already know the answer, they are asserting their authority, and belittling yours. That’s also why they’re traffic policemen. That’s also why such a series of questions is called subjectio.

诸如此类，不胜枚举。这一切的目的并非为了让交警了解你的动机和信仰。他们缺乏这种心理分析式的好奇心。正因如此，他们才被称为交警。通过让你回答他们早已知晓答案的问题，他们是在维护自身的权威，贬低你的权威。这也是他们被称为交警的原因。也正因如此，这类问题才被称为“主观性盘问”。

It’s a trick of which Mr Quentin Tarantino is inordinately fond and it makes myriad appearances in Pulp Fiction . There are subjectios about foot massages, Fonzies and driving. Subjectio is the centre of two of the most famous scenes. First, there is the great subjectio that begins, ‘What does Marsellus Wallace look like?’ To which, after a little shooting and stammering, we get the answer that he’s black. Then that he’s bald. And then comes the famous poser of: ‘Does Marsellus Wallace look like a bitch?’

昆汀·塔伦蒂诺先生对这种技巧情有独钟，在《低俗小说》中更是屡见不鲜。片中充斥着各种关于足底按摩、方兹（Fonzie）和驾驶的提问。其中两个最著名的场景都围绕着提问展开。首先，有一个经典的提问，开头是“马塞勒斯·华莱士长什么样？”。经过一番射击和结结巴巴的回答后，我们得知他是黑人。然后又得知他是秃头。接下来就是那个著名的提问：“马塞勒斯·华莱士长得像个娘们儿吗？”

It is clear both from the baldness and the general context that Marsellus Wallace does not in the slightest bit resemble a bitch. And even someone who has never seen the film will already suspect that it’s a mix-up rarely made. It’s also clear that everybody in the room already knows exactly what Mr Wallace looks like. But the poor chap is made, with some more shooting, to answer in the negative. Which is how we come to the climactic question of the subjectio: ‘Then why you trying to fuck him like a bitch?’

从秃顶和整体氛围来看，马塞勒斯·华莱士显然一点也不像个娘们儿。即使是没看过这部电影的人，也会觉得这绝对是个罕见的误会。显然，房间里的每个人都知道华莱士先生长什么样。但可怜的家伙却被迫在几轮枪战后否认这一点。这就引出了影片的高潮问题：“那你为什么要像对待娘们儿一样操他？”

Is it possible to pigeonhole every type of rhetorical question? Not quite. Which is, perhaps, why the Ancients thought up so many terms to such little effect. Take this intricate enquiry from Inspector Harry Callahan (unwashed):

能否将所有类型的反问句都归类？恐怕不能。或许正因如此，古人创造了那么多词汇，却收效甚微。就拿哈里·卡拉汉探长（邋遢鬼）提出的这个错综复杂的问题来说吧：

I know what you’re thinking, punk. You’re thinking ‘Did he fire six shots or only five?’ Now to tell you the truth I forgot myself in all this excitement. But being this is a .44 Magnum, the most powerful handgun in the world, and will blow your head clean off, you’ve got to ask yourself a question: ‘Do I feel lucky?’ Well, do you, punk?

我知道你在想什么，小子。你在想“他开了六枪还是五枪？”说实话，我当时太兴奋了，都忘了自己是谁了。但这是.44马格南，世界上威力最大的手枪，能把你脑袋打爆，你得问问自己：“我今天走运吗？”怎么样，小子？

Inspector Callahan was a master of the combined rhetorical question. There seems to be an anthypophora, but it remains unanswered so you could call it an erotesis. And then there’s the appeal to the interests of the audience (presuming that they are interested in not getting their heads blown clean off), which would be an odd sort of anacoenosis. And then we seem to end with a subjectio where he requires an answer. But even then there is ambiguity, because this line is used twice: at the beginning of the film and at the end of the film.

卡拉汉探长是运用复合反问句的高手。这里似乎存在一个隐含疑问句，但由于没有给出答案，所以也可以称之为反问。此外，他还诉诸观众的利益（假设他们不想被爆头），这算是一种奇特的反问。最后，他似乎又提出了一个需要回答的疑问句。但即便如此，仍然存在歧义，因为这句话出现了两次：一次在影片开头，一次在影片结尾。

At the beginning there is a bank robbery and, after some exciting shooting, all that’s left is Harry Callahan with his maybe loaded .44 Magnum in his hand and a bank robber with a definitely loaded shotgun just within reach. Mr Callahan weaves his web of questions and the poor bank robber, of course, decides that he is not feeling lucky. Thus it is subjectio.

故事开头是一起银行抢劫案，经过一番激烈的枪战后，只剩下哈里·卡拉汉，手里拿着一把可能已经上膛的.44马格南手枪，而一名银行劫匪则拿着一把肯定已经上膛的霰弹枪，触手可及。卡拉汉先生开始抛出一连串的问题，而可怜的银行劫匪自然觉得自己运气不佳。于是，事情就此展开。

At the end of the film Mr Callahan is faced with an almost identical situation, except that the role of the bank robber is now being filled by a giggling psychopath. Callahan repeats his lines word for word; and the killer leaps for the gun.

影片结尾，卡拉汉先生面临着几乎相同的局面，只不过这次银行劫匪的角色换成了一个咯咯怪笑的变态杀手。卡拉汉一字不差地重复着他的台词；杀手随即扑向了枪。

So perhaps this is also a case of aporia.

所以，这或许也是一种困境。

Sometimes, people ask questions because they actually don’t know the answer. This works rhetorically. When Hamlet asks ‘To be or not to be’ he doesn’t just come down with a hypophoric ‘To be!’ Instead, he stops and thinks. He restates the question as a choice between suffering slings and arrows or taking arms. Then he lists the good points of death (ending heartaches and natural shocks). Then he sees death’s one bad point (the afterlife, the fear of something after death). Then he comes to a sort of conclusion that as we don’t know what happens when you die, it ain’t worth the risk. 4

有时，人们提出问题，是因为他们确实不知道答案。这在修辞上很有效。当哈姆雷特问“生存还是毁灭”时，他并没有直接回答“生存！”。相反，他停下来思考。他把问题重新表述为在忍受箭雨和拿起武器之间做出选择。然后，他列举了死亡的好处（结束痛苦和自然灾害）。接着，他看到了死亡的唯一弊端（来世，对死后世界的恐惧）。最后，他得出了一个结论：既然我们不知道死后会发生什么，那么冒险就得不偿失。<sup>4</sup>

Asking a question when you really don’t know the answer is called aporia. It is the moment of doubt, when you’re really not sure whether to top yourself.

当你真的不知道答案时提出问题，这叫做困惑。这是充满怀疑的时刻，你真的不确定是否应该结束自己的生命。

The same sorts of doubt assailed poor Mr Presley when he sang ‘Are You Lonesome Tonight?’, a song whose melodic section consists only of rhetorical aporias. 5 Here, we must suppose that he really wants an answer. If she is lonesome tonight and her memory does stray to bright and osculatory summer days, then he’s a happy man. If on the other hand she’s got plenty of company tonight thank you very much, he’s in trouble. Here, there is an answer, we just don’t know what it is. How do you do what you do to me? Will you still love me tomorrow? Who’s that girl running around with you?

可怜的猫王在演唱《今夜你是否寂寞？》时，也饱受同样的疑惑。这首歌的旋律部分完全由一系列修辞性的困惑构成。⁵ 在这里，我们必须假设他真的想要一个答案。如果她今夜寂寞，思绪飘回到阳光灿烂、充满亲吻的夏日，那么他就是幸福的。但如果她今夜有许多人陪伴，那他就麻烦了。答案其实是有的，只是我们不知道是什么。你怎么能让我如此心动？明天你还会爱我吗？和你在一起的那个女孩是谁？

And finally, there is the sort of rhetorical question that Bob Dylan used in ‘Blowin’ in the Wind’; the sort where there is no answer, the sort where the questioner does not know the answer, does not expect anyone else to know the answer, and does not expect to be informed. Bob Dylan knows that the answer, my friend, is blowing in the breeze; but he asks anyway. He does not expect to find how many roads a man must walk down. Anyway, it would probably depend on the length and location of the roads, not to mention all the trouble of whether a street, alleyway or bridlepath can be taken into the count.

最后，还有一种反问句，鲍勃·迪伦在《答案在风中飘扬》里就用过；这种问句没有答案，提问者自己也不知道答案，不指望别人知道答案，也不指望得到答案。鲍勃·迪伦知道答案，我的朋友，就在微风中飘扬；但他还是问了。他并不指望能找到一个人要走多少条路。再说，这可能还取决于路的长度和位置，更别提街道、小巷或马道是否也算在内了。

The same goes for William Blake’s ponderings on the Panthera tigris , which go well beyond those of most naturalists. The poem does not have a full stop. It is all questions from beginning to end. But just as a prayer is a request to which you would be surprised to receive a yes or no, so Blake did not seriously expect a tiger to write him a letter answering the question:

威廉·布莱克对老虎的思考也是如此，远远超出了大多数博物学家的范畴。这首诗没有句号，从头到尾都是疑问句。但正如祈祷是一种请求，你不会指望得到肯定或否定的答复一样，布莱克也并非真的指望老虎会给他写信回答这个问题：

Tiger, tiger, burning bright

虎，虎，燃烧的光芒

In the forests of the night,

在夜幕下的森林里，

What immortal hand or eye

何等不朽之手或眼

Dare frame thy fearful symmetry?

你敢描绘你那令人畏惧的对称之美吗？

Though ‘forests of the night’ is a nice example of hendiadys. Probably.

虽然《夜之森林》是谐音双关语的一个很好的例子。大概吧。

1 Lennon/McCartney.

1 列侬/麦卡特尼。

2 Although, to be fair, I would add in the uncomfortable nature of asphalt and the danger of passing traffic: two objections missed in McCartney’s procatalepsis.

2 不过，公平地说，我还要补充一点，沥青路面的不舒适性以及过往车辆的危险性：麦卡特尼的倒叙中忽略了这两个反对意见。

3 By which I mean Graham Chapman, John Cleese, Terry Gilliam, Eric Idle, Terry Jones and Michael Palin.

3 我指的是格雷厄姆·查普曼、约翰·克里斯、特里·吉列姆、埃里克·艾德尔、特里·琼斯和迈克尔·帕林。

4 This is rather peculiar, as in Act I Hamlet’s dad had appeared to him and explained exactly what happens after death, thus making Hamlet’s great speech completely inconsistent with the plot of the play.

4 这相当奇怪，因为在第一幕中，哈姆雷特的父亲曾向他解释死后究竟会发生什么，因此哈姆雷特的伟大演讲与该剧的情节完全不符。

5 The original recording of the song by Vaughan DeLeath in 1927 contains some explanatory verses. Elvis, though, cut these and sang entirely in questions. The original version does not contain the execrable spoken section.

5. 沃恩·德利斯 (Vaughan DeLeath) 于 1927 年录制的这首歌原版包含一些解释性的歌词。然而，埃尔维斯·普雷斯利 (Elvis Presley) 删掉了这些歌词，完全以问句的形式演唱。原版中并没有那段糟糕的口白。

# ↩

Chapter 14

第十四章

Hendiadys

亨迪亚迪斯

Hendiadys (pronounced hen-DIE-a-dis) is the most elusive and tricky of all rhetorical tricks. Mostly because you can never be sure whether it’s happened.

亨迪亚迪斯（发音为 hen-DIE-a-dis）是所有修辞技巧中最难以捉摸、最狡猾的一种。主要是因为你永远无法确定它是否真的发生过。

The principle of hendiadys is easy. You take an adjective and a noun, and then you change the adjective into another noun. So instead of saying ‘I’m going to the noisy city’ you say ‘I’m going to the noise and the city’. Instead of saying ‘I walked through the rainy morning’ you say ‘I walked through the rain and the morning’. Got it? The adjective-noun noisy-city becomes the noun-and-noun noise and city . Instead of saying ‘I love your beautiful eyes’ you say ‘I love your beauty and eyes’.

词形变化的原理很简单。取一个形容词和一个名词，然后把形容词变成另一个名词。所以，与其说“我要去喧闹的城市”，不如说“我要去喧闹的城市”。与其说“我走过雨中的早晨”，不如说“我走过雨和早晨”。明白了吗？形容词-名词组合“喧闹的城市”变成了名词-名词组合“喧闹的城市”。与其说“我爱你美丽的眼睛”，不如说“我爱你的美丽和眼睛”。

But here’s the problem. The writer knows that beauty and eyes meant beautiful eyes . But the reader doesn’t know that. The poor reader might think that ‘I love your beauty and eyes’ means ‘I love your beauty in general and your eyes in particular’.

但问题就在这里。作者知道“美丽”和“眼睛”指的是美丽的眼睛，但读者却不知道。可怜的读者可能会误以为“我喜欢你的美貌和眼睛”的意思是“我喜欢你的整体美貌，尤其喜欢你的眼睛”。

So when Saint Paul told the Philippians to ‘work out your salvation with fear and trembling’, it’s probably a hendiadys for fearful trembling , but it might be a hendiadys for trembling fear . And there’s at least the possibility that he really did mean both with fear and with trembling , and wasn’t using hendiadys at all.

所以，当圣保罗告诉腓立比人“当恐惧战兢地作成你们得救的工夫”时，这很可能是一个表示恐惧战兢的双关语，但也可能是表示战兢恐惧的双关语。当然，也有可能他确实既指恐惧战兢，也指战兢战兢，而根本没有使用双关语。

Is law and order a hendiadys? It looks damned like it, but I would hate to say for certain. What about rough and tumble ? House and home ? To say for certain that something is hendiadys you have to be certain about what the writer thought in the first place. It may be that God has a glorious powerful kingdom, but Jesus actually said: ‘For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory’. 1

“法律与秩序”是双关语吗？看起来很像，但我不敢妄下断言。“粗暴冲突”呢？“家与家庭”呢？要断言某事物是双关语，首先必须确定作者最初的意图。或许上帝拥有一个荣耀而强大的国度，但耶稣实际上说过：“因为国度、权柄、荣耀，全是你的。”¹

Summertime living is easy. But Summertime and the living is easy doesn’t necessarily have to be hendiadys. It just looks very, very like it.

夏日生活轻松惬意。但“夏日”和“生活轻松惬意”这两个词未必是谐音梗。它们看起来确实很像。

There’s also a variant form of hendiadys where adverb-adjective becomes adjective-adjective. If your tea is nice and hot and my champagne is nice and chilled, those would both appear to be hendiadyses for nicely hot and nicely chilled. But there is the possibility that my champagne is both nice – of good quality – and has been properly chilled.

还有一种变体形式的副词-形容词结构，其中副词-形容词变成了形容词-形容词。如果你的茶又热又香，我的香槟又冰又爽，这两者都像是“热得恰到好处”和“冰得恰到好处”的副词-形容词结构。但也有可能我的香槟既好喝（品质上乘），又冰镇得恰到好处。

There’s also (some would say) the double verb form where you try and do something rather than trying to do something or go and see somebody rather than going to see them . And I would cheerily say that the forests of the night in which William Blake’s tiger was burning bright are a hendiadys for forests at night. 2 But without summoning Mr Blake up from the dead, I’ll never be able to prove it.

还有一种（有人会说的）双动词形式，比如“try and do something”而不是“trying to do something”，或者“go and see someone”而不是“going to see them”。我会兴高采烈地说，威廉·布莱克笔下那只燃烧着明亮火焰的夜之森林，正是夜之森林的一首双行诗。² 但除非布莱克先生死而复生，否则我永远无法证明这一点。

Another odd thing about hendiadys is that it’s either common as muck or as rare as gold. Lots of everyday forgettable phrases use it ( be a good fellow and close the door is not two commands). But almost no great writers do, except Shakespeare. Those lines listed above are almost the only examples in English literature, outside Shakespeare. And Shakespeare really only used it for a few years. But those were the few years when he wrote Hamlet , Othello , Macbeth , Antony and Cleopatra and King Lear . That was the great period.

双关语的另一个奇特之处在于，它要么极其常见，要么极其罕见。许多日常琐碎的短语都使用了双关语（比如“做个好人”和“关上门”并非两条命令）。但除了莎士比亚之外，几乎没有伟大的作家使用双关语。上面列举的那些句子几乎是莎士比亚之外的英语文学中仅有的例子。而莎士比亚也只在短短几年内使用过双关语。但这几年正是他创作《哈姆雷特》、《奥赛罗》、《麦克白》、《安东尼与克莉奥佩特拉》和《李尔王》的时期。那正是他创作的黄金时代。

In Shakespeare’s early works hendiadys barely appears. Maybe popping up once or twice a play. Then, in about 1599, Shakespeare appears to have had a moment and a revelation. He suddenly decided that hendiadys was his favourite form. You can draw a graph of the frequency 3 and watch it leap up, peak, plateau, and drop away in what’s usually called his late (and not great) period. Now, I’m not arguing that hendiadys was the only thing that made those five tragedies great, but it’s worth noting that that’s when he used the rhetorical form. Hamlet is the top play, where he averages a hendiadys every 60 or so lines. ‘Angels and ministers of grace defend us!’ shouts Hamlet, when he really means ‘Angelic ministers of grace’. But obviously the first thing you do when you see the ghost of your dead father is employ a bit of hendiadys. Hamlet’s father doesn’t mind; he’s been too busy with the ‘sulphurous and tormenting flames’ of purgatory (by which he means tormentingly sulphurous ). Hamlet notes all this down in the ‘book and volume’ of his brain. This could mean voluminous book or bookish volume – that’s one of the wonderful things about hendiadys: it confuses things. It takes something that might have been clear as an azure lake in spring and muddies it. An English teacher will tell you that The Purpose Of The Adjective Is To Describe The Noun. One does a job for the other. Not in hendiadys and not in Shakespeare. Here you just get the nouns lined up, one beside the other, and though they’re holding hands, you can’t tell which is in charge. ‘The morn and liquid dew of youth’ is beautiful, but bewildering. So is ‘the grace and blush of modesty’, and ‘the dead vast and middle of the night’.

在莎士比亚的早期作品中，双行句几乎从未出现过，或许每部剧只出现一两次。然而，大约在1599年，莎士比亚似乎突然顿悟，认定双行句是他最喜欢的修辞形式。你可以绘制一张图表来观察双行句出现频率的变化³，你会发现它在通常被称为他晚期（也是他不太伟大的时期）的阶段，经历了跃升、达到顶峰、趋于平稳，然后又逐渐下降。当然，我并不是说双行句是那五部悲剧伟大之处的唯一原因，但值得注意的是，正是在那个时期，他开始运用这种修辞手法。《哈姆雷特》是其中最杰出的剧作，平均每60行左右就会出现一个双行句。哈姆雷特高喊着“天使和恩典的使者保佑我们！”，而他真正的意思是“天使般的恩典使者”。但很显然，当你看到亡父的鬼魂时，你首先会做的就是运用一些双行句。哈姆雷特的父亲并不在意；他一直忙于炼狱中“硫磺灼热的火焰”（他指的是令人痛苦的硫磺味）。哈姆雷特把这一切都记在了他脑中的“书卷”里。这可以指浩瀚的书卷，也可以指书卷——这就是并列句的奇妙之处：它让人困惑。它把原本像春天蔚蓝湖泊般清晰的事物弄得浑浊不堪。英语老师会告诉你，形容词的作用是描述名词。一个词为另一个词服务。但在并列句中并非如此，在莎士比亚的作品中也并非如此。在这里，名词只是并排排列，虽然它们手牵着手，但你却无法分辨谁才是主导者。“青春的清晨和露珠”很美，但也令人费解。所以，“谦逊的优雅和羞涩”，以及“死寂的浩瀚和午夜”。

And, of course, many times you can’t quite work out if it’s a hendiadys or not. Is it nobler in the mind to suffer the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, or were they really the slung arrows, the arrows that fortune had hurled? Is flesh heir to ‘the heartache and the thousand natural shocks’ or to a thousand natural and heart-aching shocks? Do we bear ‘the whips and scorns of time’ or the scornful whips? Shakespeare was so frantic and keen on hendiadys when he was writing Hamlet that it could be lurking almost anywhere.

当然，很多时候你很难分辨它是否属于双关语。承受命运无情的打击是否更高尚？或者，那些打击本身就是命运抛出的箭矢？肉体承受的是“心痛和千百种自然的冲击”，还是千百种自然的和令人心碎的冲击？我们承受的是“时间的鞭笞和轻蔑”，还是轻蔑的鞭笞？莎士比亚在创作《哈姆雷特》时对双关语如此痴迷，以至于它几乎无处不在。

Hendiadys is hidden all over Shakespeare’s great plays. It’s in King Lear where Edmund says, ‘I have told you what I have seen and heard; but faintly, nothing like the image and horror of it’; and, most famously, in Macbeth , where life is a tale ‘Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury’. Whether Shakespeare was thinking of furious sound or sounding fury hardly signifies. The point and beauty of hendiadys is that it sets the words next to each other, that it removes the grammar and relation, that it doubles the words out to give breadth and beauty.

并列句（hendiadys）在莎士比亚的伟大剧作中随处可见。例如在《李尔王》中，埃德蒙说道：“我已将我所见所闻告诉你们，但只是模糊地描述，远不及当时的景象和恐怖。” 最著名的例子莫过于《麦克白》，其中人生被比作“一个白痴讲述的故事，充满了喧嚣与狂怒”。莎士比亚究竟指的是狂怒的喧嚣还是狂怒的咆哮，其实并不重要。并列句的精髓和魅力在于它将词语并置，打破了语法和关系，通过词语的重复，赋予其更广阔的视野和更优美的表达。

And then Shakespeare stopped using it. Nobody knows why, but hendiadys hardly appears in the late plays at all. Perhaps he thought better of it. Perhaps he got bored with it. Perhaps he regretted it. But for one little rhetorical trick to be the favourite of the greatest writer during his greatest period means that hendiadys has had its fifteen minutes and its fame.

后来莎士比亚就不再使用这种修辞手法了。没人知道为什么，但这种修辞手法在他晚期的剧作中几乎完全消失了。或许他觉得它不太合适，或许他厌倦了它，或许他后悔了。但对于一位最伟大的作家来说，在他创作的巅峰时期，这种小小的修辞技巧竟然成了他的最爱，这意味着这种修辞手法的辉煌和名声都已消逝殆尽。

Mind you, for my money, the greatest use of hendiadys isn’t by Shakespeare, but by Leonard Cohen in his song ‘Hallelujah’:

不过，依我之见，双关语运用得最精彩的并非莎士比亚，而是莱昂纳德·科恩在他的歌曲《哈利路亚》中：

You saw her bathing on the roof.

你看到她在屋顶上洗澡了。

Her beauty and the moonlight overthrew you.

她的美貌和月光让你神魂颠倒。

The ‘and’ where we might expect ‘in’ makes the hendiadys. And that whole song is, like so many songs, an extended example of epistrophe.

原本我们可能会期待“in”的地方却用了“and”，这就构成了双行诗。而且，整首歌，就像很多歌曲一样，都是尾韵的延伸范例。

1 Matthew’s Gospel is in Greek and Jesus would have been speaking Aramaic. But hendiadys was a common form in Greek – in fact, it’s a Greek word meaning ‘ two - for - one ’ – and the trick was also common in ancient Hebrew. So the possibility of hendiadys is definitely there.

1 马太福音是用希腊语写成的，而耶稣当时说的是亚兰语。但“hendiadys”在希腊语中是一种常见的形式——事实上，它本身就是一个希腊词，意思是“买一送一”——而且这种技巧在古代希伯来语中也很常见。因此，“hendiadys”的可能性是存在的。

2 Some would object to this and call it antiptosis instead. I don’t care. To English ears it sounds and feels just like a hendiadys, as, indeed, does ‘She walks in beauty, like the night’.

2 有些人会反对这种说法，称之为反句。我不在乎。对英国人来说，它听起来和感觉起来都像一首双行诗，就像“她行走在美中，如同黑夜”这句诗一样。

3 I have. I’m a lonely man. If you want to do your own you’ll just need George T. Wright’s essay ‘Hendiadys and Hamlet’. It’s in PMLA, 1981, Vol. 96, Issue 2. Use the table of figures for all Shakespeare’s plays in Appendix II. You can use it to impress your imaginary friends. You can also go for Schulze’s list (1908) or Kerl’s (1922), but only if you speak German.

3 我有。我是一个孤独的人。如果你想自己做，只需要乔治·T·赖特的论文《亨迪亚迪斯与哈姆雷特》。它发表在1981年《美国现代语言协会会刊》（PMLA）第96卷第2期上。使用附录二中莎士比亚所有戏剧的人物表。你可以用它来给你的假想朋友留下深刻印象。你也可以参考舒尔茨（1908）或克尔（1922）的列表，但前提是你会德语。

# ↩

Chapter 15

第十五章

Epistrophe

尾声

When you end each sentence with the same word, that’s epistrophe. When each clause has the same words at the end, that’s epistrophe. When you finish each paragraph with the same word, that’s epistrophe. Even when it’s a whole phrase or a whole sentence that you repeat, it’s still, providing the repetition comes at the end, epistrophe.

当每句话都以同一个词结尾时，那就是尾韵。当每个分句都以相同的词结尾时，那就是尾韵。当每个段落都以同一个词结尾时，那就是尾韵。即使重复的是整个短语或整个句子，只要重复的部分出现在结尾，它仍然是尾韵。

This means that half the songs ever written are just extended examples of epistrophe. Whether it’s Leonard Cohen ending every verse with hallelujah , Gershwin ending every clause with the man I love or Don McLean following each verse with a whole chorus of Bye, bye, Miss American Pie etc., that’s epistrophe. When the moon hits your eye like a big pizza pie, that’s also epistrophe because it always ends with amore.

这意味着，有一半的歌曲都是尾韵的延伸。无论是莱昂纳德·科恩每段歌词都以“哈利路亚”结尾，格什温每句歌词都以“我爱的人”结尾，还是唐·麦克林每段歌词后都接上一整段“拜拜，美国派小姐”之类的副歌，这些都是尾韵。当月亮像一块大披萨一样照耀你的眼睛时，这也是尾韵，因为它总是以“爱”结尾。

In music epistrophe is so common that we barely notice it or think about it. We’re all so familiar with the way songs work that we don’t see that they work in a particular way. Because epistrophe brings with it some quite definite feelings. Wherever you start you always come back to the same thing. Wherever Bob Dylan starts off, he always ends up out there on Highway 61. Whatever is said in the verse, you can be sure that come the chorus everybody in the whole cell block will continue to dance to the jailhouse rock.

在音乐中，尾韵如此常见，以至于我们几乎不会注意到它，也不会去思考它。我们都太熟悉歌曲的运作方式了，以至于看不到它们以某种特定的方式运作。因为尾韵本身就蕴含着一些非常明确的情感。无论你从哪里开始，最终都会回到同一个主题。鲍勃·迪伦无论从哪里开始，最终都会回到61号公路。无论歌词唱的是什么，你都可以肯定，到了副歌，整个牢房里的每个人都会继续随着监狱摇滚的节奏起舞。

Epistrophe is the trope of obsession. It’s the trope of emphasising one point again and again. And it’s the trope of not being able to escape that one conclusion, which is one of the reasons that songs are so suited to the idea of obsessive love, political certainty and other such unhealthy ideas. You can’t reason in an epistrophic pop song. You can’t seriously consider the alternatives, because the structure dictates that you’ll always end up at the same point, thinking about the same girl and giving peace a chance. Wherever you are in the world and whatever question Bob asks, you already know that you’ll be dancing in the street while the answer blows in the wind. It’s built into the structure. It’s epistrophe.

反复吟诵是一种执念的修辞手法。它反复强调同一个观点，让人无法摆脱最终的结论。这正是歌曲如此契合痴迷之爱、政治上的笃定以及其他类似不健康观念的原因之一。在一首反复吟诵的流行歌曲中，你无法进行理性思考。你无法认真考虑其他可能性，因为歌曲的结构决定了你最终总会回到同一个终点，想着同一个女孩，并试图寻求平静。无论你身处世界的哪个角落，无论鲍勃提出什么问题，你都早已知道，答案会在风中飘荡，而你却会在街头翩翩起舞。这早已融入歌曲的结构之中。这就是反复吟诵。

When the music stops, epistrophe can get a little more subtle. It can be merely emphatic, a kind of banging on the table, jabbing at the air for emphasis. That’s the sort that Abraham Lincoln used when he said ‘government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth’. I’m pretty sure that there would have been a hand gesture repeated for each people . The same goes for Othello as he says, ‘A fine woman! a fair woman! a sweet woman!’, or Shylock with, ‘I’ll have my bond! Speak not against my bond! / I have sworn an oath that I will have my bond.’ It’s also the sort of useful reminder when a witness promises to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. And it’s the sort of threatening bluster when, in The Treasure of the Sierra Madre , a bandit leader refuses to prove that he’s a policeman: ‘Badges? We ain’t got no badges. We don’t need no badges! I don’t have to show you any stinkin’ badges!’

当音乐停止时，尾声的运用会变得更加微妙。它可能仅仅是一种强调，一种敲击桌面、用手指戳空气来强调的方式。亚伯拉罕·林肯在说“民有、民治、民享的政府将永存”时就使用了这种手法。我确信，他当时会用手势来重复“人民”这个词。奥赛罗说“一位美丽的女子！一位美丽的女子！一位温柔的女子！”时也是如此，夏洛克说“我要我的保释金！不许违背我的保释金！/我已发誓我要我的保释金！”时也是如此。当证人承诺说出真相，全部真相，绝无虚假时，尾声也是一种有用的提醒。在《碧血金沙》中，当一个强盗头目拒绝证明自己是警察时，尾声也是一种威胁性的虚张声势：“警徽？我们没有徽章。我们不需要徽章！我没必要给你们看什么该死的徽章！

But those are the quick epistrophes, the single-clause epistrophes, the emphasis epistrophes. Epistrophe gets bigger and stronger the longer you delay it. Probably the most famous example of this in modern rhetoric is Barack Obama’s various epistrophic speeches, in which he always ended up with Yes we can . He leaves whole paragraphs of American history between them, but he always ends up with the same answer. Whatever the obstacle, whatever the objection, the answer is always the same. Yes we can. 1

但这些都是简短的结尾句，单句结尾句，强调结尾句。结尾句拖得越久，效果就越强。现代修辞中最著名的例子或许就是巴拉克·奥巴马的各种结尾句演讲，他总是以“是的，我们能做到”结尾。他会在结尾句之间穿插整段整段的美国历史，但最终的答案总是相同的。无论遇到什么障碍，无论遭到什么反对，答案始终如一：是的，我们能做到。¹

It’s the same hopeful, cheer-every-repetition formula that made the greatest speech in the 1939 novel The Grapes of Wrath by John Steinbeck:

这与约翰·斯坦贝克 1939 年的小说《愤怒的葡萄》中最伟大的演讲所采用的充满希望、每次重复都令人欢呼的模式如出一辙：

Wherever there’s a fight so hungry people can eat, I’ll be there. Wherever there’s a cop beating up a guy, I’ll be there. I’ll be in the way guys yell when they’re mad and – I’ll be in the way kids laugh when they’re hungry and they know supper’s ready. And when our folk eat the stuff they raise and live in the houses they build – why, I’ll be there.
