但这个双关语让我们更接近真正的悖论，因为它至少看起来像个悖论。奥斯卡·王尔德曾说“我们生活在一个非必需品才是我们唯一必需品的时代”，他虽然说的是实话，但却正朝着核心矛盾的方向迈进。对人类而言，奢侈品是必需品；而那些通常被称为必需品的东西，其实都可以舍弃。机遇是确定的，而活着只是死亡的缓慢过程。在这里，我们发现自己正努力探寻“一切的意义所在”，但却止步于此。即使是莎士比亚说的“我必须残忍才能仁慈”，也未能真正触及那个临界点。王尔德从未完全掌握那个引人入胜的矛盾，他从未说过任何不合逻辑或经不起推敲的话。他或许会为了好的悖论不惜一切代价，但他不会这么做。

The true paradox is one of the more peculiar points of rhetoric in its long war against reality. We will happily dream the impossible dream, even if logic and the laws of the universe say that it’s … impossible. The true paradox is arresting because it breaks all laws, but calming because that is so easy in language. It is easy to write that black is white, that up is down and that good is evil. It’s as easy as typing, and as difficult. I can’t do it, and I just did.

真正的悖论是修辞学在与现实的长期斗争中最奇特的一点。我们乐于做着不可能的梦，即使逻辑和宇宙法则都表明这是不可能的。真正的悖论之所以引人注目，是因为它打破了所有法则；但它又令人平静，因为用语言表达这种矛盾是如此容易。写出“黑即白”、“上即下”、“善即恶”很容易。这就像打字一样简单，也同样困难。我做不到，但我刚刚做到了。

But by breaking the laws of the universe, the true paradox lifts us out of it. The true paradox is, necessarily, a mystical moment, despite the fact that from a writer’s point of view it’s immensely easy. My fingers need only tap the keyboard for every cop to be a criminal and all the sinners saints. But the reader can meditate on the words for ever.

但真正的悖论，正是通过打破宇宙法则，将我们从中解脱出来。真正的悖论必然是一个神秘的时刻，尽管从作家的角度来看，它极其容易实现。我只需敲击键盘，就能让所有警察都变成罪犯，所有罪人都变成圣人。但读者却可以永远沉思这些文字。

It is easy, therefore, to see the true paradox as being false; as being an easy trick and therefore worthless. It is an easy trick, but it is in no way worthless. A well executed paradox stirs the soul and mixes language and philosophy in a way that no other figure does. Paul Simon was on to something when he titled his song ‘The Sound of Silence’, and his verse about people talking without speaking, and about people hearing without listening, was easy for him, but that makes it no less beautiful to us.

因此，人们很容易将真正的悖论视为虚假的，视为一种简单的技巧，因而毫无价值。它的确是一种简单的技巧，但绝非毫无价值。一个精心设计的悖论能够触动灵魂，将语言与哲学以其他任何方式都无法企及的方式融合在一起。保罗·西蒙将他的歌曲命名为《寂静之声》，他显然领悟到了其中的精髓。他歌词中关于人们不言而喻、不倾听却在聆听的描写，对他而言或许轻而易举，但这丝毫不影响它在我们心中的美。

The paradox is most at home in religion. Before Abraham was, I am. God’s service is perfect freedom. He is a circle whose centre is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere. These ideas may not be geometrically workable from an engineering point of view, but the ideas that they stir are of thought outside mere reality, and by their very operation on the human mind, they show themselves to have value, because such operation is itself proof, to have such thoughts is to prove that such thoughts can exist. And though that may not matter, it does.

这种悖论在宗教中体现得最为淋漓尽致。在亚伯拉罕之前，我已存在。侍奉上帝即是完全的自由。祂是一个圆，圆心无处不在，圆周却无处可寻。从工程学的角度来看，这些理念或许在几何上行不通，但它们所激发的思想超越了单纯的现实，并且它们在人类心灵中的作用本身就证明了自身的价值，因为这种作用本身就是一种证明——拥有这样的思想就证明了这样的思想是可以存在的。虽然这或许无关紧要，但实际上却至关重要。

So it is no surprise to us to hear paradoxes from the mouth of a mystic. We hear the words ‘The first shall be last, and the last shall be first’ and we react in a mystical way. Or at least, most chaps do; for myself I just consider it a good example of chiasmus.

所以，听到神秘主义者说出悖论，我们并不感到惊讶。我们听到“在前的将要在后，在后的将要在前”这句话，就会产生一种神秘的联想。至少大多数人会这样；而我个人则认为这只是一个交错结构的典型例子。

# ↩

Chapter 24

第24章

Chiasmus

交叉结构

Human beings, for some reason or another, like symmetry. You leave a bunch of them next to a jungle for a couple of days and you’ll come back to find an ornamental garden. We take stones and turn them into the Taj Mahal or St Paul’s Cathedral. Of course, a few things in nature are symmetrical anyway – snowflakes and leaves and the like – but their symmetry is never at a glance; you have to hold the leaf up at the right angle or run through the blizzard with a magnifying glass. When a chap makes something symmetrical he tends to set up a grand avenue so that you can see it is, and then he puts trees on either side. Nature is not symmetrical and symmetry is not natural.

人类不知为何，偏爱对称。你把一堆石头放在丛林边几天，回来就会发现那里已经长成了一座观赏花园。我们用石头建造泰姬陵或圣保罗大教堂。当然，自然界中有些东西本身就是对称的——比如雪花、树叶等等——但它们的对称性并非一目了然；你必须把树叶举到合适的角度，或者冒着暴风雪拿着放大镜才能看清。如果有人想建造一个对称的东西，他往往会设计一条宽阔的大道，让你一眼就能看出它的对称性，然后在两旁种上树木。自然界并非对称，对称也并非自然之物。

This love of symmetry carries straight over into words. At the smallest level you have the palindrome where the letters answer one another across the sentence. The palindrome is an old tradition: the first thing that man ever said was, probably, ‘Madam, I’m Adam’. And it has caused terrible distress to even the greatest literary minds. The only reason that T.S. Eliot insisted on the middle initial was that he was painfully aware of what his name would have been without it, backwards. For a short while, he became so paranoid that he decided to use his middle name instead and introduced himself as T. Stearns Eliot. The phase did not last, but it’s probably why his first great poem was called ‘The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock’.

这种对对称的喜爱也体现在文字中。最基本的体现就是回文，即句子中的字母彼此呼应。回文是一种古老的传统：人类最早说的话很可能是“夫人，我是亚当”。它甚至让最伟大的文学家都感到无比困扰。T·S·艾略特坚持使用中间名首字母的唯一原因，是他痛苦地意识到，如果去掉中间名，他的名字倒过来会是什么样子。有一段时间，他甚至为此感到极度焦虑，于是决定改用中间名，并以T·斯特恩斯·艾略特的身份自我介绍。这种做法并没有持续多久，但这或许就是他第一首伟大的诗作名为《J·阿尔弗雷德·普鲁弗洛克的情歌》的原因。

But beyond the microscopic symmetries of the palindrome there are the grander and more obvious ones of chiasmus, where the words of the first half are mirrored in the second. There was a musical that came out in 1925 called No, No, Nanette . But the only lines anybody can remember now are:

除了回文的微观对称性之外，还有更宏大、更显而易见的交叉对称性，即前半部分的文字在后半部分中相互呼应。1925年有一部音乐剧叫做《不，不，娜内特》（No, No, Nanette）。但现在人们唯一能记住的台词只有：

Tea for two and two for tea

双人茶和两人茶

Me for you and you for me

我为你，你为我

There’s something lovely about the symmetry here, not because it’s visual like a palindrome, but because the thoughts replicate each other. ‘Me for you’ is mirrored, requited and answered by ‘you for me’. Also everybody likes a cup of tea now and then. Requited love is only a pleasing symmetry, and symmetry is a kind of justice. The Three Musketeers had a cry of ‘One for all and all for one’. The symmetry makes it memorable but also reflects the reciprocity. It is that great human symmetry: the deal.

这里的对称之美令人赞叹，并非因为它像回文一样具有视觉上的对称性，而是因为其中的思想彼此呼应。“我为你”与“你为我”相互映照、互惠、回应。而且，谁不喜欢偶尔喝杯茶呢？两情相悦的爱情本身就是一种令人愉悦的对称，而对称本身就是一种正义。《三个火枪手》中曾响起“我为人人，人人为我”的口号。这种对称不仅使它令人难忘，也体现了互惠互利。这就是伟大的人性对称：交易。

Socrates may or may not have said, ‘Eat to live, not live to eat’. We remember the line because the two thoughts are held up as in a mirror: one reversing the other. It also, I suspect, reflects the fact that the Ancient Greek diet involved a lot of porridge.

苏格拉底或许说过“为了生存而吃，而不是为了吃而生存”，也或许没有说过这句话。我们之所以记住这句话，是因为这两种想法就像镜子一样相互映照：一个颠倒了另一个。我怀疑，这句话也反映了古希腊人饮食中粥的大量存在。

Mind you, just reversing words is almost as hard as a palindrome. It gets you stuck. Stuck. You get it? Thus writers can allow themselves a little give, a little wiggle-room, a little loosening of the literary belt. For example, a contemporary American writer with the peculiar name of Snoop Doggy Dogg (God, God poons) wrote a confessional poem about having ‘my mind on my money and my money on my mind’. While another, more financially optimistic chap called Tupac (Caput) observed jovially that ‘money don’t make the man, but man I’m making money’.

不过，倒序单词几乎和回文一样难。它会让你卡住，卡住。你明白我的意思吗？因此，作家可以给自己一点余地，一点回旋余地，稍微放松一下文学创作的束缚。例如，一位名叫Snoop Doggy Dogg（天哪，天哪）的当代美国作家写了一首自白诗，诗中写道“我的心思全在钱上，钱也占据了我的心”。而另一位名叫Tupac（卡普特）的作家，对金钱更加乐观，则戏谑地说道：“金钱造就不了人，但我确实在赚钱。”

Americans seem particularly fond of such verbal symmetries, and tend to elect anybody who can come up with a symmetrical sentence. The current President told his troops: ‘You stood up for America, now America must stand up for you.’ The one before didn’t care ‘whether we bring our enemies to justice, or bring justice to our enemies’. Before that it was: ‘People the world over have always been more impressed by the power of our example than by the example of our power’, and so on and so forth.

美国人似乎特别喜欢这种语言上的对称，他们往往会选出那些能说出对称句子的人。现任总统对他的部队说：“你们为美国挺身而出，现在美国必须为你们挺身而出。”前任总统则不在乎“我们是将敌人绳之以法，还是将正义带给敌人”。再往前是：“全世界的人们总是更被我们榜样的力量所折服，而不是被我们武力的威慑”，等等等等。

Even those who have never made it to President have given chiasmus a go because their chances are gone without chiasmus. Mitt Romney tried ‘Freedom requires religion, just as religion requires freedom’, and Hillary Clinton tried for the White House with: ‘In the end, the true test is not the speeches a president delivers, it’s whether the president delivers on the speeches.’

即使是那些从未当上总统的人也尝试过使用交叉结构，因为不用交叉结构他们就没机会了。米特·罗姆尼尝试过“自由需要宗教，正如宗教需要自由一样”，希拉里·克林顿竞选总统时则用了这样一句口号：“最终，真正的考验不在于总统发表了多少演讲，而在于总统能否兑现演讲内容。”

All of this goes back to JFK’s inauguration speech, which was chiasmus-crazy. With the Cold War at its coldest, Kennedy told America that ‘Mankind must put an end to war, or war will put an end to mankind’. His method was peaceful: ‘Let us never negotiate out of fear, but let us never fear to negotiate.’ And most famously of all he told Americans: ‘Ask not what your country can do for you, but what you can do for your country.’

这一切都要追溯到肯尼迪的就职演说，那篇演说简直是交叉结构运用的典范。在冷战最严峻的时期，肯尼迪告诉美国民众：“人类必须结束战争，否则战争将终结人类。”他采取的方法是和平的：“我们永远不要因为恐惧而谈判，但我们也永远不要害怕谈判。”而他最著名的演讲莫过于他对美国民众说：“不要问你的国家能为你做什么，而要问你能为你的国家做什么。”

Kennedy started the craze for chiasmus in American politics, but he himself had probably got the idea from his father. Joseph Kennedy, quite aside from being a businessman, diplomat and politician, is the prime suspect for originating the phrase later immortalised by Billy Ocean: ‘When the going gets tough, the tough get going.’

肯尼迪在美国政坛掀起了交叉结构热潮，但他本人很可能是从父亲那里得到的灵感。约瑟夫·肯尼迪，除了是一位商人、外交家和政治家之外，很可能是后来被比利·奥申传唱的那句名言的原创者：“逆境来临时，强者迎难而上。”

Chiasmus always sounds the same – the carefully thought-out artificial symmetry – but it can take various forms. First of all, there’s the straight repetition, of which Edward Lear was so fond:

交错结构听起来总是千篇一律——精心设计的对称性——但它可以采取多种形式。首先是直接重复，爱德华·李尔就非常喜欢这种形式：

They went to sea in a Sieve, they did,

他们乘着一艘筛子出海了，真的。

In a Sieve they went to sea:

他们乘着筛子出海了：

Or:

或者：

Oh, lovely Pussy, oh, Pussy, my love,

哦，可爱的小猫咪，哦，小猫咪，我的爱人，

What a beautiful Pussy you are …

你真是个漂亮的小猫咪……

The cat sat on the mat, and on the mat sat the cat. This form of chiasmus is just repetition in a mirror. It’s easy to do, and to do it is easy. Chiasmus really comes into its own when the inversion of the words gives you an inversion of thought as well. JFK’s great chiasmus works because you and your country are swapped around. The doer becomes the done for and the done for becomes the doer. It’s the same idea that Jesus used with ‘The Sabbath was made for man and not man for the Sabbath’ or ‘Judge not, that ye be not judged’.

猫坐在垫子上，垫子上也坐着猫。这种交叉结构其实就是镜像重复。它很容易做到，而且做起来也很容易。当词语的倒装也带来思维的颠倒时，交叉结构就真正展现出它的魅力。肯尼迪总统那句精彩的交叉结构之所以有效，是因为你和你的国家互换了位置。施为者变成了受为者，受为者变成了施为者。这与耶稣所说的“安息日是为人设立的，人不是为安息日设立的”或“你们不要论断人，免得你们被论断”的道理如出一辙。

Here the thoughts seem to be symmetrical, and thus they somehow seem to be logical as well. The sentence has the air of a clear, well-thought-out argument. The world makes sense in a chiasmus like this. The rational, or at least symmetrical, mind of man has a place for everything, and everything in its place. As Keats put it, ‘Beauty is truth, truth beauty’. Or as Edward Fitzgerald said: ‘The moving finger writes; and, having writ; / Moves on.’

这里的思路似乎是对称的，因此也显得合乎逻辑。这句话给人一种清晰、深思熟虑的论证之感。在这种交叉结构中，世界显得合情合理。人类理性的，或者至少是对称的思维，为万物都找到了归宿，万物各得其所。正如济慈所说，“美即真，真即美”。又如爱德华·菲茨杰拉德所言：“移动的手指书写；写完之后；/继续移动。”

The repetition and logic come together in the chiasmus of the Venn diagram. Byron pointed out that ‘Pleasure’s a sin, and sometimes sin’s a pleasure’, which I suppose was a subject on which he was the expert. Oscar Wilde said that ‘All crime is vulgar, just as all vulgarity is crime’, and then got sent off to Reading Gaol to reconsider and write ballads. Both these lines use chiasmus to get around one of the problems of precise logic: if all tomatoes are red, does that mean that all red things are tomatoes? Chiasmus lets you explain, and sound rather elegant while you’re doing so.

重复与逻辑在维恩图的交叉结构中完美结合。拜伦指出“享乐是一种罪过，有时罪过也是一种享乐”，我想这大概是他擅长的领域。奥斯卡·王尔德说过“一切犯罪都是庸俗的，正如一切庸俗都是犯罪一样”，然后就被送进了雷丁监狱，让他反思自己的观点并创作民谣。这两句话都运用了交叉结构来规避精确逻辑的一个难题：如果所有的西红柿都是红色的，那是不是意味着所有红色的东西都是西红柿？交叉结构让你能够解释清楚，而且解释起来还相当优雅。

Chiasmus can also be used for something very like a pun. Mae West said, ‘It’s not the men in my life, it’s the life in my men’, where life is being used in two different senses (CV vs. vigour). Dorothy Parker allegedly went one further. The story (unconfirmed) goes that her editor at The New Yorker sent a telegram to Parker while she was on her honeymoon. The editor wanted to remind her about the deadline for an article she was meant to be writing. Dorothy Parker sent one back saying: ‘I’ve been too fucking busy, and vice versa.’ This seems remarkably unlikely, as you couldn’t normally send swear words in a telegram, which of course had to be dictated to the chap at the post office. So maybe another version of the tale is true, where a colleague complained of being too fucking busy, and Parker merely murmured, ‘Or vice versa’. Or maybe it was all made up. It is, nonetheless, a rare case of chiasmus implied, but not stated.

交错结构也可以用来玩类似双关的文字游戏。梅·韦斯特曾说过：“不是我生命中的男人，而是我男人身上的生命力”，这里的“生命力”有两种不同的含义（简历和活力）。据说多萝西·帕克更进一步。这个故事（未经证实）是这样的：帕克在度蜜月期间，《纽约客》的编辑给她发了一封电报，提醒她一篇稿件的截稿日期。帕克回电说：“我他妈的太忙了，反之亦然。”这似乎不太可能，因为电报里通常不能用脏话，电报当然是要口述给邮局的工作人员的。所以，也许这个故事还有另一个版本：一位同事抱怨自己他妈的太忙了，帕克只是咕哝了一句“反之亦然”。或者，这一切都是编造的。然而，这是一个罕见的隐含交叉结构但未明确指出的例子。

One of the things that makes Dorothy Parker’s chiasmus a trifle unlikely is that a good chiasmus needs to be thought out. Chiasmus is clever, but not natural. Kennedy’s inauguration speech could never have been improvised and Mae West, one suspects, took a while to work hers out. Chiasmus is the grand statement, it’s the victory of symmetry, it’s the Taj Mahal. There is, though, a more subtle form: the grammatical chiasmus.

多萝西·帕克的交错结构之所以略显牵强，原因之一在于，好的交错结构需要精心构思。交错结构固然巧妙，但并非自然而然。肯尼迪的就职演说绝不可能即兴发挥，而梅·韦斯特的演讲稿，人们也怀疑，是经过反复推敲才最终成型的。交错结构是宏伟的宣言，是对称的胜利，是泰姬陵的象征。然而，还有一种更为精妙的形式：语法上的交错结构。

Adjective noun : noun adjective , or as Milton put it in the closing line of Lycidas : ‘Tomorrow to fresh woods and pastures new.’ It’s a bit of a wrench to move that ‘new’ to the end, but it completes a symmetry. More accomplished is the opening line ‘I see trees of green, red roses too’ from ‘What a Wonderful World’, 1 where the sentence is plant colour : colour plant . An unwary chap may sing that line all day without noticing the chiasmus.

形容词名词：名词形容词，或者正如弥尔顿在《利西达斯》结尾处所写：“明日将前往崭新的森林和牧场。” 将“新的”移到句末确实有些突兀，但却形成了一种对称结构。更精妙的是《多么美好的世界》的开头一句“我看到绿树，还有红玫瑰”，这句的句子结构是植物颜色：颜色植物。粗心的人可能整天都在唱这句歌词，却丝毫不会注意到其中的交叉结构。

It is possible, just possible, to make things symmetrical without anybody really noticing. They still like what they hear, but they’re not sure why. Here, the grand oratory of Kennedy or the ingenuity of Mae West are gone, and in their place are the gentle symmetries of Dr Johnson. Johnson wrote in The Vanity of Human Wishes about the world of pleasure-seekers who indulged in ‘By day the frolic, and the dance by night’, which sounds rather agreeable, not just because a schedule of 24-hour dancing and frolicking is a good schedule, but because the sentence runs time activity : activity time .

有可能，仅仅是有可能，在不引起任何人注意的情况下，让事物变得对称。人们仍然喜欢他们听到的内容，但他们不确定为什么。在这里，肯尼迪的雄辩或梅·韦斯特的机智已不复存在，取而代之的是约翰逊博士温和的对称。约翰逊在《人类愿望的虚荣》中写道，享乐主义者的世界里，人们沉溺于“白天嬉戏，夜晚跳舞”，这听起来相当令人愉悦，不仅因为24小时不间断的跳舞和嬉戏是一种不错的安排，还因为这句话本身就体现了“活动时间”的概念。

Coleridge did the same subtle thing in ‘Kubla Khan’ when he dreamt of his ‘sunny pleasure-dome with caves of ice’. But that poem also contains the rarest, subtlest, strangest kind of chiasmus there is. It’s a species of chiasmus that is as hard to spot in the wild as the Abominable Snowman, and therefore as hard to study, and it occurs in the great opening line:

柯勒律治在《忽必烈汗》中也运用了同样的微妙手法，他梦见了自己“阳光普照、冰雪环绕的享乐宫殿”。但这首诗还包含着一种极为罕见、精妙绝伦、奇特的交叉结构。这种交叉结构如同雪人一般难以寻觅，因此也难以研究，它就出现在这首诗的开篇第一句：

In Xanadu did Kubla Khan …

在上都，忽必烈汗……

Did you see it? Look again. Nothing? It’s not a symmetry of grammar, or words being mirrored; yet there is a reason why that line rolls off the tongue like the milk of paradise. Give up?

你看到了吗？再仔细看看。什么都没看到？这不是语法对称，也不是词语镜像对称；但这句诗之所以朗朗上口，如天堂之乳般甘甜，自有其道理。放弃了吗？

An – Ah – Oo – i – Oo – Ah – An

安 – 啊 – 哦 – 我 – 哦 – 啊 – 安

In Xanadu did Kubla Khan

在上都，忽必烈汗

It’s a chiasmus of vowels. Tennyson wrote:

这是一个元音交叉结构。丁尼生写道：

Beneath the thunders of the upper deep

在深渊之上的雷鸣声中

Ee – e – u – e – o – e – u – e – ee

ee – e – u – e – o – e – u – e – ee

A symmetry of assonance.

谐音的对称性。

1 By Bob Thiele and George David Weiss, released 1967.

1 由鲍勃·蒂勒和乔治·大卫·韦斯创作，于 1967 年发行。

# ↩

Chapter 25

第25章

Assonance

谐音

Assonance is repeating a vowel sound: d ee p h ea t or bl ue m oo n . It is, I’m afraid, the thin and flimsy cousin of alliteration. Well, it is in English. Welsh poetry, I’m told, thrives on assonance, as did Old German and Hebrew. But in English it’s hard to tell whether it’s there at all. There are probably a few reasons for this. First of all, English doesn’t use many vowels.

元音韵是指重复元音，例如 deep heat（深热）或 blue moon（蓝月亮）。恐怕它只是头韵的薄弱表亲。至少在英语中是这样。据说威尔士诗歌非常依赖元音韵，古德语和希伯来语也是如此。但在英语中，我们很难判断是否存在元音韵。这可能有几个原因。首先，英语使用的元音并不多。

Half the vowels in English aren’t what you thought they were. They’re schwas . A proper vowel is formed in a particular part of the mouth. So E is near the front, I is at the top, and Ooo is at the back. A schwa is formed in the middle. It sounds a bit like all the vowels, and is really none of them. It’s a lazy compromise between all the proper vowels, and we use it all the time. The word another may be spelt An-Oth-Er but you pronounce it uh-nuh-thuh. You may pronounce the bout in about clearly, but what’s the first vowel? It’s a schwa. Uh-bout.

英语里一半的元音跟你想的不一样。它们是弱元音（schwa）。一个标准的元音是由口腔的特定部位发音的。比如，E 靠近口腔前部，I 在口腔顶部，Ooo 在口腔后部。而弱元音则发音在口腔中部。它的发音听起来有点像所有元音，但实际上又不像任何一个元音。它是所有标准元音之间一种偷懒的折中方案，我们经常使用它。单词 another 的拼写可能是 An-Oth-Er，但发音是 uh-nuh-thuh。你可能能清楚地发音 about 中的 bout，但第一个元音是什么？它是一个弱元音。Uh-bout。

There’s even a letter for this grunty, nothing sound: . If you start using this lett you get an ide of how ubiqu t s schwa is. It’s the most comm n vow l in English – not A or E or any of the vow ls you learnt at school, but schwa. Not lot of peop l know that.

甚至还有一个字母专门用来表示这种咕哝的、无意义的声音： 。如果你开始使用这个字母 ，你就会明白 弱元音有多么普遍 t 。它是英语中最常见的 t元音 l——不是A或E，也不是你在学校学过的任何元音， l]，而是弱元音。 很多人知道这一点。 t

The importance of all this for assonance is that English is missing a bunch of its vowels, or at least uses a vague, half-arsed compromise vowel that sounds like all and none. There is a second problem, though. Vowels change.

这一切对押韵的重要性在于，英语缺少很多元音，或者至少使用了一种模糊不清、敷衍了事的折中元音，听起来像“all”又像“none”。然而，还有第二个问题：元音会发生变化。

Over the centuries and over the classes, consonants tend to stay roughly the same, while vowels slip around like eels. As long as the consonant is there, the word is still recognisable. A middle-class Englishman ate lunch, the Queen et lunch, and a Cockney street urchin ite it. So nobody is utterly sure how Shakespeare pronounced his vowels. Shakespeare makes a habit of rhyming love with prove . That may be because Shakespeare pronounced prove as pruv , or it might just be that Shakespeare pronounce love as luve . If he did, then ‘If music be the food of love, play on’ has an awful lot of assonance in it: muse , fude , luve . But as Shakespeare didn’t have a tape-recorder we’ll never know. The point for this chapter is, I’m afraid, that Shakespeare’s works may have been filled with lovely assonances that are now lost for ever. ‘Is this’ has assonance on ‘i’. ‘A dagger that’ has assonance on ‘a’. ‘I see before me’ has assonance on ‘ee’. But it might not have done in the original.

几个世纪以来，随着阶级的变迁，辅音往往保持大致不变，而元音却像鳗鱼一样四处游移。只要辅音还在，单词就还能被识别。一个英国中产阶级男子吃午餐（ate lunch），女王吃午餐（et lunch），一个伦敦东区街头顽童吃它（ite it）。所以，没人能完全确定莎士比亚是如何发音的。莎士比亚习惯把“love”（爱）和“prove”（证明）押韵。这可能是因为他把“prove”发音为“pruv”，也可能是因为他把“love”（爱）发音为“luve”。如果真是这样，那么“If music be the food of love, play on”（如果音乐是爱情的食粮，那就继续演奏吧）这句诗里就充满了丰富的谐音：muse（缪斯）、fude（乐曲）、luve（爱）。但由于莎士比亚没有录音机，我们永远也无法得知真相。恐怕本章的重点在于，莎士比亚的作品中可能充满了优美的谐音，而这些如今已永远消失了。 “Is this”的“i”发音押韵。“A dagger that”的“a”发音押韵。“I see before me”的“ee”发音押韵。但在原文中可能并非如此。

And even in the cases where you can find it, it’s hard to be certain that it’s anything more than a coincidence. There are only so many vowel sounds. It’s terribly tempting to look at Tennyson’s great line

即使在你能找到的情况下，也很难确定这仅仅是巧合。元音的种类就那么多。人们很容易会想到丁尼生的那句名言。

To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield

努力奋斗，不断探索，永不屈服

… and say ‘Golly, it’s four verbs that go i ee i ee .’ But that might be a coincidence. Did Auden write ‘Stop all the clocks’ because he liked the assonance of ‘o’, or because he was writing about … well … stopping clocks? When Dylan Thomas raged against the dying of the light , perhaps he just didn’t want the light to die. The only phrase where I’d say with some certainty that assonance made it famous is:

……然后说“哎呀，这四个动词的发音都是‘i ee i ee’。”但这可能只是巧合。奥登写《停止所有的钟表》是因为他喜欢“o”的谐音，还是因为他写的是……嗯……停止钟表？当狄兰·托马斯怒斥光明消逝时，也许他只是不想让光明消逝。我唯一能比较肯定地说，谐音使之名扬天下的句子是：

I met a traveller from an antique land

我遇见了一位来自古老国度的旅行者

Three an s in a row, with the very odd word ‘antique’ evidence of how deliberate it is. But that, after much searching, is my best candidate. It’s not like alliteration.

连续三个“an”，还夹杂着非常奇怪的词“antique”，这足以证明这是刻意为之。但经过反复查找，这已经是我能想到的最佳答案了。它不像是在玩头韵。

The one place that you can be sure that a little bit of assonance has been important is in proverbs and phrases. Why are you as high as a kite and not a cloud? Why as happy as Larry and not Peter? How now, brown cow?

谚语和短语中，押韵的运用可谓举足轻重。你为何像风筝一样高，而不是像云朵一样高？为何像拉里一样快乐，而不是像彼得一样快乐？棕色的母牛，你好吗？

The only reason that a stitch in time saves nine is the assonance. If it saved eight the phrase would be forgotten. English cats have nine lives, in Germany they have sechs Leben . You may, of course, be wondering why either of these phrases needed a particular number; that’s all down to the Fourteenth Rule.

“及时缝一针，省九针”之所以成立，唯一的原因是押韵。如果“及时缝一针，省八针”，这句谚语早就被人遗忘了。英国的猫有九条命，德国的猫有六条命。你当然可能会好奇，为什么这两个说法都需要用到特定的数字；这都得归功于第十四条规则。

# ↩

Chapter 26

第二十六章

The Fourteenth Rule 1

第十四条规则

Some people think that the number thirteen is unlucky. Why they should think this is utterly unclear. All sorts of explanations get offered – thirteen people at the Last Supper, thirteen steps to the gallows – but they all look like nonsense. You might as well believe that seven is lucky or that the answer to the question of life, the universe and everything is 42.

有些人认为13是不吉利的数字。至于他们为什么这么想，实在令人费解。各种各样的解释层出不穷——最后的晚餐有13个人，绞刑架有13级台阶——但这些解释听起来都像是无稽之谈。你还不如相信7是幸运数字，或者相信生命、宇宙以及一切的答案是42。

The idea that a number can have some sort of special significance is called numerology. And there are as many systems of numerology as there have been cultures, periods of history, and plonkers to think them up. Well, to be fair they weren’t all plonkers. Pythagoras was a clever chap but he still mucked around with numerology and believed that odd numbers were masculine and even feminine. But I don’t think you need to be too much of a spoilsport sceptic to suspect that numerology is nonsense.

认为数字具有某种特殊意义的想法被称为命理学。命理学的体系之多，几乎与历史上不同文化、不同时期以及提出这些体系的愚人一样多。当然，公平地说，他们并非全是愚人。毕达哥拉斯是个聪明人，但他仍然涉猎命理学，认为奇数代表男性，甚至代表女性。但我认为，你无需成为一个过于死板的怀疑论者，就能怀疑命理学纯属无稽之谈。

The fact that something that’s so obviously nonsense is so popular shows that it must appeal to something deep, deep within us. That the West thinks that seven is lucky and the Chinese think eight is shows both that numerology is wrong and that it’s popular across the world. Numbers feel mysterious and significant. So all you need to do to sound mysterious and significant is to pick a number, any number.

如此荒谬的东西竟然如此流行，这说明它一定触动了我们内心深处的某种东西。西方人认为七是吉利数字，中国人认为八是吉利数字，这既表明数字命理学是错误的，也说明它在世界各地都很流行。数字给人一种神秘而重要的感觉。所以，要想听起来神秘而重要，你只需要随便选一个数字就行了。

You would have to have a heart of stone and a soul of Formica to listen to ‘A Whiter Shade of Pale’ without wondering to yourself why there are sixteen vestal virgins. What? What does the number mean? Why sixteen? What’s the reason? There is, of course, no reason and the truth is plain to see: it feels so mysterious. If she had been one of several vestal virgins, the song would be Much Less Memorable.

除非你铁石心肠、麻木不仁，否则听《苍白的浅影》这首歌时，一定会忍不住好奇为什么歌里唱的是十六位贞女。什么？这个数字代表什么？为什么是十六？原因是什么？当然，并没有什么原因，真相显而易见：它给人一种神秘莫测的感觉。如果歌里唱的只是众多贞女中的一个，那这首歌恐怕就没那么令人难忘了。

Folk songs and fairy tales are bursting with such strangely significant numbers. It has to be four-and-twenty blackbirds baked in the pie, and three blind mice, and fifteen men on a dead man’s chest because if you replace those numbers with ‘several’ or ‘a lot of’ the whole feeling is lost – the feeling of significance, of something ancient and mysterious.

民歌和童话故事里充满了这种意义非凡的数字。必须是馅饼里烤着二十四只黑鸟，三只瞎老鼠，死人胸前躺着十五个人，因为如果把这些数字换成“几个”或“很多”，那种意义感——那种古老而神秘的感觉——就全都消失了。

Coleridge knew all about the power of numbers. The Rime of the Ancient Mariner is a classic example. It’s almost an exercise in enumeration. He starts it off in the second line:

柯勒律治深谙数字的力量。《古舟子咏》就是一个经典的例子。它几乎就是一次计数练习。他在第二行就写道：

It is an ancient Mariner,

这是一位古老的航海家，

And he stoppeth one of three.

他阻止了三人中的一个。

Why three? Perhaps it represents the Christian trinity? Or perhaps there’s no particular point to the number. And Coleridge doesn’t stop there. There aren’t just lots of people on the ship, there are:

为什么是三？也许它代表基督教的三位一体？或者这个数字本身并没有什么特别的含义。柯勒律治的解释还不止于此。船上不仅人很多，还有：

Four times fifty living men

五十个活人的四倍

… who are condemned when a pale lady ‘whistles thrice’. Things don’t happen in weeks, they happen in:

……当一位面色苍白的女士“吹三声口哨”时，他们便会受到谴责。事情不会在几周内发生，而是在以下时间内发生：

Seven days, seven nights, I saw that curse,

七天七夜，我目睹了那诅咒。

And yet I could not die.

然而，我却死不了。

Like one that hath been seven days drowned

就像一个溺水七天的人

My body lay afloat;

我的身体漂浮在水面上；

The albatross accompanies the ship for precisely nine days, and the spirit follows the boat not ‘deep in the sea’, as most poets would have put it, but exactly ‘nine fathoms deep’.

信天翁陪伴船只整整九天，它的灵魂跟随船只，不是像大多数诗人所说的那样“深入大海”，而是恰好“九英寻深”。

A hundred and one other authors have used the trick: Tolkien’s Nine Ring Wraiths and Lawrence of Arabia’s Seven Pillars of Wisdom. 2 As Rudyard Kipling observed:

还有一百零一位作家也用过这种手法：托尔金的《九戒灵》和阿拉伯的劳伦斯的《智慧七柱》。正如鲁德亚德·吉卜林所观察到的：

… my Totem saw the shame; from his ridgepole shrine he came,

……我的图腾目睹了这耻辱；他从屋脊上的神龛中走了出来，

And he told me in a vision of the night:—

他在夜间的异象中告诉我：

‘There are nine and sixty ways of constructing tribal lays,

“构建部落诗歌的方式有六十九种，

And every single one of them is right!’

他们说的每一个都对！

But the most prolific enumerator is almost certainly Bob Dylan. Bob Dylan writes folk songs and there is something inescapably folky about numbers. He puts numbers everywhere: sad forests (seven), wild horses (six), jugglers (fifteen), believers (five) and fourth time around. There are at least 573 other examples, including ‘Love Minus Zero’, which is an example of catachresis.

但最擅长使用数字的几乎肯定是鲍勃·迪伦。鲍勃·迪伦创作民谣，而数字本身就带有某种无法抗拒的民谣气息。他把数字运用得淋漓尽致：悲伤的森林（七）、野马（六）、杂耍艺人（十五）、信徒（五）以及第四次。至少还有573个类似的例子，包括《爱减零》（Love Minus Zero），这首歌本身就是一个误用的例子。

1 This is the only rule I’m including that is not part of classical rhetoric.

1 这是我唯一要加入的、不属于古典修辞学的规则。

2 This is taken from the Bible, Proverbs 9, verse 1, but the point remains.

2 这句话出自圣经箴言 9 章 1 节，但道理仍然适用。

# ↩

Chapter 27

第27章

Catachresis

误用

Catachresis is rather difficult to define, but it’s essentially when a sentence is so startlingly wrong that it’s right. Catachresis is the slap in the face. It’s the ice-block in your underwear. Catachresis is bam! Unfortunately, the most famous example is barely noticeable.

误用很难定义，但本质上是指一个句子错得离谱，反而显得正确。误用就像当头一棒，就像冰块塞进内裤里，砰！可惜的是，最著名的例子却几乎难以察觉。

Even the bravest of chaps can have a loss of nerve when faced with the harrowing and fearful task of chatting to his mother. A dutiful son has to remember not to slouch or swear or, in Hamlet’s case, murder the old bat. So he gives himself a pep talk full of reminders:

即使最勇敢的人，面对与母亲交谈这种令人胆战心惊的任务时，也会怯场。一个孝顺的儿子必须记住不能驼背、不能说脏话，更不能像哈姆雷特那样，谋杀老太婆。于是，他给自己打气，反复提醒自己：

… now to my mother.

……现在轮到我母亲了。

O heart, lose not thy nature; let not ever

哦，我的心啊，不要失去你的本性；不要永远

The soul of Nero enter this firm bosom:

尼禄的灵魂进入了这坚实的胸膛：

Let me be cruel, not unnatural:

让我残忍一些，但不要违背人性：

I will speak daggers to her, but use none.

我会用言语狠狠地刺她，但不会真的动手。

Nero was notorious for putting his own mother to death, among other indiscretions, and Hamlet’s words would make a wonderful Mother’s Day card. Yet the important phrase here is the catachresis ‘I will speak daggers’. If you stop and think about it, the sentence doesn’t make sense. You can’t speak a dagger. 1

尼禄因处死自己的母亲而臭名昭著，这只是他众多暴行之一。哈姆雷特的这番话倒像是绝佳的母亲节贺卡。然而，这里的关键在于误用句“我将以匕首之语说话”。仔细想想，这句话本身就不通顺。你不可能用匕首之语说话。¹

You can speak any adverb. You can speak loudly, softly, gradually, democratically and deliciously. You can speak a few nouns: English and the truth. Or you could speak words as sharp as daggers, or as cruel. But you can’t speak daggers any more than you can speak grenades or bullets or blunderbusses. And that’s why the phrase stuck. Speaking daggers is so unusual that it became part of the language. And then it became usual. And a couple of hundred years later we got looking daggers (1834) and nobody really notices any more. It’s the fate of everyone who sets out to shock: you shock, you are noticed, you are remembered, but what is remembered ceases to be noticed and shocks no more. Sic transit l’enfant terrible d’antan .

你可以说任何副词。你可以大声说、轻声说、缓缓说、民主地说、妙语连珠地说。你可以说几个名词：英语和真理。或者你可以说出像匕首一样锋利、像残酷一样的话语。但你不可能说出匕首，就像你不可能说出手榴弹、子弹或短管火枪一样。这就是为什么这个短语流传下来的原因。“说话像匕首一样”如此罕见，以至于它成为了语言的一部分。然后它变得习以为常。几百年后，我们有了“眼神像匕首一样”（1834年），但现在已经没人注意到了。这就是所有试图制造轰动的人的命运：你制造轰动，你被注意到，你被记住，但被记住的东西不再被注意到，也不再令人震惊。这就是过去“可怕的孩子”的命运。

The same thing happened to Lewis Carroll and his great catachresis. Alice drinks the drink that says ‘Drink Me’ and it makes her small. Then she eats the cake that says ‘Eat Me’ and it makes her big. And then:

刘易斯·卡罗尔也遇到了同样的情况，他犯了一个严重的误用错误。爱丽丝喝了写着“喝我”的饮料，结果变小了。然后她吃了写着“吃我”的蛋糕，结果变大了。然后：

‘Curiouser and curiouser!’ cried Alice (she was so much surprised, that for the moment she quite forgot how to speak good English).

“真是越来越奇怪了！”爱丽丝喊道（她太惊讶了，以至于一时忘记了如何说一口流利的英语）。

But the Oxford English Dictionary now has an entry of its own just for curiouser and curiouser (meaning 16 C under ‘curious’), with Carroll as the first citation.

但牛津英语词典现在专门为 curiouser and curiouser（意为“好奇的”）一词添加了一个词条，该词条出自 16 世纪的“好奇的”一词，卡罗尔是第一个引用的例子。

But catachresis continues in a cycle of novelty and absorption. It is very hard to explain grammatically why it is that ‘Thunderbirds are go’. But if Thunderbirds were going it would never have caught on. It’s that single word that hits you like first love, and, like a first love, seems rather familiar 40 years later.

但误用现象在新鲜感和被吸收的循环中不断发生。很难从语法上解释为什么是“Thunderbirds are go”。但如果是“Thunderbirds were going”，它就不会流行起来。这一个词就像初恋一样击中你，而且，就像初恋一样，40年后听起来依然很熟悉。

Songwriters love to use love as a catachresis. For example, there’s Leonard Cohen’s ‘Dance Me to the End of Love’. That’s a perfect catachresis. You would expect the sentence to end with a noun of space or time – ‘Dance Me to the End of the Night’ or ‘Dance Me to the End of the Street’ – and instead you get love, which isn’t a place, unless you believe The Doors’ line ‘She lives on Love Street’, which is another love-catachresis. Bananarama had ‘Love in the First Degree’, Moon Martin had a ‘Bad Case of Loving You’, and KLF had asked ‘What Time Is Love?’ Rolf Harris attempted his own catachresis with ‘Tie Me Kangaroo Down, Sport’, but the most beautiful catachresis is probably Roxette’s opening line, ‘Lay a whisper on my pillow’.

词曲作者们喜欢用“爱”这个词来玩弄语境。例如，莱昂纳德·科恩的《Dance Me to the End of Love》就是一个绝妙的语境转换。你可能会期待这句话以表示空间或时间的名词结尾——比如“Dance Me to the End of the Night”或“Dance Me to the End of the Street”——但结果却是“爱”，它并非一个地点，除非你相信The Doors乐队的歌词“She lives on Love Street”，而这又是另一个关于爱的语境转换。Bananarama乐队有《Love in the First Degree》，Moon Martin有《Bad Case of Loving You》，KLF乐队则提出了“What Time Is Love?”这个问题。Rolf Harris也尝试过用“Tie Me Kangaroo Down, Sport”来玩弄语境转换，但最美妙的语境转换或许要数Roxette乐队的开篇歌词“Lay a whisper on my pillow”了。

A catachresis is any sentence that makes you stop, scratch your head and say ‘that’s wrong’, before you suddenly realise that it’s right. It’s Andrew Marvell in ‘The Garden’:

误用句是指那些让你停下来，挠挠头，然后说“这不对”的句子，但你突然意识到它是正确的。安德鲁·马维尔在《花园》中就用了这种手法：

Annihilating all that’s made

彻底摧毁一切已造之物

To a green thought in a green shade.

一片绿色的思绪。

Or it’s the modern host asking his guest: ‘Would you like some I Can’t Believe It’s Not Butter?’

或者，现代主人会问他的客人：“您想来点‘我不敢相信这不是黄油’吗？”

Although that’s also a litotes.

虽然这也是一种反语。

1 Shakespeare was reusing a trick he’d first tried in Much Ado About Nothing where Benedick says that Beatrice ‘speaks poinards, and every word stabs’.

1 莎士比亚重用了他在《无事生非》中首次尝试过的技巧，当时本尼迪克说比阿特丽斯“说话像刀子，每个字都像刀子”。

# ↩

Chapter 28

第28章

Litotes

轻体

Litotes is affirming something by denying its opposite. It’s not difficult. Supposing you’re writing a song about something that happens every day. You could start each line with the words ‘It’s usual’, or you could use litotes and start them with the words ‘It’s not unusual’. Litotes is a form of understatement-by-negative, and is not without its uses.

反语是通过否定其反面来肯定某事。这并不难理解。假设你要写一首歌，歌词是关于每天都会发生的事。你可以每句都以“这很平常”开头，也可以用反语，以“这不奇怪”开头。反语是一种用否定来表达轻描淡写的方式，而且并非没有用处。

Understatement is a tricky business, because it works only if you know the truth. If Franz Liszt told you that he played the piano a little, it would be an understatement. If I said the same it would just be true. So, in a sense, understaters need you to know what they’re saying before they say it. Or, at the very least, they need you to get it instantly. ‘The Burial of Sir John Moore at Corunna’ begins:

轻描淡写是一门学问，因为它只有在你知道真相的情况下才有效。如果弗朗茨·李斯特告诉你他只会弹一点钢琴，那就是轻描淡写。如果我这么说，那就是实话。所以，从某种意义上说，轻描淡写的人需要你在他们开口之前就知道他们在说什么。或者至少，他们需要你立刻明白他们的意思。《科伦纳的约翰·摩尔爵士葬礼》的开头是：

Not a drum was heard, not a funeral note,

没有听到鼓声，也没有听到丧歌。

As his corpse to the rampart we hurried.

我们匆匆将他的尸体抬到城墙上。

And the reader has to pick up on the fact that there was silence. A logician might say that it was still possible that there was cheering and heavy traffic and sirens going off, but logicians have no place near poetry. When Tom Jones sees you hanging around with anyone, we know that he cries and cries consistently.

读者必须注意到，当时一片寂静。逻辑学家或许会说，当时可能还有欢呼声、车水马龙和警笛声，但逻辑学家与诗歌格格不入。汤姆·琼斯只要看到你和任何人在一起，我们就知道他会哭个不停。

The context is often a help. Antarctic explorers can joke to each other about how it’s ‘not warm’ all day long (and remember that during exploring season the day is four months at the South Pole). Or you can refer to something universally acknowledged: ‘Bill Gates isn’t short of a bob or two.’ But even context can let you down. On 15 August 1945, Emperor Hirohito made a broadcast to the Japanese nation. It was the first time an Emperor had ever spoken on the radio, so the Japanese people knew that something was up. Moreover, two atomic bombs had just been dropped. Hirohito announced to his listening nation that ‘the war situation has developed not necessarily to Japan’s advantage’, which is perhaps the most extreme example of litotes in all humanity’s huge history. But it wasn’t quite clear enough. Many listeners didn’t realise what he was saying until the speech was over and the announcer cut in to say that Japan had surrendered to the Allies.

语境往往能起到帮助作用。南极探险家们可以互相开玩笑说那里“一整天都不暖和”（别忘了，在探险季，南极点一天要持续四个月）。或者你可以引用一些公认的事实：“比尔·盖茨可不缺钱。” 但即便如此，语境也可能出错。1945年8月15日，裕仁天皇向日本全国发表了广播讲话。这是天皇首次通过广播讲话，因此日本民众意识到肯定有大事发生。此外，两颗原子弹刚刚被投下。裕仁天皇向收听广播的全国民众宣布，“战争形势的发展未必对日本有利”，这或许是人类漫长历史中最极端的反语用法。但这番话并没有表达清楚。许多听众直到讲话结束，播音员插播宣布日本已向盟军投降时，才明白天皇的意思。

Litotes requires you to know your audience, and preferably have them in the room with you. When the Empress of India (and Queen of Great Britain and Ireland) tried her litotes she kept it short-range and brutal.

使用讽刺手法需要了解你的听众，最好能让他们与你身处同一空间。印度女皇（同时也是大不列颠及爱尔兰女王）尝试使用讽刺手法时，她的手法简洁有力，毫不留情。

Her [Queen Victoria’s] remarks can freeze as well as crystallise. There is a tale of the unfortunate equerry who ventured during dinner at Windsor to tell a story with a spice of scandal or impropriety in it. ‘We are not amused,’ said the Queen when he had finished.

维多利亚女王的言论既能凝固成永恒，也能隽永成。曾有这样一个故事：一位不幸的侍从在温莎城堡的晚宴上，胆敢讲述一个带有丑闻或不雅色彩的故事。“我们一点也不觉得好笑，”女王在他讲完后说道。

Litotes is a complicated beast. It’s closely related to the double-negative, but it’s not quite the same. Leaving no stone unturned is not litotes, because it has no understatement to it. When Shakespeare wrote in The Tempest , ‘I have no hope that he’s undrowned’, it wasn’t a litotes because it wasn’t an understatement, it was just confusing. Litotes is a special kind of understatement that happens to use negatives. And understatement is a kind of irony.

反语（litotes）是一种复杂的修辞手法。它与双重否定密切相关，但又不完全相同。“不遗余力”并非反语，因为它没有含蓄的表达。莎士比亚在《暴风雨》中写道：“我并不希望他能活着回来”，这并非反语，因为它并非含蓄的表达，而只是令人费解。反语是一种特殊的含蓄表达，它恰好使用了否定词。而含蓄表达本身就是一种反讽。

Irony is an odd fish because, contrary to popular belief, irony draws people together. Irony is an untruth that both parties know is untrue, that both parties agree is untrue. 1 When two strangers meet in the pouring rain and one says to the other, ‘Lovely weather we’re having’, he’s appealing to the one thing that he knows they both have in common and the one truth they both recognise. When a couple are arguing furiously and one says sarcastically to the other, ‘Oh, because you’d know all about being faithful’, they may be arguing, but that statement appeals to knowledge they share.

反讽很奇特，因为与人们普遍的认知相反，它能拉近人与人之间的距离。反讽是一种双方都知道是假的、并且双方都认同的谎言。当两个陌生人在倾盆大雨中相遇，其中一人对另一人说：“今天天气真好啊”，他是在诉诸他们共同拥有的、也是他们都认同的真理。当一对情侣激烈争吵，其中一人讽刺地对另一人说：“哦，因为你肯定最懂忠诚”，他们或许正在争吵，但这句话却触及了他们共同拥有的认知。

Irony is always about what people have in common, and so is litotes. It’s a sociable figure. Though it can be used to end wars, bury generals and crush courtiers, litotes is most at home among friends. It is a gentlemanly figure, a civilised figure, an agreeable one. It is the sort of figure you should toss out with an amiable smile and a raised eyebrow.

反讽总是关乎人们的共同点，反语也是如此。它是一种善于交际的语言。虽然它可以用来结束战争、埋葬将军、打压朝臣，但反语最常用于朋友之间。它是一种绅士风度，一种文明礼貌，一种令人愉悦的语言。你应该带着和蔼的微笑和挑起的眉毛，轻松地把它抛出去。

‘Well I’ll be damned if it isn’t old Bertie. How are you?’

“哎呀，没想到竟然是老伯蒂。你好吗？”

‘Can’t complain, old boy, can’t complain.’

“没啥可抱怨的，老兄，没啥可抱怨的。”

‘Would it be awfully wrong to tempt you with a drink?’

“如果我请你喝一杯，是不是太过分了？”

‘I wouldn’t say no.’

“我不会拒绝。”

However, there are those who don’t like litotes at all, and they are not without their reasons. George Orwell wrote a long essay attacking hackneyed metaphors and language that wasn’t crystal clear – or, as he would have put it, diamond clear. His general theory was that unclear language reflected unclear thought, which allowed evil politicians to oppress people. So litotes is a dictator’s henchman.

然而，有些人完全不喜欢反语，而且他们的理由并非毫无道理。乔治·奥威尔曾写过一篇长文，抨击陈词滥调的比喻和晦涩难懂的语言——或者用他自己的话说，是“像钻石一样清晰”。他的总体理论是，晦涩的语言反映了混乱的思想，这使得邪恶的政客得以压迫人民。因此，反语是独裁者的帮凶。

Orwell reckoned that ‘it should also be possible to laugh the not un- formation out of existence’. He advised all writers to memorise the sentence A not unblack dog was chasing a not unsmall rabbit across a not ungreen field . However, writers didn’t memorise that sentence and litotes continued untroubled until its reputation was nearly destroyed by the cruel despot John Major.

奥威尔认为“也可以用笑声来消除‘非非形式’”。他建议所有作家都记住这句话：“一只不黑的狗正在追逐一只不小的兔子，穿过一片不绿的田野。”然而，作家们并没有记住这句话，反讽也因此得以继续使用，直到残暴的独裁者约翰·梅杰几乎将其名声摧毁。

Hansard , the record of the proceedings of the British Parliament, has absolutely no record of John Major ever saying the words ‘not inconsiderable’; 2 but it became his catchphrase nonetheless. These days no journalist ever refers to the twentieth century’s second longest serving Prime Minister without working the phrase in somewhere. Though he never said it, the litotes seemed to sum up all that the public found wrong in him. Where Thatcher would have said ‘big’ and Churchill ‘vast’, Major footled about with a double-negative. Where was the oratory? Where was the charisma? Why didn’t he just come out and say ‘considerable’? It was a slur, but it was a slur that stuck.

英国议会记录《汉萨德议事录》中完全没有约翰·梅杰说过“并非微不足道”这句话的记录；然而，这句话却成了他的口头禅。如今，任何记者在提及这位二十世纪任期第二长的首相时，都会不经意地提到这句话。尽管他从未说过这句话，但这些贬义词似乎概括了公众对他的所有不满。如果撒切尔夫人会用“大”，丘吉尔会用“浩瀚”，梅杰却总是用双重否定来含糊其辞。他的雄辩呢？他的个人魅力呢？他为什么不直接说“相当可观”呢？这是一种贬义，但却是一种根深蒂固的贬义。

Litotes isn’t the best figure to use when you’re trying to be grand. Litotes does not stir the soul, it’s more suited to stirring tea. Even Wordsworth couldn’t make it work like that. He was pretty damned good at raising the spirits and soul, but he had the silly habit of using the phrase ‘not seldom’. ‘Not seldom, clad in radiant vest, / Deceitfully goes forth the Morn’, ‘Not seldom from the uproar I retired’, ‘Not seldom did we stop to watch some tuft / Of dandelion seed’, ‘not seldom in my walks / A momentary trance comes over me’, and on and on until you want to grab him, slap him, pull out a dictionary and show him the word ‘often’.

如果你想营造一种宏大的氛围，那么使用弱化修辞法（litotes）就不是个好主意。弱化修辞法无法触动灵魂，它更像是用来搅拌茶水。即使是华兹华斯也无法驾驭这种修辞手法。他确实很擅长鼓舞人心，但他有个愚蠢的习惯，就是喜欢用“not seldom”这个词。“Not seldom, clad in radiant vest, / Deceitfully goes forth the Morn”（清晨，身披耀眼的背心，/ 诡谲地向前走去），“Not seldom from the uproar I demo”（我常常从喧嚣中退却），“Not seldom did we stop to watch some tuft / Of dandelion seed”（我们常常停下来观看一些蒲公英的种子），“not seldom in my walks / A momentary trance comes over me”（漫步时，/ 一阵短暂的恍惚袭来），诸如此类，不胜枚举，直到你恨不得抓住他，扇他耳光，然后拿出字典，给他看“often”（经常）这个词。

So Orwell wasn’t wrong, but he wasn’t quite right either. Litotes has no place in politics or pastoral poetry. Litotes cannot stand on a podium or cry from a mountaintop, it is much more at home in the drawing room or the bathtub. It’s the sort of figure that should be used by Bertie Wooster. In fact, it was used by Bertie Wooster:

所以奥威尔说的不算错，但也不算完全对。弱化修辞在政治或田园诗中都无容身之地。弱化修辞既不能高高在上，也不能在山巅呐喊，它更适合出现在客厅或浴缸里。这种修辞手法应该由伯蒂·伍斯特来使用。事实上，伯蒂·伍斯特也确实用过它：

As I sat in the bathtub, soaping a meditative foot and singing, if I remember correctly, ‘Pale Hands I Loved Beside the Shalimar’, it would be deceiving my public to say that I was feeling boomps-a-daisy. 3

当我坐在浴缸里，一边冥想般地搓洗着脚，一边哼着歌——如果我没记错的话——《我曾在沙利玛河畔爱过的苍白双手》——如果我说我当时感觉棒极了，那我就是在欺骗我的公众。3

Where ‘Pale Hands I Loved Beside the Shalimar’ is an example of synecdoche.

其中，“我在沙利玛河畔爱过的苍白双手”就是一个提喻的例子。

1 I’m excluding dramatic, proleptic and situational irony.

1. 我不包括戏剧性反讽、预言性反讽和情境性反讽。

2 I have been unable to find any reference to Major ever actually using these words in any context except once in a 1992 speech where he said: ‘It is, of course, as Private Eye or the Guardian would have me say, a time “of not inconsiderable interest in Europe”.’ Of course, it’s not easy to prove a negative.

2 除了在 1992 年的一次演讲中，他曾说过：“当然，正如《私人眼》或《卫报》会让我说的那样，现在是欧洲‘相当引人关注的时期’。”之外，我找不到任何资料表明梅杰在任何场合真正使用过这些词语。当然，要证明某件事不存在并不容易。

3 Jeeves and the Feudal Spirit (1954) by P.G. Wodehouse.

3. P.G.伍德豪斯著《吉夫斯与封建精神》（1954）。

# ↩

Chapter 29

第29章

Metonymy and Synecdoche

转喻和提喻

Everybody knows about metaphors and similes; metonym and synecdoche are the exact opposite. In metaphor and simile you say that two things have a couple of qualities in common. It generally has to be at least two: one obvious one and one that is strongly implied. Suppose that a chap tells the girl he loves that her eyes are as green as emeralds: she’ll probably take that as a compliment, not because emeralds are green but because they’re valuable. If he tells the girl that her eyes are as green as mould, he’ll get a slap; not because he’s inaccurate but because it’s always the second, implied comparison that’s important. Green as beer-bottles suggests that she’s drunk, and green as traffic-lights will probably get him arrested. ‘Your heart is as cold as ice’ is completely different to ‘Your heart is as cold as ice cream’, even though the temperatures are the same.

每个人都知道比喻和明喻；转喻和提喻则恰恰相反。比喻和明喻是指两个事物具有一些共同的特征。通常至少需要两个共同特征：一个显而易见，另一个则强烈暗示。假设一个男人告诉他心爱的女孩，她的眼睛像祖母绿一样绿：她很可能会把这当作赞美，不是因为祖母绿是绿色的，而是因为它们很珍贵。如果他告诉女孩她的眼睛像霉菌一样绿，他肯定会挨一巴掌；不是因为他的描述不准确，而是因为真正重要的是第二个暗示的比较。像啤酒瓶一样绿暗示她喝醉了，而像交通信号灯一样绿则很可能会让他被逮捕。“你的心像冰一样冷”和“你的心像冰淇淋一样冷”截然不同，即使它们的温度相同。

I wandered lonely as a cloud …

我像一朵孤独的云，四处游荡……

Clouds are not lonely. Especially in the Lake District where Wordsworth wrote that line. In the Lake District clouds are remarkably sociable creatures that bring their friends and relatives and stay for weeks. But nobody even notices that the comparison is all wrong because the mind always skips to the second connection which is that clouds do wander aimlessly. It’s not that Wordsworth didn’t know about meteorology, it’s that he did know about metaphor.

云并不孤独。尤其是在华兹华斯写下这句诗的湖区。在湖区，云是极其合群的生物，它们会带着朋友和亲戚，停留数周之久。但没有人注意到这个比喻完全错误，因为人们的思绪总是会跳到第二个联系：云的确漫无目的地游荡。并非华兹华斯不懂气象学，而是他深谙比喻之道。

In the same year that Wordsworth was writing about hiking on English hillsides – 1804 – William Blake was writing a poem about hiking on English hillsides. Blake’s poem is a bit different. For starters it’s about the medieval legend that Jesus spent his twenties in Britain. There is no evidence for this whatsoever, and, so far as historians can tell, Britain’s tourism industry was scandalously underdeveloped at the time. The idea was too ridiculous even for Blake, which is why he hedges his bets and phrases everything as a question. The other difference is that Blake doesn’t use metaphor, he uses metonymy, and more precisely synecdoche.

1804年，华兹华斯创作了描写英国山坡徒步的诗歌，而威廉·布莱克也创作了一首关于英国山坡徒步的诗。布莱克的诗与华兹华斯的诗略有不同。首先，它取材于一个中世纪的传说：耶稣在英国度过了他的二十多岁。然而，没有任何证据支持这一说法，而且据历史学家所知，当时英国的旅游业发展极其滞后。即使对布莱克来说，这个想法也过于荒谬，因此他采取了含糊其辞的方式，将一切都以疑问句的形式表达出来。另一个不同之处在于，布莱克没有使用隐喻，而是使用了转喻，更准确地说是提喻。

Metaphor is when two things are connected because they are similar, metonymy is when two things are connected because they are really physically connected. It’s the favourite rhetorical figure of Fleet Street. Consider the following news report:

隐喻是指将两个事物联系起来，因为它们相似；转喻是指将两个事物联系起来，因为它们在物理上是相连的。这是舰队街最常用的修辞手法。请看以下新闻报道：

Downing Street was left red-faced last night at news that the White House was planning to attack the British Crown with the support of Wall Street. Number 10 said it was ‘unacceptable’ though the Vatican refused to get involved. Meanwhile, the army’s top brass have been ordered to send in the Green Jackets, which will confuse the Americans as they were expecting the Redcoats.

昨晚，唐宁街得知白宫计划在华尔街的支持下攻击英国王室，顿时颜面尽失。首相府表示此举“不可接受”，但梵蒂冈拒绝介入。与此同时，英国陆军高层已奉命派遣绿夹克步兵团，此举令美方措手不及，因为他们原本以为会是红衫军。

Rather than mentioning people, you mention something that they are physically touching. You are no longer you. You are your clothes, you are the building you’re standing in, the medals pinned to your chest or the hat on your head. You are a suit, a blue-stocking, a bit of skirt.

与其提及人，不如提及他们实际接触的事物。你不再是你自己。你变成了你的衣服，你变成了你身处的建筑物，你胸前佩戴的勋章，或是你头上的帽子。你变成了一套西装，一个女学者，或一条短裙。

The extreme form of metonymy is synecdoche, where you become one of your body parts. You are your feet, your lips or your liver.

转喻的极端形式是提喻，在这种修辞中，你变成了你身体的某个部位。你就是你的脚、你的嘴唇或你的肝脏。

All eyes were on the government as they tried to alleviate the famine with a charity theatre matinée. A spokesman said if they got enough bums on seats they could feed all the hungry mouths, but it would have to be all hands on deck as this was about getting feet on the ground. The government said they had their top brains working on it and that the gate from a full house could buy a hundred head of cattle.

所有人的目光都聚焦在政府身上，他们试图通过一场慈善剧院午场演出来缓解饥荒。一位发言人表示，如果能吸引足够多的观众，就能解决所有饥饿的问题，但这需要全员参与，因为关键在于让民众切实参与进来。政府称，他们已派出最顶尖的专家团队参与筹备，如果剧院爆满，门票收入就能购买一百头牛。

So how do you apply that to a poem about Jesus going for stroll?

那么，如何将这个概念应用到一首关于耶稣散步的诗中呢？

And did those feet in ancient time

那些脚在古代也曾存在过吗？

Walk upon England’s mountains green?

漫步在英格兰翠绿的山峦间？

And was the countenance divine

那容貌是神圣的吗？

On England’s pleasant pastures seen?

见过英格兰宜人的牧场吗？

William Blake loved synecdoche. His poems are filled with stray body-parts.

威廉·布莱克喜爱提喻法。他的诗歌中充满了零散的身体部位。

What immortal hand or eye

何等不朽之手或眼

Could frame thy fearful symmetry?

能否勾勒出你那令人恐惧的对称之美？

Or

或者

And what shoulder and what art

以及什么样的肩膀和什么样的艺术

Could twist the sinews of thy heart?

能让你心如刀绞吗？

And when that heart began to beat,

当那颗心脏开始跳动时，

What dread hands and what dread feet?

多么可怕的手和多么可怕的脚？

What makes Blake’s synecdoches so powerful is that we get glimpses. It’s like the opening of a film where we see just a close-up of feet walking on green grass, a hand or an eye in the night-time forests. But whereas in a film the camera would pull out to show the whole scene, Blake never reveals. We see the feet and the shining countenance, but when he pulls out they’ve been replaced by a lamb. Blake works in fragments; when you read his synecdoches you have to see the world in a grain of sand.

布莱克的提喻之所以如此有力，在于它让我们得以窥见一斑。这就像电影的开头，我们看到的只是绿草地上行走的脚的特写，或是夜幕降临后森林中的一只手或一只眼睛。但电影中，镜头会拉远展现整个场景，而布莱克却从未揭示。我们看到了脚和闪亮的面容，但当镜头拉远时，它们已被一只羔羊所取代。布莱克的创作以碎片化的方式呈现；当你阅读他的提喻时，你必须从一粒沙子中看到整个世界。

And synecdoches can be so vivid, that’s the power of the close-up. When Dr Faustus sold his soul to the Devil, part of his price was to see the most beautiful woman who had ever lived: Helen of Troy. She was brought before him and he asked:

提喻法可以如此生动，这就是特写镜头的力量。浮士德博士将灵魂卖给魔鬼时，他付出的代价之一就是见到有史以来最美丽的女人：特洛伊的海伦。她被带到他面前，他问道：

Was this the face that launched a thousand ships

这就是引发千船齐鸣的那张脸吗？

And burnt the topless towers of Ilium?

然后烧毁了伊利昂的无顶塔楼？

He didn’t need to phrase it like that. He could have said:

他没必要那样说。他本可以说：

Is this the woman for the sake of whose beauty the Greeks launched a large naval force and besieged the city of Troy (also known as Ilium), a siege that eventually resulted in the city being sacked and burnt?

这位女子是否就是希腊人为了她的美貌而派出庞大的海军力量围攻特洛伊城（又称伊利昂城），最终导致该城被洗劫一空并焚毁的那位呢？

The meaning would have been exactly the same. But Christopher Marlowe didn’t write it like that. He used three synecdoches. Helen is only a face. The Trojan War is a snapshot image of a thousand ships setting sail. Troy is only burning towers. Ten years of elaborate Greek mythology in three clear images: a face, a flotilla, and turrets set ablaze.

意思本应完全相同。但克里斯托弗·马洛并没有那样写。他运用了三种提喻。海伦只是一张脸。特洛伊战争只是一幅千艘战船扬帆起航的画面。特洛伊城只是燃烧的塔楼。十年的复杂希腊神话浓缩成三个清晰的意象：一张脸、一支舰队和熊熊燃烧的塔楼。

All this relies, of course, on the historical synecdoche, where one part of a story stands for the whole thing, not because it’s a symbol of it, but because it’s part of it. The Boston Tea Party, the storming of the Bastille, and the fall of the Berlin Wall are all synecdoches. They are fragments that narrate a whole story.

当然，这一切都依赖于历史提喻，即用故事的一部分来代表整体，并非因为它象征着整体，而是因为它本身就是整体的一部分。波士顿倾茶事件、攻占巴士底狱和柏林墙倒塌都是提喻的例子。它们是叙述完整故事的片段。

The hand that rocks the cradle rules the world, and the right fragment implies the world. And we are nothing more than hungry eyes, cheating hearts, lying lips, and faithless arms. Although all those are also transferred epithets.

摇篮的手主宰世界，正确的碎片象征着世界。而我们不过是饥渴的双眼、欺骗的心、说谎的嘴唇和背信弃义的双臂。尽管这些也都是引申义。

# ↩

Chapter 30

第三十章

Transferred Epithets

转移别名

A transferred epithet is when an adjective is applied to the wrong noun. So instead of writing ‘The nervous man smoked a cigarette’ you write ‘The man smoked a nervous cigarette’. Cigarettes, of course, do not have feelings; yet we understand immediately what that second sentence means. A transferred epithet is a good thing, or, rather, a good epithet is a transferred thing.

修饰语转移是指将形容词用在了错误的名词上。例如，与其写“那个紧张的男人抽了一支烟”，不如写成“那个男人抽了一支紧张的香烟”。当然，香烟没有感觉；但我们立刻就能明白第二句话的意思。修饰语转移是件好事，或者更确切地说，好的修饰语本身就是一种转移。

It’s astonishing how often epithets are transferred and how little we notice. Nobody ever stops to think about a disabled toilet, and why and how it has been disabled. Perhaps the flush has been sabotaged or the U-bend deliberately blocked. Once you point out the transfer, it becomes rather amusing. P.G. Wodehouse was the great master of this technique. His transfers are just a little too ridiculous to work. ‘I lit a rather pleased cigarette’ is just a bit too much, as is ‘I balanced a thoughtful lump of sugar on the teaspoon’; but Wodehouse’s best, for my considered money, was: ‘His eyes widened and an astonished piece of toast fell from his grasp.’ 1 The idea of astonished toast is just too much, and we let out a surprised chortle.

令人惊讶的是，形容词的转移如此频繁，而我们却对此浑然不觉。没人会停下来思考残疾人厕所，以及它为何以及如何被改造成残疾人厕所。或许是冲水装置被人动了手脚，又或许是U型弯管被人故意堵塞。一旦你指出这种转移，它就变得颇为滑稽。P·G·伍德豪斯是运用这种技巧的高手。他的转移手法略显荒诞，难以令人信服。“我兴高采烈地点燃了一支香烟”就有点过火，就像“我若有所思地把一块方糖放在茶匙上”一样；但依我看来，伍德豪斯最精彩的描写是：“他瞪大了眼睛，一块惊愕的吐司从他手中滑落。”¹ “惊愕的吐司”这个概念实在太过夸张，我们不禁发出惊讶的轻笑。

But the transferred epithet is not always fun and games. ‘Dulce et Decorum Est’ by Wilfred Owen is a pretty grim poem about the effects of mustard gas, but the transferred clumsy fits right in:

但这种移位修饰并非总是轻松愉快的。威尔弗雷德·欧文的《甜美而光荣》（Dulce et Decorum Est）是一首描写芥子气危害的相当阴郁的诗，但“笨拙”这个修饰却恰如其分地贴切在诗中：

Gas! Gas! Quick, boys! – An ecstasy of fumbling,

加油！加油！快，伙计们！——一阵慌乱的摸索，

Fitting the clumsy helmets just in time …

及时戴上了笨重的头盔……

And in Gray’s Elegy it feels really rather … elegiac:

而格雷的挽歌则给人一种非常……哀伤的感觉：

The ploughman homeward plods his weary way

农夫拖着疲惫的步伐，艰难地走回家。

We don’t laugh at the idea that the way is weary rather than the ploughman. It feels natural, particularly, for some reason, with roads. We accept that miles can be weary, roads lonesome and highways lost, because we know that in each case the adjective describes the weary, lonesome, lost chap and not the thoroughfare.

我们不会嘲笑“道路疲惫不堪”而非“耕夫疲惫不堪”这种说法。这感觉很自然，尤其是在谈到道路时，不知为何更是如此。我们接受“路途漫长令人疲惫”、“道路寂寞难耐”、“高速公路迷失方向”的说法，因为我们知道，在这些例子中，形容词描述的是疲惫、寂寞、迷失方向的人，而不是道路本身。

T.S. Eliot was a compulsive transferrer of epithets. In a mere three lines of ‘Prufrock’ retreats mutter, nights are restless, hotels are one-night, and restaurants are made of, or possibly serve saw-dust, it isn’t clear which. Presumably the saw-dust is on the floor, but one of the odd things about the transferred epithet is that you don’t need to even mention the noun that should be taking the adjective. You can leave it to be guessed. You need only mention the dizzy heights and imagination will supply the human.

T·S·艾略特是个喜欢把形容词移位的诗人。在《普鲁弗洛克》这首诗短短三行里，就出现了这样的比喻：隐居处低声细语，夜晚躁动不安，酒店只提供一夜情，餐厅是用锯末做的，或者可能供应锯末——具体是哪一种并不明确。想必锯末是在地板上，但这种移位形容词的奇特之处在于，你甚至不需要提及应该被形容词修饰的名词。你可以让它留给读者去猜测。你只需要提及令人眩晕的高度，想象力就会赋予它人性。

Epithets are almost always transferred between humans and their surroundings, and it’s almost always a one-way street. The emotions leak out from us. The loneliness seeps through the soles of our shoes onto the road. Our clumsiness springs from our fingers onto the recalcitrant helmets. Wordsworth wrote of lonely rooms, but he never wrote about third-floor people containing en-suite bathrooms.

人与环境之间几乎总是相互影响，而且这种影响几乎总是单向的。情感从我们身上流淌而出。孤独感透过鞋底渗入路面。笨拙的举止从指尖传递到顽固的头盔上。华兹华斯描写过孤独的房间，但他从未描写过住在三楼、拥有独立卫浴的人。

The transferred epithet makes the world come alive. Prufrock’s city mutters restlessly and Gray’s fields tinkle drowsily. This is particularly true when the first noun is missing. You can say ‘The nervous man smoked a cigarette’. You can say ‘The man smoked a nervous cigarette’. But you can also say ‘A nervous cigarette was smoked’. Dizzy heights and guilty secrets can stand on their own. The man has vanished altogether. All that’s left are objects with human emotions.

移位修饰语使世界鲜活起来。普鲁弗洛克的城市躁动不安地低语，格雷的田野昏昏欲睡地叮当作响。当第一个名词缺失时，这种感觉尤为强烈。你可以说“那个紧张的男人抽了一支烟”。你可以说“那个男人抽了一支紧张的烟”。但你也可以说“一支紧张的烟被抽了”。令人眩晕的高度和不可告人的秘密可以独立存在。那个男人彻底消失了。剩下的只有具有人类情感的物体。

Charles Dickens would have been the greatest master of the transferred epithet, except that he rarely used it. He went much, much further:

查尔斯·狄更斯本可以成为运用移位修饰语的最伟大大师，但他很少使用这种修辞手法。他在这方面走得更远：

Mr Jaggers never laughed; but he wore great bright creaking boots; and, in poising himself on these boots, with his large head bent down and his eyebrows joined together, awaiting an answer he sometimes caused the boots to creak, as if they laughed in a dry and suspicious way.

贾格斯先生从不笑；但他穿着又大又亮又吱吱作响的靴子；当他用这双靴子站稳，低着头，眉毛紧蹙，等待着回答时，他有时会让靴子发出吱吱声，仿佛它们在以一种干巴巴、可疑的方式笑着。

It’s as though Dickens tried using the transferred epithet and then decided, ‘It’s not enough. I need more!’ So he went and built a world in which all objects are alive. In Dickens’ strange mind, mists were lazy, houses crazy, and snowflakes went into mourning and wore black. It’s terrifying and it’s beautiful, but the simple movement of the adjective has been left far behind. You can never tell, when Dickens talks about a threatening house or a miserable mist, whether anybody was meant to have these emotions in the first place. This was not the classic transferred epithet, it was the dark heart of Dickens’ mind, and we should leave in a hurry.

仿佛狄更斯先尝试了移位形容词，然后觉得“这还不够，我需要更多！”于是他构建了一个万物皆有灵的世界。在狄更斯奇特的想象中，雾气懒散，房屋疯狂，雪花也披上了黑色的丧服。这既令人恐惧又令人着迷，但形容词简单的变化早已被抛诸脑后。当狄更斯描写阴森的房子或令人沮丧的雾气时，你永远无法确定，这些感受是否真的存在于现实生活中。这并非经典的移位形容词，而是狄更斯内心深处的黑暗，我们最好还是赶紧离开。

The transferred epithet has very vague borders. Do happy days and lonely nights count? What about a knowing smile or sarcastic laugh? When Brutus stabbed Caesar and Shakespeare wrote:

这种转移的形容词界限非常模糊。快乐的日子和孤独的夜晚算吗？心照不宣的微笑或讽刺的笑声呢？当布鲁图斯刺杀凯撒时，莎士比亚写道：

This was the most unkindest cut of all

这是最残酷的一刀。

I can’t decide whether that’s a transferred epithet or just an accurate description of a cut. But it is certainly a case of pleonasm.

我无法确定这究竟是修饰语还是对切口的准确描述。但可以肯定的是，这是一种赘述。

1 For a fuller analysis see ‘The Transferred Epithet in P.G. Wodehouse’ by Robert A. Hall, Jr., Linguistic Inquiry , Vol. 4, No. 1 (Winter, 1973), pp. 92–4.

1 有关更详细的分析，请参阅 Robert A. Hall, Jr. 的《P.G. Wodehouse 中的转移绰号》，载于《语言学研究》第 4 卷第 1 期（1973 年冬季），第 92-94 页。
