Chapter 31

第31章

Pleonasm

赘言

Pleonasm is the use of unneeded words that are superfluous and unnecessary in a sentence that doesn’t require them. It’s repeating the same thing again twice, and it annoys and irritates people. Some cannot see a pleonasm without flying into a furious rage. But that is rather silly. There are three different varieties of pleonasm: the tiny, the lazy, and the lovely.

赘述是指在句子中使用多余的、不必要的词语。它相当于重复相同的内容两次，令人厌烦。有些人一看到赘述就勃然大怒，但这其实很荒谬。赘述有三种类型：微不足道的、懒惰的和可爱的。

Let us start with the tiny. Psalm 121 begins thus:

让我们从最细微之处开始。《诗篇》121篇开头是这样的：

I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help.

我要向山举目，我的帮助从何而来？

There are people who would find that line inspiring. They would read it and run off to live better lives of purity and holiness up a hill somewhere. There are others who would find it infuriating. Twice. They would read it and as they did so the veins would stand out on their furious foreheads, the saliva would drip from their maddened mouths, and they would take a big red marker pen out of their pockets and delete two words.

有些人会觉得这句话很鼓舞人心。他们读完后会立刻逃离，遁入山林，过上纯洁圣洁的生活。而另一些人则会觉得这句话令人怒不可遏，甚至怒不可遏。他们会一边读着这句话，一边怒火中烧，额头青筋暴起，口水直流，然后从口袋里掏出一支粗红的记号笔，把那两个字删掉。

First, there’s the word ‘up’. What other direction can you lift something? It’s almost as bad as ‘fall down’ or ‘enter into’. It is (some would say) an insult to the intelligence and an abuse of the English language. But it’s not nearly as bad as ‘from whence’. Whence means from where . So what does ‘from whence’ mean? ‘From from where’? It’s enough to make you shoot yourself, and then write an angry letter to the paper.

首先是“up”这个词。除了向上，你还能往哪个方向举东西？它几乎和“fall down”或“enter into”一样糟糕。（有些人会说）这简直是对智商的侮辱，是对英语的滥用。但它远不及“from whence”那么糟糕。“whence”的意思是“从哪里”。那么，“from whence”到底是什么意思呢？“从哪里”？简直让人想自杀，然后给报社写封愤怒的信。

People who think like this lead terrible lives. They have never married, simply because they couldn’t bear to hear the words:

有这种想法的人过着糟糕的生活。他们从未结婚，仅仅因为他们无法忍受听到以下这些话：

Dearly beloved , we are gathered together in the sight of God, and in the face of this congregation, to join together this man and this woman in Holy Matrimony …

亲爱的弟兄姐妹们，我们今天聚集在上帝面前，在各位会众面前，共同见证这对新人缔结神圣的婚姻……

They can’t enjoy Hamlet because of the unnecessary ‘that’ in ‘To be or not to be, that is the question’. And they can’t even throw themselves in front of a train and put an end to their lives of misery and woe, because they’re not sure about railway tracks .

他们欣赏不了《哈姆雷特》，因为“生存还是毁灭，这是一个问题”里多余地加了个“那个”。他们甚至不敢跳到火车前结束自己痛苦不堪的生活，因为他们连铁轨都搞不清楚。

The reason usually given for such anger is that the unnecessary word, the pleonasm, is wasting the reader’s time. As though anybody’s time were so valuable that reading the word ‘up’ might mess up their schedule. Those with the time to complain about time-wasting have too much time on their hands.

人们通常对这种愤怒的解释是，多余的词语（赘述）浪费了读者的时间。仿佛任何人的时间都如此宝贵，以至于读到“向上”这个词就会打乱他们的计划似的。那些有时间抱怨浪费时间的人，真是闲得慌。

The second kind of pleonasm is quite different. It’s the lazy adjective noun. This is a world of personal friends, added bonuses and free gifts. They are annoying for two contradictory reasons: first of all nobody talks like that, and secondly everybody talks like that.

第二种赘述方式截然不同，它是一种懒惰的形容词名词。这种赘述充斥着私人朋友、额外福利和免费赠品。它令人厌烦的原因有两个，而且这两个原因本身就自相矛盾：首先，没人会那样说话；其次，每个人都那样说话。

I have never said the words ‘free gift’. It would seem a sinister thing to say when gathered around the Christmas tree. ‘Here’s my free gift, and, as an added bonus, here’s a festive Christmas card.’ People would think I’d gone mad. Yet, if you wander into a shop or make the terrible mistake of turning on the television or radio, you will hear of havens that are safe, co-operation that is mutual, and prizes that are, it turns out, to be won.

我从未说过“免费礼物”这几个字。在圣诞树下，大家围坐在一起，说这话似乎有点不吉利。“这是我的免费礼物，另外，还附赠一张圣诞贺卡。”人们会觉得我疯了。然而，如果你走进一家商店，或者犯了打开电视或收音机的可怕错误，你就会听到各种关于安全港湾、互惠合作以及奖品的故事——而这些奖品，原来是可以赢得的。

Such phrases lumber about the language like zombies. They were created long ago by insanely evil marketing executives who were desperate to progress forward and sell their foreign imports to the general public. But, like Frankenstein’s monster, they could not be stopped. They still lurk in shops and howl from televisions; even though their original inventor is past history.

这类短语如同僵尸般在语言中游荡。它们是很久以前由那些疯狂邪恶的营销主管炮制出来的，这些人为了推进业务发展，急于将进口商品推销给大众，不惜一切代价。但就像弗兰肯斯坦的怪物一样，它们无法被彻底消灭。即使它们的创造者早已成为历史，它们仍然潜伏在商店里，在电视机里咆哮。

And finally, there is the third and best kind of pleonasm: the lovely pleonasm of emphasis. A free gift may be put down to thoughtlessness, but ‘free, gratis and for nothing’ is quite deliberate. It is certainly pleonasm, but it is also effective. It is the pneumatic drill of repetition that gives emphasis and insistence to the notion that you don’t have to pay a penny. A pedant may scream at the phrase ‘I saw it with my own two eyes’, but in conversation it means something. When Shakespeare wrote of ‘Th’inaudible and noiseless foot of time’, it wasn’t that he hadn’t thought it through. It was the same deliberate mind that had Hamlet complain:

最后，还有第三种也是最妙的一种赘述：强调式的赘述。免费赠送礼物或许会被归咎于粗心大意，但“免费、无偿、不劳而获”却是经过深思熟虑的。这当然是赘述，但也十分有效。它就像一台气动式的重复机器，强调并强化了“你无需支付一分钱”这一概念。一个迂腐的人可能会对“我亲眼所见”这句话大加挞伐，但在日常对话中，它却蕴含着意义。莎士比亚写下“时间那无声无息的脚步”时，并非是他没有深思熟虑。正是这种深思熟虑的思维，让哈姆雷特发出了这样的抱怨：

How weary, stale, flat and unprofitable

多么令人厌倦、陈旧、乏味且无利可图啊！

Seem to me all the uses of this world.

在我看来，这世间万物皆有其用。

We are all casual creatures and we say things that we don’t really mean; so, when we really mean a thing, we say it twice. Or three times. Or sixteen times in a single speech, if you’re complaining about a dead parrot that is:

我们都是随性的人，常常说一些言不由衷的话；所以，当我们真的想表达什么的时候，我们会说两遍。或者三遍。如果你是在抱怨一只死鹦鹉，那甚至可能在一句话里说十六遍：

1. Passed on

1. 已传递

2. No more

2. 不再有

3. Ceased to be

3. 不再是

4. Expired

4. 已过期

5. Gone to meet its maker

5. 去见造物主了

6. Stiff

6. 僵硬

7. Bereft of life

7. 失去生命

8. Rests in peace

8. 安息

And so on and so forth until we get to …

如此往复，直到我们到达……

16. Ex

16. 例如

This is pleonasm, but it’s pleonasm for an effect. The tragic truth of the parrot’s mortality can be communicated only through repetition. And the only comfort can be found in the funeral service’s ‘sure and certain hope of the resurrection’, where the pleonasm’s power is set against the fragile ‘hope’.

这虽是赘述，却是为了达到某种效果。鹦鹉终有一死的悲剧真相只能通过重复来传达。而唯一的慰藉，则寄托于葬礼上“对复活的坚定信念”，在这里，赘述的力量与脆弱的“希望”形成了鲜明的对比。

Pleonasm is absolutely natural and absolutely necessary. Kipling was undoubtedly being pleonastic when he wrote:

赘述是完全自然且完全必要的。吉卜林写下以下文字时，无疑是在赘述：

Oh, East is East, and West is West, and never the twain shall meet,

哦，东方是东方，西方是西方，两者永不相交。

Till Earth and Sky stand presently at God’s great Judgment Seat.

直到天地万物如今都站在上帝的伟大审判台前。

But you cannot take a red marker pen to that sentence without destroying it. Kipling needed to insist that East really, truly, actually was East; and that West really, truly, actually, factually was West. All Kipling was doing here was restating, rather memorably, the Law of Identity. The idea that a thing is itself dates back to the days of Socrates, Aristotle, togas and casual pederasty. It was formulated by Gottfried Leibniz as ‘A is A’. This truth of logic is unchanging, a point demonstrated by the twentieth-century thinker Herman Hupfeld who asserted that:

但你不能用红笔涂改这句话而不破坏它。吉卜林需要强调东方的确是东方；西方的确是西方。吉卜林在这里所做的，只是以一种令人印象深刻的方式重申了同一律。事物本身就是同一的观念可以追溯到苏格拉底、亚里士多德、托加长袍和随意的男童恋的时代。戈特弗里德·莱布尼茨将其表述为“A是A”。这一逻辑真理永恒不变，二十世纪思想家赫尔曼·胡普菲尔德就证明了这一点，他断言：

A kiss is still a kiss,

吻就是吻，

A sigh is just a sigh;

叹息只是叹息而已；

But for pure pleonasm nobody has ever beaten Gertrude Stein, who took the trouble to point out in her poem ‘Sacred Emily’ that a ‘Rose is a rose is a rose is a rose’.

但论纯粹的赘述，没有人能胜过格特鲁德·斯坦因，她特意在诗作《神圣的艾米丽》中指出，“玫瑰就是玫瑰就是玫瑰就是玫瑰”。

This was, by far, Stein’s most famous line. It’s been adapted and parodied a million and one times, most memorably by Ernest Hemingway, who fell out with Miss Stein and wrote, ‘A bitch is a bitch is a bitch is a bitch’. Stein reused the line herself, and added an ‘A’ to the beginning just in case anybody thought that she wasn’t being pleonastic and was just describing a girl whose name was Rose. Stein’s girlfriend, Alice Toklas, took to marketing dinner plates that had the phrase written all the way around the edge. The crockery version has no beginning and no end and is therefore a case of infinite pleonasm. That’s only possible, of course, because the last word of the sentence is the same as the first word, which makes it an example of epanalepsis.

这无疑是斯坦最著名的一句话。它被改编和戏仿了无数次，其中最令人印象深刻的是欧内斯特·海明威的版本。海明威与斯坦小姐闹翻后，写道：“婊子就是婊子，婊子就是婊子，婊子就是婊子。”斯坦本人也重新使用了这句话，并在开头加了一个“A”，以防有人误以为她不是在赘述，而只是在描述一个名叫罗斯的女孩。斯坦的女友爱丽丝·托克拉斯甚至开始销售印有这句话的餐盘。餐具版的这句话没有开头也没有结尾，因此是一种无限赘述。当然，这只有在句子的最后一个词与第一个词相同的情况下才有可能，这使得它成为一种重复句。

# ↩

Chapter 32

第32章

Epanalepsis

埃帕纳莱普西斯

John Lennon complained that the song ‘Yesterday’ didn’t go anywhere. You find out that the guy’s unhappy, and that he longs for the past, but it never goes beyond that. There’s no resolution. Lennon was quite right. After all, the song begins with the word ‘yesterday’ and ends 125 words later with the word ‘yesterday’.

约翰·列侬抱怨说，《Yesterday》这首歌没有后续发展。你会发现歌里的主人公并不快乐，他怀念过去，但仅此而已，没有更深入的探讨。没有结局。列侬说得没错。毕竟，这首歌以“yesterday”开头，125个字后又以“yesterday”结尾。

It’s a circular song, which ends where it began. And it even does it at a smaller level. The first verse begins and ends with the same word – ‘yesterday’ – and so does the second – ‘suddenly’ – and so does the third – ‘yesterday’ again. But that’s probably the song’s strength. It’s about a man who can’t think of anything else but yesterday, and the words mirror that rather beautifully. It’s also a double case of epanalepsis: beginning and ending with the same word.

这是一首循环往复的歌，首尾呼应，甚至在更小的层面上也体现了这一点。第一段歌词以同一个词开头和结尾——“昨天”；第二段以“突然”开头和结尾；第三段又以“昨天”开头和结尾。但这或许正是这首歌的精妙之处。它讲述的是一个满脑子都是昨天的男人，歌词恰如其分地反映了这一点。此外，这首歌还运用了双重重复手法：以同一个词开头和结尾。

Ending where you began has two effects that are, at first sight, contradictory. It gives the impression of going nowhere, and it gives the impression of moving inevitably on. So each New Year’s Day you’re back where you started: 1 January. And each New Year’s Day an old year is gone for ever and a new one is upon you. Time moves ever onwards, and Time scampers around in circles. It’s the same thing with epanalepsis.

以起点结束会产生两种乍看之下自相矛盾的效果。它给人一种原地踏步的感觉，又给人一种不可避免地继续前行的感觉。所以，每个新年，你都回到了起点：1月1日。每个新年，旧的一年永远地过去了，新的一年开始了。时间不断向前流逝，时间也在原地打转。回文也是如此。

‘The king is dead; long live the king’ sums up both sides of epanalepsis. On the one hand it announces that the old monarch is dead and gone, and that there is a new king on the throne. On the other hand, it curtly tells republicans that there will always be a monarch. Everything has changed, and everything has remained the same. 1

“国王驾崩，新王万岁”概括了复数形式的两面性。一方面，它宣告旧君主驾崩，新王登基；另一方面，它又简洁地告诉共和主义者，君主制将永远存在。一切都变了，一切又都没变。

Epanalepsis implies circularity and continuation. When Robert Burns wrote of ‘Man’s inhumanity to man’ he didn’t say that that inhumanity breeds inhumanity, but he implied it with the epanalepsis. It sounds so like ‘A lie begets a lie’ or ‘Nothing will come of nothing’ that we can’t help feeling that there’s an unending inhuman circle of dog eat dog eat dog eat dog. The phrase wouldn’t have been nearly as memorable if Burns had written ‘Man’s inhumanity to others’.

循环往复句暗示着循环和延续。罗伯特·伯恩斯在写到“人对人的不人道”时，并没有直接说这种不人道滋生不人道，而是通过循环往复句暗示了这一点。这听起来很像“谎言滋生谎言”或“无中生有”，让我们不禁觉得存在着一个永无止境的残酷循环，弱肉强食，永无止境。如果伯恩斯写的是“人对他人不人道”，这句话就不会如此令人难忘了。

‘Man’s inhumanity to man’ is only one clause of one sentence. But epanalepsis can work at any scale you like. Paul McCartney finished his song by repeating a word; but Lewis Carroll finished his poem ‘Jabberwocky’ by repeating the whole of the first verse. It has the same effect, though. The Jabberwock may be slain, but it’s still brillig, the toves are still slithy, and the mome raths continue their outgrabing. Everything has changed, but everything is still the same.

“人对人的残忍”只是句子中的一个从句。但重复句式可以运用在任何尺度上。保罗·麦卡特尼用重复一个词结束了他的歌曲；而刘易斯·卡罗尔则用重复第一节诗句的方式结束了他的诗歌《杰伯沃克》。尽管如此，效果却是一样的。杰伯沃克或许已被杀死，但它依然是布里利格（brillig，一种神秘生物），托夫斯依然是滑溜溜的，莫姆拉斯依然在抓挠。一切都变了，但一切又都依旧如故。

Of course, epanalepsis doesn’t have to be used to imply circularity and continuation, it’s just at its best when it does. Shakespeare wrote that ‘men of few words are the best men’, but it’s not a particularly memorable line. Nor is ‘Cassius from bondage will deliver Cassius’. Even his extended versions didn’t catch on. Nobody remembers:

当然，循环重复修辞手法并非一定要用来暗示循环和延续，只是当它用于此目的时效果最佳。莎士比亚写道“少言寡语者为上等之人”，但这句台词并不令人印象深刻。“卡西乌斯将解救卡西乌斯”也是如此。即使是他的加长版也没能流行起来。没人记得：

Blood hath bought blood and blows have answered blows;

血债血偿，拳打脚踢；

Strength matched with strength, and power confronted power:

以强对抗以强，以权力对抗权力：

But that’s probably because nobody reads King John . There are times when Shakespeare seems to have given up on epanalepsis altogether. In Julius Caesar he has a battle of the speeches. Antony gives his ‘Friends, Romans, countrymen’ in answer to Brutus’ much less famous ‘Romans, countrymen and lovers’ speech. Frankly, the term ‘lovers’ is a bit weird when addressing a large crowd of unwashed Romans. Shakespeare made Brutus’ speech deliberately bad. And he filled it with epanalepsis.

但那大概是因为没人读《约翰王》。莎士比亚似乎有时完全放弃了重复修辞手法。在《尤利乌斯·凯撒》中，他安排了一场演说对决。安东尼发表了“朋友们，罗马人，同胞们”，回应布鲁图斯那段远不如安东尼著名的“罗马人，同胞们，还有爱人们”的演说。坦白说，对着一大群衣衫褴褛的罗马人说“爱人们”确实有点怪异。莎士比亚故意把布鲁图斯的演说写得糟糕透顶，并且大量运用了重复修辞手法。

Romans, countrymen, and lovers! hear me for my cause, and be silent, that you may hear: believe me for mine honour, and have respect to mine honour, that you may believe:

罗马人、同胞、爱人们！请听我陈述我的缘由，并保持安静，以便你们能听见；请相信我的荣誉，并尊重我的荣誉，以便你们能相信我。

It’s as though Shakespeare was sick and tired of a rhetorical figure that had never really worked for him. But he didn’t give up on it entirely. He hit the jackpot with epanalepsis once, out on a blasted heath, with an old man shouting at the weather.

莎士比亚似乎对这种从未真正奏效的修辞手法感到厌倦。但他并没有完全放弃它。有一次，他在荒凉的旷野上，用一个老人对着天气咆哮的场景，成功地运用了倒叙手法。

If you think about it, writing a play involving wind and rain is a bold move in a world before fans and hosepipes. King Lear has to magic up his own scenery and storm. The weather was in the poetry, and Shakespeare seemed to like the challenge. He pulled out epanalepsis, not because of its circularity, but because of the pure emphasis on repetition. Lear’s epanalepsis is one of command. It’s the sort of sentence uttered by somebody who is used to being obeyed, and gets angry when he isn’t.

仔细想想，在风扇和水管出现之前的年代，创作一部涉及风雨的戏剧可谓大胆之举。《李尔王》中的场景和风暴都得靠莎士比亚的魔法来营造。天气本身就蕴藏在诗歌之中，而莎士比亚似乎乐于接受这种挑战。他运用了反复修辞手法，并非因为其循环性，而是因为它纯粹强调重复。李尔王的反复修辞是一种命令式的表达。这种句子出自一个习惯于被人服从，一旦不被服从便会勃然大怒的人之口。

Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks! rage! blow!

吹吧，风，吹裂你的脸颊！怒吼吧！吹吧！

Which is also an example of Shakespearean personification.

这也是莎士比亚式拟人手法的一个例子。

1 Except, of course, when there’s a Queen, at which point the epanalepsis is ruined.

1 当然，除非有女王，那样的话，这种变奏就毁了。

# ↩

Chapter 33

第33章

Personification 1

拟人化1

Personification is strange woman. She wanders about holding a mask and talking to herself. She’s never there when you think she is, and when she does turn up, she tries to take over your life. But most importantly, she’s very, very hard to define. Women, eh?

拟人化是个古怪的女人。她戴着面具四处游荡，自言自语。你以为她会出现的时候，她却总是不见踪影；而当她真的出现时，她又会试图掌控你的生活。但最重要的是，她真的很难定义。女人啊，真是如此。

Duty calls, money talks, sleep beckons, and work phoned up to see if you could come in on Saturday. All of these are, technically, personifications. But they don’t follow through. ‘That was work on the phone’ is an utterly natural phrase. But it would be followed by ‘ they want me to come in on Saturday’. Not he or she. ‘Work’ there is something like a group noun, or a synecdoche (q.v.). It’s not a human figure with eyes and lips and legs and bad breath.

职责召唤，金钱至上，睡意袭来，还有工作电话问你周六能不能来上班。从技术上讲，这些都是拟人化的修辞手法。但它们并没有衔接得更自然。“那是工作电话”这句话本身很自然，但后面应该接“他们想让我周六来上班”。这里不是“他”或“她”。这里的“工作”更像是一个名词，或者说是一种提喻（参见相关条目）。它不是一个有眼睛、嘴唇、腿，甚至还有口臭的人形。

Work personified could be a beautiful figure. He would be a large cruel man, I think, with a schedule in one hand and a whip in the other. He would wear a suit with money stuffed in the pockets. He would be invincible except when he did battle with the beautiful Lady Public Holiday who would arrive from the seaside on a white horse holding an ice cream and a broken alarm clock. They would fight in the stadium of …

工作的化身或许会是一个英俊的人物。我想，他会是一个身材魁梧、冷酷无情的男人，一手拿着日程表，一手拿着鞭子。他会穿着西装，口袋里塞满了钱。他所向披靡，唯独在与美丽的“公共假日女士”的战斗中才会败下阵来。这位女士会骑着白马从海边而来，手里拿着冰淇淋和一个坏掉的闹钟。他们会在体育场里决一死战……

But I’m getting carried away. Work is not personified in the phrase ‘work phoned’. And money is not personified just before it talks. Duty calls but we never really hear its gruff voice. Necessity is the mother of invention, but did she have an epidural?

但我有点跑题了。“工作来电”这句话里，工作并没有被拟人化。金钱在开口说话之前，也没有被拟人化。责任召唤，但我们从未真正听到它粗犷的声音。需要是发明之母，但她打了无痛分娩针吗？

At the other end of the spectrum there’s allegory. Allegory is proper personification, in fact it’s personification that has moved in and taken over the whole story. In allegory the person isn’t just suggested by a human verb, it’s fleshed out and dressed up and given a house to live in. The best-known example in English is The Pilgrim’s Progress , where a chap subtly named Christian meets a giant called Despair (and his wife, Diffidence) and gets bogged down in symbolic bogs and climbs a hill called Difficulty and so on and so forth until any sensible person is bored to tears.

在另一个极端，则是寓言。寓言是真正的拟人化，事实上，拟人化已经渗透并主导了整个故事。在寓言中，人物并非仅仅由人类动词暗示，而是被赋予血肉、装扮，甚至被赋予了居所。英语中最著名的例子是《天路历程》，主人公克里斯蒂安遇到了一个名叫绝望的巨人（以及他的妻子，名叫羞怯），他陷入了象征性的沼泽，攀登了一座名为困难的山，如此反复，直到任何一个理智的人都感到厌倦为止。

Now, there’s nothing wrong with allegory of this kind, but it has no place in this book. Here we are dealing only with the effects that can be achieved in a single sentence, or at most a paragraph. Allegory is for finer minds than mine, and deeper souls. Also, it tends to religion. Not just because the best examples are religious, but because personification is very close to deification. People worship money and nature, or rather Money and Nature, and turn them quickly into goddesses or gods. It’s often hard to see whether they really mean it. In King Lear Edmund says:

这种寓言本身并无不妥，但它并不适合本书。本书只探讨一句话，最多一个段落所能达到的效果。寓言是为比我更有智慧、更有深度的人准备的。而且，它往往与宗教有关。这不仅是因为最好的寓言例子都与宗教有关，还因为拟人化与神化非常接近。人们崇拜金钱和自然，或者更确切地说是金钱和自然，并迅速将它们变成女神或神。我们常常很难判断他们是否真的这么想。在《李尔王》中，埃德蒙说：

Thou, nature, art my goddess; to thy law

自然啊，你是我的女神；我服从你的法则

My services are bound.

我的服务已达成。

And you can’t quite tell whether he means it. After all, the Ancient Romans worshipped Love (Venus) and War (Mars) and ironmongery (Vulcan), and it’s not entirely clear to what extent they were personifications or gods or both and neither. It probably depended on the Ancient Roman.

你很难判断他是否真心如此。毕竟，古罗马人崇拜爱神维纳斯、战争女神玛尔斯和铁器之神伏尔甘，但这些神祇究竟是人格化的化身，还是真正的神，抑或两者兼具，却又都不是，这一点并不完全清楚。这或许取决于古罗马人自身的理解。

So at one end, we have personification that barely exists, and at the other we have personification that’s gone too far for us. Or, to put it another way, personification wears invisible shoes and a huge, flowery hat. Yet somewhere in between, somewhere around the nether regions, we have the personification that really works, and of which Shakespeare was the greatest master.

所以，一方面，拟人手法几乎不存在；另一方面，拟人手法又矫枉过正。或者换句话说，拟人手法就像穿着隐形鞋，戴着一顶巨大的花帽。然而，在两者之间，在某种模棱两可的境地，我们拥有真正有效的拟人手法，而莎士比亚正是这方面的大师。

In Othello Iago warns Othello about jealousy.

在《奥赛罗》中，伊阿古警告奥赛罗要提防嫉妒。

O, beware, my lord, of jealousy;

哦，我的大人，要提防嫉妒；

It is the green-eyed monster which doth mock

是嫉妒的绿眼怪兽在嘲弄

The meat it feeds on;

它所食用的肉类；

Iago could just have called jealousy a monster. It would have done the job. There’s no particular reason to mention the eye colour, but it’s just enough to bring the monster to life. It’s only a glimpse, a moment’s revelation; but there it is, the real monster, suddenly glaring out at you. And then the peep-hole, which was opened for a moment, is slammed shut and we’re back with Othello and Iago sitting in a room in Cyprus, discussing handkerchiefs.

伊阿古完全可以把嫉妒比作一个怪物，这样就足够了。虽然没必要特意提及眼睛的颜色，但这足以让这个怪物栩栩如生。这只是惊鸿一瞥，一瞬间的揭示；但它就在那里，真正的怪物，突然间怒目而视。然后，那只被打开过片刻的窥视孔砰地一声关上，我们又回到了奥赛罗和伊阿古坐在塞浦路斯的一间房间里，讨论着手帕的场景。

Shakespeare had tried the trick before. Like many of his best lines he took a couple of stabs at it. A few years before, in The Merchant of Venice , he’d had ‘shuddering fear, and green-eyed jealousy’, but the problem with that line is that it’s not necessarily a personification. It could just be that jealousy makes your eyes turn green. If I say that I’m in a ‘wild-eyed panic’ that just means that I’m wild-eyed.

莎士比亚以前就尝试过这种手法。就像他许多最精彩的台词一样，他曾多次尝试过。几年前，在《威尼斯商人》中，他用了“战栗的恐惧和嫉妒的绿眼”这样的表达，但问题在于，这句台词未必是拟人化的。它可能仅仅是指嫉妒会使人的眼睛变绿。如果我说我“惊恐万分”，那仅仅意味着我惊恐万分。

Either way, Shakespeare had been honing this technique since his earliest plays. Eyes and faces, glimpsed for a moment, and then gone. Just a brush from Personification’s elbow as she dashes by. Contrast and compare:

无论如何，莎士比亚从早期剧作开始就一直在磨练这种技巧。眼睛和脸庞，一闪而过，随即消失。就像拟人化的人物匆匆掠过时，手臂轻轻擦过。对比分析：

‘Bold-faced Victory’ ( Henry VI Part 1 )

《厚颜无耻的胜利》（亨利六世 第一部）

‘Close-tongued Treason’ ( The Rape of Lucrece )

《密语叛国》（《鲁克丽丝受辱记》）

‘Open-eyed Conspiracy’ ( The Tempest )

《睁眼阴谋》（《暴风雨》）

‘Fire-eyed Fury’ ( Romeo and Juliet )

“怒火中烧的愤怒”（《罗密欧与朱丽叶》）

‘The silver hand of Peace’ ( Henry IV Part 2 )

《和平的银手》（亨利四世第二部）

‘Pale-faced Fear’ ( Henry VI Part 1 )

《面色苍白的恐惧》（亨利六世 第一部）

‘The iron tongue of Midnight’ ( A Midsummer Night’s Dream )

《午夜的铁舌》（《仲夏夜之梦》）

‘Smooth-faced peace’ ( Richard III )

“表面和睦的和平”（理查三世）

‘That smooth-faced gentleman, tickling Commodity’ ( King John )

“那位面容光滑的绅士，逗弄着商品”（约翰王）

And on and on and on. And people tell you that Shakespeare was inspired. He practised. Each one has a person, a visible person, leap into existence, be glimpsed, and vanish. Usually he used a single body-part to imply the whole, but sometimes he gave his abstraction a house. In Henry VI Part 2 we glimpse, for one line, ‘Lean-faced Envy in her loathsome cave’. And then we leave her there, not even knowing why she was a woman.

就这样，没完没了。人们说莎士比亚灵感迸发，他反复练习。每一部作品中，都有一位人物，一个清晰可见的人物，跃然纸上，令人惊鸿一瞥，随即消失。他通常用一个身体部位来象征整体，但有时也会为他的抽象形象赋予一栋房子。在《亨利六世》第二部中，我们只瞥见一行字：“瘦骨嶙峋的嫉妒，在她那令人作呕的洞穴里”。然后，我们就把她留在了那里，甚至不知道她为什么是女人。

But two persons stalk through all Shakespeare’s plays: Time and Death. Each is seen only in glimpses. Time’s foot is inaudible, his hand is cruel, and he carries a sickle. Death is a fuller figure. He’s a shrunken carcass, a carrion, he wears rags but his ribs are bare. He carries a pale flag and wears a black veil over his loathsome visage. And he eats people. Shakespeare’s Death doesn’t lead people away to an afterlife, he munches them in his steel jaws, an eternal feast that takes place in the eternal cell in his secret house in a melancholy vale. Death also has sex. Not often, but he does. Cleopatra is understandable. But Juliet too:

但莎士比亚的所有戏剧中都贯穿着两个人物：时间和死亡。他们都只是惊鸿一瞥。时间的脚步悄无声息，他的手残酷无情，手中挥舞着镰刀。死亡则是一个更为丰满的身影。他像一具干瘪的尸体，一具腐肉，衣衫褴褛却肋骨毕露。他手持一面苍白的旗帜，用黑色面纱遮盖着他那令人作呕的面容。而且，他吃人。莎士比亚笔下的死亡不会引领人们走向来世，而是用他钢铁般的下颚将他们吞噬，这是一场永恒的盛宴，在他位于忧郁山谷深处的秘密居所的永恒牢房中进行。死亡也有性生活。虽然不频繁，但他的确有。克莉奥佩特拉的性欲可以理解。但朱丽叶的性欲也同样可以理解：

O son! the night before thy wedding-day

哦，儿子！你婚礼的前夜

Hath Death lain with thy wife. There she lies,

死神是否与你的妻子同眠？她就躺在那里。

Flower as she was, deflowered by him.

她原本是朵花，却被他夺去了贞洁。

Death is my son-in-law, Death is my heir;

死神是我的女婿，死神是我的继承人；

My daughter he hath wedded: I will die,

他娶了我的女儿：我将死去，

And leave him all; life, living, all is Death’s.

把一切都留给他吧；生命、生活，一切都属于死亡。

And then he eats her.

然后他把她吃了。

What this tells us about Shakespeare’s psyche, I don’t know and don’t want to know. The important thing is that you only get this complete picture of hungry, randy, ragged death if you read the whole of Shakespeare’s works and put it together. Because Shakespeare does it all in glimpses. One detail and then Death is hidden away again. It’s beautiful and it’s remarkably effective. This isn’t the half-personification of ‘duty calls’, but it’s not the full-blown allegory either. It’s one detail and no more.

这揭示了莎士比亚怎样的心理，我不知道，也不想知道。重要的是，只有通读莎士比亚的全部作品，并将它们融会贯通，你才能完整地看到一个饥渴、好色、衣衫褴褛的死神形象。因为莎士比亚总是用寥寥几笔勾勒出死神的轮廓。一个细节，死神便再次隐匿。这种手法精妙绝伦，效果惊人。这并非“职责召唤”的半拟人化，也并非完整的寓言。它只是一个细节，仅此而已。

Unfortunately this technique pretty much died with Shakespeare. There are a few examples since, and each one has been beautiful. Andrew Marvell gave Time a mode of transport:

可惜的是，这种技法几乎随着莎士比亚的去世而失传了。此后也出现过一些例子，而且每一个都堪称佳作。安德鲁·马维尔赋予了时间一种独特的载体：

But at my back I always hear

但我总能听到身后传来的声音

Time’s wingèd chariot hurrying near

时间的飞车正疾驰而来

Imagine if it had been:

想象一下如果真是那样：

Relentless Time still hurrying near

无情的时间仍在匆匆逼近

The whole beauty of the line would have been lost. But as long as you have that one wingèd chariot, you have an image. ‘The awakening Morn’ wouldn’t be anything much. So Milton wrote:

整首诗的美感都会消失殆尽。但只要保留了那辆带翼战车，就有了画面感。“醒来的早晨”也就失去了意义。所以弥尔顿写道：

For we were nursed upon the self-same hill,

因为我们都成长于同一座山上，

Fed the same flock, by fountain, shade, and rill.

同一群鸟儿，在喷泉旁、树荫下和小溪边觅食。

Together both, ere the high Lawns appeared

两者同时出现，高高的草坪显现出来。

Under the opening eye-lids of the morn

清晨，在睁开的眼睑下

Mind you, Milton stole that from the Book of Job, which has ‘the eyelids of the morning’, but he stole it well.

请注意，弥尔顿是从《约伯记》中剽窃来的，《约伯记》中有“清晨的眼睑”的描写，但他剽窃得非常出色。

And then Personification became less popular. She stayed home more and more, and grew ill. Keats tried to take her on a few dates, but she grew pale, and spectre-thin, and died. Duty still calls, money still talks, and work still phones up; but Personification isn’t what she used to be. Poor girl.

后来，拟人化不再那么受欢迎了。她越来越少待在家里，身体也越来越差。济慈曾试图约她出去几次，但她脸色苍白，骨瘦如柴，最终去世了。责任依然召唤，金钱依然摆在眼前，工作依然不时打来电话；但拟人化已不再是以前的她了。可怜的姑娘。

She’s not quite dead, though. That would be an overstatement.

她还没完全死透。这么说有点夸张了。

1 The Greek term, since you ask, is prosopopoeia. But for once we have a nice, normal English word that does the trick without lining up innumerable vowels.

1 既然你问了，希腊语的术语是prosopopoeia。但这一次，我们终于找到了一个简洁明了的英语单词，无需排列无数个元音就能达到目的。

# ↩

Chapter 34

第34章

Hyperbole

夸张

Hyperbole (pronounced hi-PER-boh-lee) is the technical term for exaggeration, and even though we have literally thousands of English words that mean the same thing, hyperbole is one of the few technical Greek rhetorical terms that absolutely everybody knows.

夸张（发音为 hi-PER-boh-lee）是夸大其词的专业术语，尽管英语中有成千上万个单词意思相同，但夸张是少数几个每个人都知道的希腊修辞学专业术语之一。

That may be because we exaggerate constantly. The human being is the great embroiderer. It’s not enough for us to say that we waited for ten minutes; we have to wait ‘for ages’. If I’ve told you twice, I’ve told you a thousand times. If you’re rich, you have a ton of money. It’s enough to make you break down in a flood of tears.

或许是因为我们总是夸大其词。人就像伟大的刺绣师，我们不会只说等了十分钟，非要说“等了很久很久”。我说了两遍，就好像说了上千遍一样。如果你很有钱，拥有很多钱，那足以让你泪流满面。

However, we do not use hyperbole enough. We lack ambition. The state of Kansas is actually flatter than a pancake. 1 It’s quite possible to have a ton of money. All you need is £2,853.93 in coppers. If you really want to make a hyperbole work, you must make sure that it is beyond anything that is even vaguely possible. What is the point in a mere ton of money? Damon Runyon (who called money ‘potatoes’ as that was the New York slang of the time) went much further:

然而，我们夸张的修辞手法运用得不够充分。我们缺乏雄心壮志。堪萨斯州实际上比煎饼还平坦。¹ 拥有巨额财富并非不可能。你只需要2853.93英镑的铜板。如果你真的想让夸张的修辞手法奏效，你必须确保它超越任何哪怕一丝可能。区区一吨钱又有什么意义呢？达蒙·鲁尼恩（他把钱称为“土豆”，因为那是当时纽约的俚语）的夸张程度更甚：

[A]nybody who ever reads the newspapers will tell you that Miss Abigail Ardsley has so many potatoes that it is really painful to think of, especially to people who have no potatoes whatever. In fact, Miss Abigail Ardsley has practically all the potatoes in the world, except maybe a few left over for general circulation.

凡是读过报纸的人都会告诉你，阿比盖尔·阿兹利小姐拥有的土豆多得令人难以置信，尤其是对那些连土豆都没有的人来说。事实上，阿比盖尔·阿兹利小姐几乎拥有全世界所有的土豆，可能只剩下一些供大众享用。

That’s a lot of potatoes, and that’s a proper hyperbole. Given that people recognise an exaggeration when they hear one, you might as well go for it. At the same time that Runyon was describing money on the East Coast, Dashiell Hammett was describing private detectives on the West.

那可是好多土豆啊，这绝对是夸张的说法。既然人们一听就知道这是夸张，那你不妨就这么用吧。就在鲁尼恩描写东海岸的金钱时，达希尔·哈米特正在描写西海岸的私家侦探。

He was a swarthy little Canadian who stood nearly five feet in his high-heeled shoes, weighed a hundred pounds minus, talked like a Scotchman’s telegram, and could have shadowed a drop of salt water from Golden Gate to Hongkong without ever losing sight of it.

他是一个皮肤黝黑的小个子加拿大人，穿着高跟鞋也差不多有五英尺高，体重不到一百磅，说话像苏格兰电报一样，而且他能从金门大桥一路追踪一滴海水到香港而不离开视线。

Indeed, the Americans seem to be the modern masters of the impossible hyperbole. Next to their mountainous overstatements, an Englishman’s languid and effete attempts are subatomically small.

的确，美国人似乎是现代夸张修辞的个中高手。与他们滔天巨作相比，英国人那些懒散乏味的尝试简直微不足道。

Yet there was a time when the English could do that sort of hyperbole too. Long, long ago, at a time when the Big Bang was still a recent and painful memory, lived a man called Sydney Smith (1771–1845). One day, Reverend Smith was informed that a chap who lived down the road had got engaged to a lady who was not exactly skinny. His response was not exactly gentlemanly, but it was properly hyperbolic.

然而，英国人也曾有过使用这种夸张手法的时期。很久很久以前，在宇宙大爆炸的记忆还很模糊、令人痛苦的年代，住着一位名叫悉尼·史密斯（1771-1845）的人。有一天，史密斯牧师听说住在附近的一位男士和一位身材并不苗条的女士订婚了。他的反应虽然称不上绅士风度，但却恰如其分地运用了夸张的修辞手法。

Marry her! Impossible! You mean a part of her; he could not marry her all himself. It would be a case not of bigamy, but trigamy; the neighbourhood or the magistrates should interfere. There is enough of her to furnish wives for a whole parish. One man marry her! – it is monstrous. You might people a colony with her; or give an assembly with her; or perhaps take your morning walk round her, always provided there were frequent resting places, and you were in rude health. I once was rash enough to try walking round her before breakfast, but only got half-way, and gave it up exhausted. Or you might read the Riot Act and disperse her; in short, you might do anything with her but marry her.

娶她！不可能！你指的是她的一部分；他不可能娶她全部。那不是重婚，而是三婚；邻居或地方法官应该会干预。她足够多的妻子供整个教区的人使用。一个人娶她！——简直是疯了。你可以用她建立一个殖民地；或者用她召开一次集会；或者，你也可以绕着她晨练，前提是沿途有充足的休息点，而且你身体健康。我曾经鲁莽地尝试在早餐前绕着她散步，结果只走了一半就筋疲力尽地放弃了。或者你可以颁布《骚乱法案》驱散她；总之，你可以对她做任何事，但就是不能娶她。

Next to these heroic efforts, most of Shakespeare’s exaggerations seem like understatements. The best he could do for ‘You’re very fat’ was his description of Falstaff as ‘this horseback-breaker, this huge hill of flesh’. It’s hardly enough. He had his moments, of course; Shakespeare usually did.

与这些英雄般的壮举相比，莎士比亚的大多数夸张之词都显得轻描淡写。他能对“你很胖”这句话做的最好的描述，也只是把福斯塔夫形容为“这个压垮马背的家伙，这座巨大的肉山”。这远远不够。当然，他也有夸张的时刻；莎士比亚通常都是如此。

Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood

海王星浩瀚的海洋能否洗净这血迹

Clean from my hand? No, this my hand will rather

我手上干净吗？不，我的手宁愿

The multitudinous seas in incarnadine,

深红色的众多海洋，

Making the green one red.

把绿色的改成红色。

But that is mainly memorable for the strange verb incarnadine . For top-grade hyperbole we need to go back and consult the Son of God.

但最令人印象深刻的还是那个奇怪的动词“incarnadine”。要论顶级的夸张修辞，我们得去请教上帝之子了。

And why do you look at the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not consider the plank in your own eye? Or how can you say to your brother, ‘Let me remove the speck from your eye’; and look, a plank is in your own eye? Hypocrite! First remove the plank from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.

为什么你只看到你弟兄眼中的刺，却看不到自己眼中的梁木呢？你怎能对你弟兄说：‘让我去掉你眼中的刺’，而你自己眼中却有梁木呢？你这假冒为善的人！先去掉自己眼中的梁木，然后才能看得清楚，去掉你弟兄眼中的刺。

All things are, of course, possible with Jesus, but having a large plank of wood in your eye and not noticing is an extreme example. It’s almost as silly as trying to get a whole camel through the eye of a needle, which is an impossibility, or, to put it technically, an adynaton.

当然，在耶稣里凡事皆有可能，但眼睛里插着一块大木板却浑然不觉，这算是一个极端例子。这几乎和试图把一整头骆驼穿过针眼一样荒谬，而这根本不可能，或者更确切地说，是不可能完成的任务。

1 See Fonstad, Pugatch, Vogt, 2003, The Annals of Improbable Research , Vol. 9.

1 参见 Fonstad、Pugatch、Vogt，2003 年，《不可能研究年鉴》，第 9 卷。

Chapter 35

第35章

Adynaton

阿迪纳顿

And again I say unto you, It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God.

我又告诉你们，骆驼穿过针眼比财主进神的国还容易呢。

Matthew 19, verse 24

马太福音19章24节

This verse has always rather worried rich men, 1 who tend to ask themselves how much a really damned big needle would cost. There’s a pretty theory that there was once a Needle Gate in the walls of Jerusalem that camels could get through, provided they went down on their knees. Unfortunately for the rich, it’s utterly untrue; but it’s a nice idea.

这句诗一直让富人们颇为烦恼¹，他们常常琢磨着一根特别粗的针到底要多少钱。有一种说法是，耶路撒冷城墙上曾经有一座针门，骆驼只要跪下就能通过。可惜的是，这对富人来说纯属无稽之谈；不过，这倒是个不错的想法。

Even the disciples, who were a pretty low-income lot, ‘were exceedingly amazed, saying, Who then can be saved?’ To which Jesus comfortingly replied that ‘with God all things are possible’. Jesus’ importance for rhetoric is therefore that he didn’t believe in adynata.

就连那些家境贫寒的门徒也“极其惊讶，问道：‘这样，谁能得救呢？’”耶稣安慰地回答说：“在神，凡事都能。”因此，耶稣在修辞学上的重要性在于，他不相信神迹奇事（adynata）。

An adynaton (pronounced ad-in-ART-on) is impossible. Before an adynaton will work, pigs will fly, Hell will freeze over and the Devil will go skiing. You might as well try to get blood out of a stone. It’s therefore a very easy, if very periphrastic, way of saying no.

异能（发音为 ad-in-ART-on）是不可能的。异能实现之前，猪都会飞，地狱都会结冰，魔鬼都会去滑雪。这就像试图从石头里榨出血一样徒劳。因此，这是一种非常简单但又非常迂回的否定说法。

John Donne could have written that honesty gets you nowhere. Instead, he wrote:

约翰·邓恩本可以写道，诚实毫无益处。但他却写道：

Go and catch a falling star,

去抓住一颗流星吧。

Get with child a mandrake root,

给孩子服用曼德拉草根，

Tell me where all past years are,

告诉我往年都去哪儿了？

Or who cleft the devil’s foot,

或者谁劈开了魔鬼的脚，

Teach me to hear mermaids singing,

教我如何聆听美人鱼的歌声，

Or to keep off envy’s stinging,

或者为了避免嫉妒的刺痛，

And find

并找到

What wind

风

Serves to advance an honest mind.

有助于培养诚实的思想。

Similarly the sentence ‘I’m not going to go out with that girl again; she’s from Scarborough’ is a trifle tedious. But if you instead agree to take her back if she can perform three impossible tasks, you can have some fun. You can demand that she make you a cambric shirt without using needle and thread, that she finds you an acre of land between the sea and the shore, and that she reaps it with a leather sickle. Chuck in some parsley, sage, rosemary and thyme and bingo. You’ve got yourself a folk song, although not a Scarborian girlfriend.

同样，“我不会再和那个女孩约会了；她来自斯卡伯勒”这句话也略显乏味。但如果你同意如果她能完成三项不可能完成的任务就和她复合，你就能从中找到乐趣。你可以要求她不用针线为你缝制一件细棉布衬衫，找到一英亩位于海边和海岸之间的土地，并用皮镰刀收割。再添上一些欧芹、鼠尾草、迷迭香和百里香，瞧！你就拥有了一首民谣，虽然你没有一个斯卡伯勒的女朋友。

Any negative can be transformed into an adynaton. There tend to be two forms: ‘you might as well try to …’ and ‘not until …’. However, they’re pretty interchangeable. A supporter of Ulysses S. Grant predicted the result of the 1869 Presidential election thus:

任何否定句都可以转化为肯定句。肯定句通常有两种形式：“不妨试试……”和“直到……”。然而，它们几乎可以互换使用。尤利西斯·S·格兰特的一位支持者曾这样预测1869年总统选举的结果：

Build a worm-fence round a winter supply of summer weather; catch a thunder-bolt in a bladder; break a hurricane to harness; hang out the ocean on a grape-vine to dry; but never, sir, never for a moment delude yourself with the idea that you can beat Grant.

用蚯蚓围住过冬的夏季天气；用膀胱接住雷电；驯服飓风；把海洋挂在葡萄藤上晾干；但是，先生，千万不要妄想你能打败格兰特。

But he could just as well have phrased it: ‘When you’ve managed to build a worm-fence [etc. etc. etc.] then you’ll beat Grant.’ Conversely you could take W.H. Auden’s exclamation of undying love:

但他也可以这样说：“等你建好防虫篱笆（等等等等）之后，你就能打败格兰特了。”反过来，你也可以看看W·H·奥登那句关于永恒之爱的感叹：

‘I’ll love you, dear, I’ll love you

“我会爱你，亲爱的，我会爱你。”

Till China and Africa meet,

直到中国和非洲相遇，

And the river jumps over the mountain

河流跃过山峦

And the salmon sing in the street,

鲑鱼在街头歌唱，

‘I’ll love you till the ocean

我会爱你直到海洋尽头

Is folded and hung up to dry

折叠好后挂起来晾干。

And the seven stars go squawking

七颗星星开始鸣叫

Like geese about the sky.’ 2 , 3

如同天空中的大雁。’2,3

And change it to ‘I’m about as likely to stop loving you as …’.

改成“我停止爱你的可能性就像……”。

The important thing is that, in terms of content, Auden’s lines only say ‘I’ll always love you’. The adynata are purely adornments. They’re verbal fun. They’re Auden sitting around dreaming up impossibilities and making them rhyme.

重要的是，就内容而言，奥登的诗句只表达了“我将永远爱你”。那些附加的音节纯粹是装饰，是语言上的趣味，是奥登闲暇时天马行空地构思并押韵的产物。

Adynaton is just Greek for ‘impossible’, but that doesn’t mean that anything impossible is an adynaton, because in rhetoric adynaton is just a long way round of saying ‘this is the case’. Almost any sentence can have an adynaton added in. ‘My name is Mark Forsyth’ can become ‘If my name isn’t Mark Forsyth, may the crayfish whistle on the mountainside’ (which is, apparently, the Russian equivalent of pigs might fly).

“Adynaton”在希腊语中是“不可能”的意思，但这并不意味着任何不可能的事情都是“adynaton”，因为在修辞学中，“adynaton”只是表达“事实如此”的一种迂回方式。几乎任何句子都可以添加“adynaton”。例如，“我的名字是马克·福赛斯”可以变成“如果我的名字不是马克·福赛斯，愿小龙虾在山坡上吹口哨”（这显然是俄语中“猪会飞”的对应说法）。

So when Auden reused the image of the sea drying up in ‘Funeral Blues’: 4 , 5

所以当奥登在《葬礼蓝调》中再次使用大海干涸的意象时：4,5

Pour away the ocean and sweep up the wood

倾倒海水，扫除木柴

For nothing now can ever come to any good.

现在什么事都不会有好结果了。

… it’s not an adynaton, he was just being sad. The same goes for Chesterton’s ‘When fishes flew and forests walked’, or for the great Mormon Sex In Chains case of 1977, where a former Miss Wyoming abducted and ravaged a Mormon missionary, later stating: ‘I loved Kirk so much I would have skied down Mount Everest in the nude with a carnation up my nose.’ That’s not a proper rhetorical adynaton, it’s just love.

……这不是修辞上的夸张，他只是在表达悲伤。切斯特顿的《当鱼儿飞翔，森林行走》也是如此，1977年著名的摩门教性奴案也是如此。那起案件中，一位前怀俄明小姐绑架并强奸了一位摩门教传教士，事后她说：“我太爱柯克了，就算他一丝不挂，鼻子上插着康乃馨，我也愿意滑雪下珠穆朗玛峰。”这不是修辞上的夸张，这只是爱。

Sometimes, the lines get a bit blurry. The famous graffito, ‘A woman needs a man like a fish needs a bicycle’, is kind of an adynaton, and kind of not. And sometimes something can be a rhetorical adynaton without really being impossible. Hamlet’s poem of true love to Ophelia was meant to describe a series of impossibilities:

有时候，界限会变得模糊不清。著名的涂鸦“女人需要男人就像鱼需要自行车一样”既算是修辞上的悖论，又不算。有时，某种说法在修辞上是悖论，但实际上并非不可能。哈姆雷特写给奥菲莉娅的那首关于真爱的诗，意在描述一系列不可能之事：

Doubt thou the stars are fire;

你若怀疑星辰是火，岂不更可悲？

Doubt that the sun doth move;

怀疑太阳是否会移动；

Doubt truth to be a liar;

怀疑真相就是说谎；

But never doubt I love.

但请永远不要怀疑我对你的爱。

But the Danish Prince was unfortunate in all things. First Copernicus put paid to the moving sun, and then Arthur Eddington in 1920 pointed out that stars are not fire, but instead produce their light through the fusion of hydrogen to helium. If Ophelia had had even a passing knowledge of modern astrophysics she would have realised that their relationship was doomed.

但这位丹麦王子真是诸事不顺。先是哥白尼否定了太阳自转的理论，然后1920年，爱丁顿又指出恒星并非燃烧，而是通过氢聚变成氦发光。如果奥菲莉娅对现代天体物理学稍有了解，她就会意识到他们的关系注定失败。

In the prologue to the medieval religious dream poem Piers Plowman , the poet says that you ‘Might as well measure the mist on Malvern Hills’ 6 as get a lawyer to talk without first paying him a fee. Unfortunately there is now a weather station on Malvern Hills, and the humidity is measured and reported. 7

在中世纪宗教梦幻诗《农夫皮尔斯》的序言中，诗人写道，你“还不如去测量马尔文山上的雾气”<sup>6</sup>，就像不先付钱就去找律师一样。不幸的是，现在马尔文山上确实有一个气象站，湿度会被测量并公布<sup>7</sup>。

It’s sad to see Time’s toothless mouth laughing the poets to scorn. The stars are all explained and the mist is all measured, and there is no magic left in this dreary world. But the legal profession still charge exorbitant fees. That at least is a truth we can cling to. After all, Shakespeare’s first famous line, as we have seen, was ‘The first thing we do, let’s kill all the lawyers’.

令人悲哀的是，时间那张无齿的嘴巴嘲笑着诗人。星辰已被解释，迷雾已被测量，这凄凉的世界里已无任何魔法可言。但律师行业依然收取着天价费用。至少这是我们可以抓住的真理。毕竟，正如我们所见，莎士比亚的第一句名言是“我们做的第一件事，就是杀光所有律师”。

Which is an example of prolepsis.

这是前推的一个例子。

1 Rich women, it seems, are in the clear.

1 看来，富有的女性似乎可以免受牵连。

2 ‘As I Walked Out One Evening’. Copyright © 1940. By W.H. Auden, renewed. Reprinted by permission of Curtis Brown, Ltd.

2 《一天晚上我外出散步时》。版权所有 © 1940。作者：W.H. 奥登，已续期。经柯蒂斯·布朗有限公司许可转载。

3 While we’re at it, you may also want to notice the diacope, polysyndeton, catachresis, alliteration and anaphora (q.v.).

3 顺便提一下，你可能还想注意一下叠音、多连接词、误用、头韵和首字母重复（参见相关条目）。

4 Copyright © 1940. By W.H. Auden, renewed. Reprinted by permission of Curtis Brown, Ltd.

4 版权所有 © 1940 年，W.H. 奥登所有，已续展。经柯蒂斯·布朗有限公司许可转载。

5 Burns had the same line: ‘Till a’ the seas gang dry, my dear, / And the rocks melt wi’ the sun.’ But the adynaton is rather overdone – impossibility is one thing, but warm sunshine in Scotland is ridiculous.

5 伯恩斯也写过类似的诗句：“直到大海干涸，亲爱的，/岩石在阳光下融化。”但这种夸张的说法有点过头了——不可能是一回事，但苏格兰温暖的阳光就太荒谬了。

6 ‘Thou mightest beter meten the myst on Malverne hulles / Then geten a mom of heore mouth til moneye be schewed.’

6 ‘Thou mightest beter meten the myst on Malverne hulles / Then geten a mom of heore mouth til moneye be swewed.’

7 www.malvernwx.co.uk/Graphs/2013/2013_humidity.gif

7 www.malvernwx.co.uk/Graphs/2013/2013_humidity.gif

# ↩

Chapter 36

第三十六章

Prolepsis

预演

They’re simple things, pronouns. Your English teacher probably explained them to you like this. You use a noun and afterwards, when you want to refer to it , you can use a pronoun, like ‘it’. The reader knows what the pronoun refers to because it appeared earlier in the sentence. Or it appeared earlier in the paragraph.

代词很简单。你的英语老师可能这样解释过：你先用名词，之后想指代它的时候，可以用代词，比如“它”。读者之所以知道代词指代的是什么，是因为它在句子前面出现过。或者它在段落前面出现过。

About pronouns they were sometimes wrong, the old masters ; because you can use a pronoun before saying what it refers to. It’s an odd little technique, and it’s called prolepsis. 1

关于代词，老一辈大师们有时也会犯错；因为你可以在说出代词所指代的对象之前使用它。这是一种奇特的小技巧，叫做预叙法。¹

It’s perfectly natural, prolepsis. We use it all the time in conversation, but we rarely write it down. Somehow the rules that our teachers taught us reach out their chalky hands and stop the pen. It takes a very good poet to unlearn the rules. When we do, the effect is remarkable. After all:

预叙是很自然的。我们在日常对话中经常使用，但很少把它写下来。不知怎的，老师教给我们的那些规则就像沾满粉笔的手一样，阻止了我们写作。只有真正优秀的诗人才能摒弃这些规则。一旦我们做到了，效果就非常显著。毕竟：

They fuck you up, your mum and dad.

你的父母会毁了你。

They may not mean to, but they do.

他们或许并非有意如此，但事实的确如此。

is not an amazing observation, especially for an observer of Philip Larkin’s talents. (I, for one, would replace the F with a B.) But even if you take the Freudian view and agree with the content, many would baulk at the coarse simplification of the message. Nonetheless, it’s one of the most famous first lines in twentieth-century poetry. To work out why, you just need to see what it would look like without the prolepsis:

这并非什么惊人的发现，尤其对于一位了解菲利普·拉金才华的人来说更是如此。（就我个人而言，我会把F换成B。）即便你接受弗洛伊德的观点并认同其内容，许多人也会对这种粗暴的简化处理感到不满。尽管如此，它仍然是二十世纪诗歌中最著名的开篇之一。要弄明白个中缘由，你只需看看去掉预叙之后会是什么样子：

Your mum and dad, they fuck you up

你爸妈把你毁了

Or, if you insist on keeping the rhyme:

或者，如果你坚持要押韵：

You’re fucked up by your mum and dad

你被你爸妈毁了

But no. They’ve lost it, those alternatives, they’ve lost it good and proper. The mysterious prolepsis always gives you a good line, especially a first one. Philip Larkin (1971) had probably learnt that lesson from the first line of Stevie Smith’s ‘Not Waving But Drowning’ (1957), which uses exactly the same technique for its first line:

但不行。他们失去了那些选择，彻底失去了它们。神秘的预叙总能带来一句精彩的句子，尤其是第一句。菲利普·拉金（1971）可能从史蒂薇·史密斯的《不是挥手而是溺水》（1957）的第一句中汲取了这一教训，因为那首诗的第一句就运用了完全相同的技巧：

Nobody heard him, the dead man,

没有人听到他说话，死者的声音。

But still he lay moaning;

但他仍然躺着呻吟；

And Stevie Smith had probably learnt it from the first line of W.H. Auden’s ‘Musée Des Beaux Arts’ 2 (1938), which uses exactly the same technique:

而史蒂薇·史密斯很可能是从 W.H. 奥登的《美术馆》（1938 年）的第一句诗中学到的，这首诗使用了完全相同的技巧：

About suffering they were never wrong,

在苦难这件事上，他们从未犯错。

The old Masters: how well they understood …

古代大师们：他们对……的理解多么深刻……

And W.H. Auden had probably learnt it from the first line of Ernest Dowson’s ‘Vitae Summa Brevis’ (1896), which uses exactly the same technique again:

W.H. 奥登很可能是从欧内斯特·道森的《人生简史》（1896 年）的第一行中学到的，因为那句话再次使用了完全相同的技巧：

They are not long, the weeping and the laughter,

哭泣和欢笑并不长久，

Love and desire and hate;

爱、欲望和恨；

I think they have no portion in us after

我认为他们与我们之间没有任何瓜葛。

We pass the gate.

我们穿过大门。

And then repeats it for the even more famous second verse:

然后，他又重复了一遍，唱出了更为著名的第二段歌词：

They are not long, the days of wine and roses,

美酒与玫瑰的时光并不长久。

Out of a misty dream

从迷雾般的梦境中

Our path emerges for a while, then closes

我们的道路出现了一段时间，然后又消失了。

Within a dream.

在梦中。

Prolepsis has two great advantages. First, it has mystery, but not too much. When a poem opens with a pronoun, a little bit of your mind thinks to itself: ‘What? What the hell’s going on? Who? Who are they ?’ For a moment it weeps and wonders, but only for a moment, because a few words later, before the full stop is even upon us, you find out that they are the old masters, or your mum and dad, or the days of wine and roses. The mystery is opened, your attention is grabbed, and then the mystery is solved.

预叙法有两个优点。首先，它营造了一种神秘感，但又不会过分。当一首诗以代词开头时，你的脑海中会浮现出一丝疑惑：“什么？这到底是怎么回事？是谁？他们是谁？” 你会短暂地感到困惑和疑惑，但这种困惑转瞬即逝，因为几个字之后，甚至在句号出现之前，你就会发现，他们可能是古代大师，可能是你的父母，也可能是美好的旧时光。谜团被揭开，你的注意力被牢牢抓住，然后谜底也随之揭晓。

This sort of thing can go horribly wrong if you get too ambitious with your mystery pronouns. There’s a certain kind of thriller novel that always opens:

如果你在悬疑部分使用过于花哨的代词，这类事情可能会变得非常糟糕。有一种悬疑小说总是以这样的开头：

There were three of them. He’d known that all along. But why had she sent them? He thought of telling them that he didn’t have it any more, any of it. But if they knew those were gone, they might tell her that he didn’t have them. Then he’d really be for it.

一共三个。他一直都知道。但她为什么要送来？他想过告诉他们他什么都没有了。但如果他们知道那些东西不见了，他们可能会告诉她他没有那些东西。那样的话，他就真的会同意了。

Such openings drive any sane reader insane, and only play into the hands of book-burners. But the principle is sound, and used much more subtly and successfully by the greatest poets in the English language.

这样的开头会让任何一个理智的读者抓狂，只会正中焚书者的下怀。但其背后的原理是合理的，英语世界最伟大的诗人运用得更加巧妙和成功。

The second reason that prolepsis is so effective is that it is thoughtful and natural. We have all, after thinking about something for a while, lost in meditation, suddenly said something like ‘That’s it!’ or ‘They’re all in it together!’ or ‘She couldn’t possibly have known that, at the time of the murder, the clocks would all have been turned back an hour.’ And then, noticing that there are others in the room who won’t have understood what we’re talking about, we add an explanatory noun: ‘Beer’ or ‘the CIA and the cartels’ or ‘Lady Chlamydia Glossop’. So when Auden starts his poem with ‘About suffering they were never wrong’, it’s as though he’s actually been sitting in the Musée Des Beaux Arts, staring at a painting and lost in thought. And when he says ‘The old Masters’, it’s as though he’s suddenly realised he’s been talking aloud, and now wishes to explain himself.

预叙如此有效的第二个原因是它深思熟虑且自然流畅。我们都曾有过这样的经历：思考某事许久，陷入沉思之后，突然脱口而出：“就是它！”或者“他们都是一伙的！”又或者“她不可能知道，谋杀案发生时，时钟都拨慢了一个小时。”然后，意识到房间里还有其他人可能听不懂我们在说什么，我们便会加上一个解释性的名词：“啤酒”、“中央情报局和贩毒集团”或者“衣原体格洛索普夫人”。所以，当奥登以“论苦难，他们从未错”作为诗歌的开头时，就好像他真的坐在巴黎美术博物馆里，凝视着一幅画作，陷入沉思。而当他说到“古代大师们”时，就好像他突然意识到自己一直在自言自语，现在想要解释一番。

Similarly, you can imagine somebody standing at dawn on Westminster Bridge, looking at London. After a while, he says, to nobody in particular, ‘Earth has not anything to show more fair’. He doesn’t mention what the anything is, because he’s talking to himself, still caught up in the fairness of it all. Then he notices you, and, by way of justification, adds:

同样，你可以想象一个人黎明时分站在威斯敏斯特桥上，眺望着伦敦。过了一会儿，他自言自语道：“世间再无比这更美好的事物。”他没有说明“世间再无”指的是什么，因为他只是在自言自语，仍然沉浸在这美好的景象之中。然后他注意到你，为了证明自己所言非虚，他又补充道：

Dull would he be of soul who could pass by

一个能轻易路过的人，他的灵魂该是多么迟钝啊。

A sight so touching in its majesty:

如此壮丽的景象，令人动容：

This City now doth, like a garment, wear

这座城市如今如同一件衣服，披着

The beauty of the morning; silent, bare,

清晨之美；寂静，空旷，

Ships, towers, domes, theatres and temples lie

船只、塔楼、圆顶、剧院和寺庙都静静地躺在那里。

Open unto the fields, and to the sky

面向田野，面向天空

To which a cruel passer-by would say, ‘If it’s wearing the morning like a garment, how come it’s bare? Eh?’ But a more understanding soul would say: ‘Ships, towers, domes, theatres, and temples. Well done, Mr Wordsworth. That’s a lovely congeries.’

这时，一个刻薄的路人会说：“如果它把晨曦当作一件衣服，为什么它却光秃秃的呢？嗯？”但一个更通情达理的人会说：“船只、塔楼、圆顶、剧院和寺庙。干得好，华兹华斯先生。这是一幅美丽的画卷。”

1 Most rhetorical terms are awkward (see Epilogue ), but prolepsis is one of the worst as it has five more rhetorical or grammatical meanings that are pretty much unrelated, as prolepsis is merely the Greek for ‘anticipation’. So it can also mean anticipating your opponent’s argument : ‘He’ll probably tell you X, but I can prove that X is wrong.’ It can also mean referring to something in its future state : ‘You’re a dead man walking.’ It can be a form of irony where a character in a play says something that later turns out to be untrue. It can be a grammatical construction in which a verb agrees with a whole but not the parts. It can mean a rhetorical device in which the subject is outlined in brief before being dealt with in detail: ‘This paper will show that …’ It also has a couple of medical and botanical meanings.

大多数修辞术语都比较拗口（参见后记），而“prolepsis”（预叙）一词尤其令人难以理解，因为它还有五个几乎毫不相关的修辞或语法含义，而“prolepsis”仅仅是希腊语中“预期”的意思。因此，它也可以指预判对手的论点：“他可能会告诉你X，但我可以证明X是错的。”它还可以指指某事物未来的状态：“你死定了。”它也可以指一种反讽形式，即戏剧中的人物说了一句后来证明是假的话。它还可以指一种语法结构，其中动词与整体一致，但与各部分不一致。它还可以指一种修辞手法，即在详细论述之前先简要概述主题：“本文将表明……”此外，它还有一些医学和植物学方面的含义。

2 Copyright © 1940. By W.H. Auden, renewed. Reprinted by permission of Curtis Brown, Ltd.

Chapter 37

第三十七章

Congeries

集团公司

The best thing about congeries is that it’s a singular noun. Otherwise I’d use the word ‘list’. List means exactly the same thing, but it has none of the exoticism of congeries, no spice, no adventure, no derring-do, no whiff of the palm tree and the jungle, no pizzazz, no fairy-dust, no magic. Also everybody knows how to pronounce ‘list’, but no two dictionaries can agree on congeries, which makes it much more fun. The plural, incidentally is congeries.

“congeries”这个词最棒的地方在于它是单数名词。否则我就用“list”了。“list”的意思完全一样，但它一点也不像“congeries”那样充满异域风情，没有刺激，没有冒险，没有英勇无畏，没有棕榈树和丛林的气息，没有活力，没有魔幻，没有魔法。而且，每个人都知道“list”怎么发音，但“congeries”的发音却众说纷纭，这反而更有趣。顺便一提，它的复数形式是“congeries”。

Congeries is Latin for a heap, and in rhetoric it applies to any piling up of adjectives or nouns in a list. So when St Paul said:

Congeries在拉丁语中是“堆”的意思，在修辞学中，它指的是将形容词或名词堆砌成列表。所以当圣保罗说：

Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are these; Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness, Idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies, Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like […] But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance …

情欲的事都是显而易见的，就如奸淫、污秽、邪荡、拜偶像、邪术、仇恨、争竞、忌恨、恼怒、结党、纷争、异端、嫉妒、凶杀、醉酒、荒宴，以及类似的事。[…] 圣灵所结的果子，就是仁爱、喜乐、和平、忍耐、恩慈、良善、信实、温柔、节制……

He was making a congeries. He was also doing something completely unnatural, because humans don’t naturally make lists. Or, to be more precise, we don’t talk in lists. If I were to ask what your 50 favourite films were, you would probably settle down with a pencil and paper and spend an hour or so puzzling over it. If I didn’t let you have any stationery, you’d start to talk, but you’d talk very, very slowly. You’d roll your eyes around and look at the ceiling for inspiration. So would I. So would anybody.

他当时正在列清单。而且，他做的这件事完全不自然，因为人类天生不会列清单。或者更准确地说，我们不会用清单的方式说话。如果我问你最喜欢的50部电影是什么，你可能会拿出纸笔，花上一个小时左右的时间好好琢磨琢磨。如果我不让你用纸笔，你也会开始说话，但你会说得非常非常慢。你会翻白眼，抬头望向天花板寻找灵感。我也会这样。任何人都会这样。

If you took one deep breath and reeled off the full list in one, syllable-perfect, and in ascending order, I would think you either a superhuman, or the sort of person who has worked it all out with pencil and paper some lonely Sunday and then memorised it in the hope, in the desperate hope, that you would someday be asked Just That Question. Either way, I would think you peculiar. Nobody but a God or a fool talks in lists.

如果你深吸一口气，一字不差地把整个列表按升序完整地念出来，我会觉得你不是超人，就是那种在某个寂寞的星期天用纸笔把所有东西都算出来，然后死记硬背下来，满怀希望地盼望着有一天会被问到这个问题的人。不管怎样，我都会觉得你很古怪。除了神和傻瓜，没人会用列表说话。

Which is why they are so effective. They startle and bewilder. If a normal person were asked to describe a Christmas tree they would murmur something about presents and tinsel. Here is how Dickens did it:

这就是它们如此有效的原因。它们令人惊叹，令人困惑。如果让一个普通人描述圣诞树，他们可能会含糊其辞地说些关于礼物和彩带之类的东西。狄更斯是这样写的：

The tree was planted in the middle of a great round table, and towered high above their heads. It was brilliantly lighted by a multitude of little tapers; and everywhere sparkled and glittered with bright objects. There were rosy-cheeked dolls, hiding behind the green leaves; and there were real watches (with movable hands, at least, and an endless capacity of being wound up) dangling from innumerable twigs; there were French-polished tables, chairs, bedsteads, wardrobes, eight-day clocks, and various other articles of domestic furniture (wonderfully made, in tin, at Wolverhampton), perched among the boughs, as if in preparation for some fairy housekeeping; there were jolly, broad-faced little men, much more agreeable in appearance than many real men – and no wonder, for their heads took off, and showed them to be full of sugar-plums; there were fiddles and drums; there were tambourines, books, work-boxes, paint-boxes, sweetmeat-boxes, peep-show boxes, 1 and all kinds of boxes; there were trinkets for the elder girls, far brighter than any grown-up gold and jewels; there were baskets and pincushions in all devices; there were guns, swords, and banners; there were witches standing in enchanted rings of pasteboard, to tell fortunes; there were teetotums, humming-tops, needle-cases, pen-wipers, smelling-bottles, conversation-cards, bouquet-holders; real fruit, made artificially dazzling with gold leaf; imitation apples, pears, and walnuts, crammed with surprises; in short, as a pretty child, before me, delightedly whispered to another pretty child, her bosom friend, ‘There was everything, and more.’

那棵树栽种在一张巨大的圆桌中央，高耸入云，高过他们的头顶。无数小蜡烛照亮了它，树上到处闪烁着明亮的光芒。绿叶后藏着脸颊红润的娃娃；无数树枝上挂着真正的怀表（至少指针可以转动，而且可以无限上弦）；树枝间摆放着抛光的桌子、椅子、床架、衣柜、八日钟以及其他各种家用家具（这些家具都是在伍尔弗汉普顿用锡精心制作的），仿佛在为仙女们准备家务；还有一些笑容可掬、脸庞宽阔的小矮人，他们的外表比许多真人还要讨人喜欢——这也不奇怪，因为他们的脑袋可以摘下来，露出里面装满了糖梅；还有小提琴和鼓；那里有铃鼓、书籍、工作盒、颜料盒、糖果盒、窥视盒，以及各种各样的盒子；有给大女孩们的饰品，比任何成年人的金银珠宝都更加闪亮；有各种形状的篮子和针垫；有枪、剑和旗帜；有站在纸板魔法圈里的女巫，用来算命；有陀螺、嗡嗡作响的陀螺、针盒、笔擦、香水瓶、对话卡片、花束架；真正的水果，用金箔装饰得闪闪发光；人造苹果、梨和核桃，里面塞满了惊喜；总之，正如我面前一个漂亮的小女孩，高兴地对她亲密的朋友，另一个漂亮的小女孩耳语道：“那里什么都有，而且远不止这些。”

That’s a list, a list nobody could say or speak unless they had spent six months memorising it. But what an image! Noun after noun after noun. You cannot help but see the Christmas tree in all its detailed glory. It is a heap of pretty images. And that’s how Dickens wanted to get his image across. The reader is simply bludgeoned into submission.

那是一份清单，一份除非花了六个月时间背诵，否则没人能说出口的清单。但那画面感十足！名词一个接一个，令人目不暇接。你无法不去想象那棵圣诞树，它细节丰富，美轮美奂。这简直就是一堆精美的意象。而这正是狄更斯想要传达的意象。读者就这样被强行灌输，最终屈服。

Congeries work precisely because readers and listeners aren’t used to them. We can deal with gold-tongued flattery and snarled threats, but a list? It hits below the belt. And a list doesn’t need to be as long as Dickens’ Christmas tree. Shakespeare got the same sort of effect with:

罗列式的表达之所以有效，恰恰是因为读者和听众不习惯这种形式。我们可以接受花言巧语的奉承和恶狠狠的威胁，但罗列式的表达？那就太伤人了。而且，罗列式的表达也不需要像狄更斯笔下的圣诞树那样冗长。莎士比亚也用过类似的表达方式：

The cloud-capp’d towers, the gorgeous palaces,

云雾缭绕的塔楼，华丽的宫殿，

The solemn temples, the great globe itself

庄严的庙宇，巨大的地球仪本身

Shakespeare loved lists, especially when he was insulting people.

莎士比亚喜欢列举清单，尤其是在他侮辱别人的时候。

… you starveling, you elf-skin, you dried neat’s tongue, you bull’s pizzle, you stock-fish! O for breath to utter what is like thee! You tailor’s-yard, you sheath, you bowcase; you vile standing-tuck …

……你这饥饿的家伙，你这精灵皮，你这干牛舌，你这牛鞭，你这干鳕鱼！哦，多么渴望能说出比你更糟糕的词！你这裁缝的院子，你这鞘，你这弓袋；你这卑鄙的立领……

The technical name for a heap of insults is bdelygmia, and the best thing about a good bdelygmia (aside from the pronunciation: no letter is silent) is that you don’t even need to know what any of the words mean. I have no idea what a tailor’s-yard is, or why it might be an insult. Yet it works, as part of a list. Take this beauty from Gabriel Harvey in the late sixteenth century:

一堆侮辱性词语的专业术语是“bdelygmia”，而好的“bdelygmia”最棒的地方（除了发音：每个字母都发音）在于，你甚至不需要知道任何一个词的意思。我不知道“裁缝店”是什么，也不知道它为什么会成为侮辱。但它作为列表的一部分却很有效。看看十六世纪末加布里埃尔·哈维的这句妙语：

Fie on impure Ganymedes, Hermaphrodites, Neronists, Messalinists, Dodecomechanists, Capricians, Inventors of new, or Revivers of old lecheries, and the whole brood of venereous libertines.

呸！不洁的伽倪墨得斯、雌雄同体者、尼禄主义者、梅萨利尼主义者、十二机械主义者、任性者、发明新淫乱或复兴旧淫乱之徒，以及所有好色的放荡之徒。

You would need a damned fine classical education to even have a hint of what you were being accused of. But as a bdelygmia, it’s beautiful.

你需要接受过非常优秀的古典教育，才能勉强理解你被指控的罪名。但作为一件bdelygmia（一种印度传统服饰），它很美。

Of course, a congeries doesn’t have to be made of nouns; adjectives will pummel just as well. They don’t paint a picture in the way that nouns do, but they beat their way in. Shakespeare described sex and wanting to have sex thus:

当然，构成一个整体的词语不一定非得是名词；形容词也能起到同样的作用。它们不像名词那样描绘画面，但它们也能有效地融入其中。莎士比亚曾这样描述性以及对性的渴望：

The expense of spirit 2 in a waste of shame

精神2的代价是浪费耻辱

Is lust in action: and till action, lust

欲望是行动：直到行动，欲望……

Is perjured, murderous, bloody, full of blame,

作伪证、杀人、血腥、充满罪责

Savage, extreme, rude, cruel, not to trust;

野蛮、极端、粗鲁、残忍、不可信任；

Which shows that the poor chap was probably as bad with women as he was good with words. A good list is the love of every good writer. Joyce rejoiced in them, Beckett revelled, Wilde went wild, and Homer counted ships. There is something liberating about simply putting together words with no need to bother with structuring them. Even when a congeries is simply found lying around it has a certain magic to it. Take this list from 1953 of words approved by the East German government for describing the British:

这说明，这可怜的家伙可能在女人方面和他擅长文字一样糟糕。好的词汇表是每个优秀作家的心头好。乔伊斯沉醉其中，贝克特如痴如醉，王尔德如痴如醉，荷马则数着船只。把词语随意组合在一起，无需费心组织结构，这本身就有一种解放感。即使只是随意拾取的词汇表，也自带某种魔力。比如这份1953年东德政府批准用来形容英国人的词汇表：

Paralytic sycophants, effete betrayers of humanity, carrion-eating servile imitators, arch-cowards and collaborators, gang of woman-murderers, degenerate rabble, parasitic traditionalists, playboy soldiers, conceited dandies.

麻木的马屁精，颓废的人类叛徒，食腐的奴性模仿者，胆小如鼠的合作者，杀害妇女的团伙，堕落的乌合之众，寄生虫般的传统主义者，花花公子士兵，自负的纨绔子弟。

Splendid sentence. But no verb.

句子很精彩，可惜缺少动词。

1 A ‘ peep - show box’ in that more innocent age was a box with a magnifying glass in the side through which you could see little painted wonders. In the twentieth century some bright and drooling spark had the idea of putting dirty pictures inside, and eventually somebody decided to shove a whole girl in there. This is called Progress.

在那个更纯真的年代，“窥视盒”指的是一个侧面装有放大镜的盒子，透过放大镜可以看到一些彩绘小画。到了二十世纪，某个头脑简单、思想龌龊的人突发奇想，把不雅图片放进去，最终有人竟然把一个完整的女孩塞了进去。这就是所谓的进步。

2 Semen.

2 精液。

Chapter 38

第38章

Scesis Onomaton

Scesis Onomaton

Some people believe that a sentence has to have a main verb. Nonsense! It’s quite possible to hold a long conversation without a verb in sight. ‘Drink?’ ‘Thanks.’ ‘Your round.’ ‘Really?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘Damn.’

有些人认为句子必须有主要动词。胡说！完全可以进行一段很长的对话，中间却看不到一个动词。“喝点什么？”“谢谢。”“你请客。”“真的吗？”“是的。”“真棒。”

And it’s quite possible to write without main verbs. You can’t do it for ever, but you can have a go. No verbs. Only fragments. A noun here; a participle there. The first sentence of Bleak House .

完全可以不用主要动词来写作。虽然不可能永远这样写下去，但你可以尝试一下。没有动词，只有动词片段。这里一个名词，那里一个分词。《荒凉山庄》的第一句话就是如此。

London.

伦敦。

That’s a good first sentence. That’s a writer who knew what he wanted to say. He wanted to say London, and everything it stood for. Start there and then we can narrow down. The next sentence has no main verb either:

这是个不错的开头句。这位作家很清楚自己想表达什么。他想表达的是伦敦，以及它所代表的一切。就从这里入手，然后我们再缩小范围。下一句也没有主要动词：

Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting in Lincoln’s Inn Hall.

米迦勒节学期刚刚结束，大法官正在林肯律师学院大厅就座。

Just to be clear, ‘sitting’ is a participle acting as an adjective to ‘Lord Chancellor’. Then:

需要说明的是，“sitting”是作形容词修饰“Lord Chancellor”的分词形式。然后：

Implacable November weather.

十一月的天气阴冷无情。

And so it goes on. Ten more full stops. 343 more words until you finally get to a sentence with a main verb in it. Nothing actually does anything. It hangs there like fog. ‘Fog everywhere.’ The scene is set perfectly, because that’s what scesis onomaton (SKEE-sis o-NO-mat-on) does best. Setting scenes. The simple noun that tells you all you need to know.

就这样继续下去。又过了十个句号。又过了343个字，你才终于看到一个包含主要动词的句子。但实际上什么也没发生。它像雾一样笼罩着那里。“到处都是雾。”场景设置得恰到好处，因为这就是拟声词（scesis onomaton）最擅长的：营造场景。一个简单的名词，就能告诉你所有你需要知道的信息。

Space: the final frontier.

太空：最后的边疆。

It wouldn’t be nearly as good if it ran:

如果它能运行，那就远不如现在这样好了：

This is Space, which is the final frontier.

这里是太空，是人类的最终疆界。

Who needs an ‘is’ when you have all those nouns? Eternity. A sentence without a tense. ‘This is Space’, ‘this was Space’, or ‘this will be Space’ would limit it in time. If you dispense with main verbs then it could be past, present or future. Dickens’ London is, was and will be London. It doesn’t matter what those in London now do with the city, because Dickens claimed it in one timeless word. His is a London where dinosaurs ruled the earth; he’s quite explicit about it:

有了这么多名词，谁还需要“是”？永恒。一个没有时态的句子。“这是空间”、“这是曾经的空间”或“这将是空间”都会限制其时间范围。如果省略主要动词，那么它可以是过去、现在或将来。狄更斯的伦敦是、曾经是、将来也永远是伦敦。如今伦敦人如何对待这座城市并不重要，因为狄更斯用一个永恒的词语就宣告了它的永恒。在他的伦敦，恐龙统治着地球；他对此毫不掩饰：

As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill.

街道上满是泥泞，仿佛水刚刚从地球上消失一般，如果遇到一头四十英尺长的巨齿龙，像一头大象蜥蜴一样摇摇摆摆地爬上霍尔本山，那将是一件非常奇妙的事情。

London: the eternal city. As timeless as Star Trek ’s void. And when Dickens finally does get to a main verb (because you can’t keep scesis onomaton up for ever), he deliberately throws his readers:

伦敦：永恒之城。如同《星际迷航》中的虚空一般永恒。当狄更斯终于用上一个主要动词时（因为你不可能永远用拟声词），他故意抛给读者一个难题：

Most of the shops lighted two hours before their time – as the gas seems to know, for it has a haggard and unwilling look.

大多数商店都比平时提前两个小时亮灯——煤气似乎也知道这一点，因为它看起来疲惫不堪，很不情愿。

Past and present in one sentence. Dickens didn’t want to be tied down to a time just yet. Scesis onomaton can therefore set an eternal scene, but it can also state an eternal principle, one that’s not pinned down within History’s muddy field. When Winston Churchill wrote his history of the Second World War he had a lot to say about the events of 1939–45, events that he had in large part brought about. But the book begins with a simple, verbless heading: ‘The Moral of the Work’. And underneath that is written:

过去与现在，尽在一句话之中。狄更斯并不想被束缚于某个特定的时代。因此，拟声词既可以描绘永恒的场景，也可以阐述永恒的原则，一个不受历史泥沼束缚的原则。温斯顿·丘吉尔撰写二战史时，对1939年至1945年间发生的事件有很多话要说，而这些事件在很大程度上正是由他一手促成的。但这本书的开篇却是一个简洁的、没有动词的标题：“作品的寓意”。标题下方写着：

In War: Resolution.

战争：决议。

In Defeat: Defiance.

在失败中：反抗。

In Victory: Magnanimity.

胜利的真谛：宽宏大量。

In Peace: Good Will.

和平之中：善意。

He could have made it a boast: ‘In war, I had resolution’; or a patriotic victory: ‘We had resolution’. He could have made it an order along the lines of the Ten Commandments: ‘In War thou shalt have resolution.’ Or he could have made it a proclamation of the future: ‘In War we shall always have resolution.’ But any of those alternatives would have limited him, and limited his words. This was not the history. That would follow in Chapter 1. This was, is and will be The Moral of the Work and a moral has no time. No birth. No death.

他本可以把它当作一种夸耀：“在战争中，我意志坚定”；或者把它当作一场爱国的胜利：“我们意志坚定”。他本可以把它当作一条类似十诫的命令：“在战争中，你应当意志坚定”。或者，他本可以把它当作一个未来的宣言：“在战争中，我们将永远意志坚定”。但任何一种选择都会限制他，也会限制他的言辞。这并非历史。历史将在第一章讲述。这过去是、现在是、将来也永远是这部作品的寓意，而寓意没有时间限制。它没有诞生，也没有消亡。

Churchill’s eternal truths were rather noble. But scesis onomaton works for even the pettiest rule. ‘Finders keepers’ does not deign to tell us whether they were, are, will be or should be. It’s a rule, a verbless rule (and was actually an underlying principle of parts of the British Empire). The same goes for ‘Each to his own’, ‘Like father, like son’ and ‘Third time lucky’.

丘吉尔的永恒真理固然高尚。但即使是最琐碎的规则，拟声词也能适用。“先到先得”并不屑于告诉我们东西过去是、现在是、将来是还是应该归谁所有。它只是一条规则，一条无动词的规则（实际上，它曾是部分大英帝国的基本原则）。“各得其所”、“有其父必有其子”和“事不过三”也是如此。

This timeless aspect of scesis onomaton has been rather brought down by its use in politics. Few figures can last long in that world without being scalded by all the hot air. There have been enough protest placards calling for ‘War!’ or ‘No War!’, for ‘Justice!’ or, in minority cases, ‘Injustice!’, that the bare noun has started to look rather bare. Yet in other fields, the scesis onomaton still bears fruit. Tennyson used it for ‘Crossing the Bar’:

拟声词的永恒特质，因其在政治领域的运用而大打折扣。在这个圈子里，鲜少有人能长久立足而不被铺天盖地的喧嚣所吞噬。抗议标语上充斥着“战争！”或“反对战争！”、“正义！”，以及少数情况下“不公正！”的呼声，以至于原本的名词形式显得苍白无力。然而，在其他领域，拟声词依然大有可为。丁尼生就曾用它来指代“渡过沙洲”。

Sunset and evening star,

日落和晚星

And one clear call for me!

给我打一个明确的电话！

The verblessness is perfect for a poem about going ‘from out our bourn of Time and Place’. But he uses it even more effectively as a closing. In In Memoriam , part 50, he runs through a whole poem of fully verbed-up sentences. So you aren’t expecting the end. But as usual with Tennyson, mortality and eternity are the themes. Tennyson was a great poet, but I can’t imagine that he was that much fun to spend a month with. All beard and misery. The last verse begins with a main verb and looks thoroughly traditional and grammatical:

这种无动词的表达方式，对于一首关于“离开时空”的诗来说堪称完美。但他更巧妙地将其运用在结尾。在《悼念集》第五十首中，他用一整首诗都使用了完整的动词句。因此，你不会预料到结尾。但正如丁尼生一贯的风格，死亡与永恒是这首诗的主题。丁尼生是一位伟大的诗人，但我很难想象和他一起度过一个月会是怎样一番乐事。满脸胡须，愁容满面。最后一节以一个主要动词开头，看起来完全符合传统语法：

Be near me when I fade away,

当我离世之时，请陪伴在我身边。

To point the term of human strife,

指出人类冲突的时期，

And on the low dark verge of life

在生命的低谷和黑暗边缘

The twilight of eternal day.

永恒白昼的黄昏。

And time and verbs have vanished. Nothing to cling to. That is the great feat of scesis. Of course, it has other effects. ‘Me Tarzan. You Jane’ manages to avoid eternal truth. It also never popped up in any of the films, even as a clapper-board.

时间和动词都消失了。没有什么可以依附。这就是超验的伟大壮举。当然，它还有其他影响。“我是泰山，你是简”成功地避开了永恒的真理。它也从未在任何一部电影中出现过，哪怕是以场记板的形式。

It’s very hard to say what the most popular play of Renaissance London was. The longest single run of any play was Thomas Middleton’s A Game At Chess , which ran for nine whole nights, at which point it was banned for being too politically interesting for contemporary audiences (and hence too tedious for anyone today). However, A Game at Chess wasn’t famous for its memorable lines. That honour went to The Spanish Tragedy by Thomas Kyd.

很难说文艺复兴时期伦敦最受欢迎的戏剧是什么。演出时间最长的剧目是托马斯·米德尔顿的《棋局》，连续上演了九个晚上，之后因政治内容过于敏感（对当时的观众来说也过于乏味）而被禁演。然而，《棋局》并非以其令人难忘的台词而闻名。这一殊荣属于托马斯·基德的《西班牙悲剧》。

The Spanish Tragedy stood in relation to Renaissance drama in the way that Casablanca stands in relation to cinema. It wasn’t quite the first, but it was pretty much the first anyone cared about. It may not have been the best, but it was the classic. Casablanca was big and melodramatic in a way that you could get away with in the 1940s and that everyone still secretly loves, even if we feel we’re too clever for it today. The Spanish Tragedy was big and melodramatic in a way you could get away with in the late 1580s, and that everyone still loved in 1610, even if they felt that they were too clever for it by then. People would get drunk and then recite the lines in a tearful manner. This happened enough that there were scenes in other plays taking the mickey out of how people re-enacted the scenes of The Spanish Tragedy .

《西班牙悲剧》之于文艺复兴戏剧，正如《卡萨布兰卡》之于电影。它并非第一部，但却是第一部真正引起人们关注的作品。它或许并非最佳，但却是经典之作。《卡萨布兰卡》的宏大和戏剧化，在20世纪40年代依然适用，至今仍为人所喜爱，即便我们如今自认为高人一等，不屑一顾。《西班牙悲剧》的宏大和戏剧化，在16世纪80年代末期依然适用，即便到了1610年，人们依然喜爱，即便他们自认为那时已不再那么高人一等。人们会喝得酩酊大醉，然后声泪俱下地背诵台词。这种情况屡见不鲜，以至于其他戏剧中出现了专门讽刺人们重现《西班牙悲剧》场景的桥段。

Thomas Kyd was a hell of a writer. There is only one contemporary account of seeing Hamlet in the theatre. Not Shakespeare’s version. Nobody thought that worth writing about. No. Thomas Kyd’s original. 1 Not the Shakespeare remake. And The Spanish Tragedy was Kyd’s best play and the best lines in The Spanish Tragedy were the main-verbless …

托马斯·基德是一位杰出的作家。现存只有一份同时代人对在剧院观看《哈姆雷特》的记录。不是莎士比亚的版本。没人觉得那值得写。不，是托马斯·基德的原作。¹ 不是莎士比亚的改编版。《西班牙悲剧》是基德最好的剧作，而《西班牙悲剧》中最精彩的台词是……

O eyes! No eyes, but fountains fraught with tears!

哦，眼睛！没有眼睛，只有泪水涌出的泉眼！

O life! No life, but lively form of death!

哦，生命！并非生命，而是死亡的生动形态！

O world! No world, but mass of public wrongs,

哦，世界啊！这世间不过是一堆公共罪恶罢了。

Confused and filled with murder and misdeeds!

混乱不堪，充满了谋杀和罪恶！

O Heavens!

天哪！

Which is a good example of isocolon, alliteration, metaphor, and anaphora.

这是等长句、头韵、隐喻和反复修辞的一个很好的例子。

1 Most scholars seem to agree that the first Hamlet was probably written by Kyd, but there’s no solid evidence. The only line that survives is ‘Hamlet! Revenge!’

1 大多数学者似乎都认为第一部《哈姆雷特》很可能是基德所作，但没有确凿的证据。唯一流传下来的台词是“哈姆雷特！复仇！”

# ↩

Chapter 39

第39章

Anaphora

回指

Anaphora (an-AFF-or-a) is starting each sentence with the same words. It’s the king of rhetorical figures. I hate to confess it, but it’s true. Hendiadys has her eccentric charm, polyptoton slaves away in the background, catachresis wanders around smashing things up, but anaphora has all the power.

首语重复（Anaphora）是指每个句子都以相同的词语开头。它是修辞手法之王。我不得不承认，这是事实。复句（Hendiadys）自有其独特的魅力，多音句（Polyptoton）默默地在幕后运作，误用句（Catachresis）四处游荡，破坏一切，但首语重复却拥有全部的力量。

It’s so preposterously easy to do. It’s so preposterously easy to pick some words. It’s so preposterously easy to repeat them. Everyone can do it. Everyone can start a sentence the same way. It takes no skill. It takes …

这简直易如反掌。挑选几个词简直易如反掌。重复这些词简直易如反掌。人人都能做到。人人都能用同样的方式开头造句。这不需要任何技巧。它只需要……

I could go on like this all day, and be thinking about something else. But anaphora is dangerous. It’s almost too powerful. Or to put it more precisely, it’s like a gun: very useful, but you need to point it the right way before pulling the trigger. With anaphora people always remember the opening words, but they usually forget the rest.

我可以这样一直说下去，然后想着别的事情。但是，反复修辞很危险，它几乎太强大了。或者更准确地说，它就像一把枪：非常有用，但你必须在扣动扳机之前瞄准正确的方向。人们总是会记住反复修辞的开头几句话，但通常会忘记后面的内容。

Do you remember Winston Churchill’s description of the invasion of Britain? Do you remember how he spoke of the Germans defeating our navy, landing on the south coast, taking London and reducing British resistance to a few guerrilla fighters in Wales or the Lake District or somewhere like that? Do you remember that? No?

你还记得温斯顿·丘吉尔对英国沦陷的描述吗？你还记得他是如何描述德国人击败英国海军、在南部海岸登陆、占领伦敦，并将英国抵抗力量削弱到只剩下威尔士、湖区或类似地方的少数游击队员吗？你还记得吗？不记得了？

That’s odd, because you do. You just never listened to the speech. You listened to the anaphora. Churchill used to write his speeches out on separate lines. So his description of the German conquest of Britain, delivered to Parliament in 1940 when Britain stood alone, ally-less and facing almost certain defeat, would have looked, in his notes, like this:

这很奇怪，因为你的确听进去了。你只是没听演讲内容，只听了反复出现的句式。丘吉尔习惯把演讲稿单独写在几行。所以，1940年，当英国孤立无援、几乎注定失败时，他在议会发表的关于德国征服英国的演讲，在他的笔记里应该是这样的：

We shall not flag or fail.

我们不会出现任何问题或失败。

We shall go on to the end.

我们将继续进行到最后。

We shall fight in France,

我们将在法国作战。

We shall fight on the seas and oceans [North and Atlantic],

我们将在海洋（北海和大西洋）上战斗，

We shall fight with growing confidence and growing strength in the air,

我们将以日益增长的信心和力量在空中作战，

We shall defend our island, whatever the cost may be,

我们将不惜一切代价保卫我们的岛屿。

We shall fight on the beaches [of Britain],

我们将在（英国的）海滩上战斗，

We shall fight on the landing grounds [of Britain],

我们将在英国的登陆场作战，

We shall fight in the fields [of Kent] and in the streets [of London],

我们将在肯特郡的田野上和伦敦的街头战斗，

We shall fight in the hills [Somewhere up North].

我们将在山上战斗（在北方的某个地方）。

We shall never surrender. 1

我们永不投降。

It’s pretty clear what he’s describing. He’s describing defeat, defeat with honour.

他描述的是什么，很明显。他描述的是失败，但也是光荣的失败。

But Churchill also knew exactly what he was doing with anaphora. People never hear the rest, they hear the words ‘We shall fight’ and that’s good enough for them. They hear, and because they’ve heard it several times, they believe. Churchill needed to get across two messages: we shall fight, and we shall probably lose. The anaphora allowed him to push one, while slipping the other in unnoticed.

但丘吉尔也深谙其道，他运用反复修辞的技巧炉火纯青。人们听不到后面的内容，他们只听到“我们将战斗”这几个字，这就足够了。他们听到了，而且因为听过好几遍，所以就信以为真。丘吉尔需要传达两个信息：我们将战斗，而且我们很可能会失败。反复修辞让他能够突出其中一个信息，同时又悄无声息地融入另一个信息。

He phrased exactly the same thing privately to his Cabinet. But he told them: ‘If at last the long story [of Britain] is to end, it were better it should end, not through surrender, but only when we are rolling senseless on the ground.’ 2

他私下里对内阁成员也说了同样的话。但他告诉他们：“如果英国漫长的历史最终要结束，那么最好不是以投降的方式结束，而是在我们彻底崩溃、奄奄一息地倒在地上的时候结束。”²

Do you remember Martin Luther King and his dream? Do you remember what the dream was? All the details? I mean, I’m sure you remember the speech in general. But what three states are named? No? Nobody remembers. They remember the dream and not the details.

你还记得马丁·路德·金和他的梦想吗？你还记得他的梦想是什么吗？所有的细节？我的意思是，我相信你大致记得他的演讲。但是他提到了哪三个州的名字呢？不记得了？没人记得。人们记住的是他的梦想，而不是细节。

Of course, anaphora doesn’t have to use a whole phrase. You can get by with only a word. The effect is slightly less powerful, but beautifully hypnotic. There was an eighteenth-century poet called Christopher Smart. Smart did all of the things that you might expect of an eighteenth-century poet: getting into debt, writing scurrilous poems, writing religious poems, signing silly contracts with booksellers. In the end it all got too much for him and he was confined to a madhouse with nothing to keep him company except a cat called Jeoffrey.

当然，反复修辞并不一定非要用整个短语。有时只用一个词也行。效果虽然稍逊一筹，却同样引人入胜。十八世纪有一位名叫克里斯托弗·斯马特的诗人。斯马特做了所有十八世纪诗人会做的事：负债累累、写些粗俗的诗、写些宗教诗、和书商签些荒唐的合同。最终，这一切让他不堪重负，他被关进了疯人院，陪伴他的只有一只名叫杰弗里的猫。

So Smart wrote a poem. It’s a very odd poem by any measure. For starters, it’s in Free Verse, which wasn’t really meant to exist back then. For seconds, it’s utterly insane in a terribly religious way (lines like ‘Let Samuel, the Minister from a child, without ceasing praise with the Porcupine, which is the creature of defence and stands upon his arms continually’ should give you some idea). But the oddest thing is that all the lines on each page begin with the same word. On some pages this word is ‘Let’, and on other pages this word is ‘For’.

所以，斯马特写了一首诗。无论从哪个角度来看，这都是一首非常奇特的诗。首先，它是自由诗，而自由诗在当时并不常见。其次，这首诗充满了宗教色彩，荒诞不经（比如“让自幼的牧师塞缪尔，不停地赞美豪猪，豪猪是防御的象征，它总是站在他的手臂上”这样的诗句，你应该能体会到它的怪异之处）。但最奇怪的是，每一页上的所有诗行都以同一个词开头。有些页上这个词是“Let”，有些页上这个词是“For”。

So, in a sense, it’s not free verse. Anaphora is the verse form. It is pure anaphoric poetry. And the most beautiful passage is the one about his cat, Jeoffrey.

所以，从某种意义上说，它不是自由诗。它的诗体是首字母重复诗。它是纯粹的首字母重复诗。其中最美的一段是关于他的猫杰弗里的。

For he purrs in thankfulness, when God tells him he’s a good Cat.

当上帝夸他是只好猫时，他会发出感激的呼噜声。

For he is an instrument for the children to learn benevolence upon.

因为他是孩子们学习仁慈的工具。

For every house is incomplete without him and a blessing is lacking in the spirit.

因为没有他，每个家庭都不完整，灵里也缺少祝福。

For the Lord commanded Moses concerning the cats at the departure of the Children of Israel from Egypt.

因为耶和华在以色列人出埃及的时候，曾吩咐摩西要他们处理猫的事。

For every family had one cat at least in the bag.

几乎每个家庭都至少有一只猫装在袋子里。

For the English Cats are the best in Europe.

英国猫是欧洲最好的猫。

For he is the cleanest in the use of his fore-paws of any quadruped.

因为他是所有四足动物中前爪使用最干净的。

For the dexterity of his defence is an instance of the love of God to him exceedingly.

他巧妙的辩护体现了上帝对他极大的爱。

For he is the quickest to his mark of any creature.

因为他是所有生物中到达目标速度最快的。

For he is tenacious of his point.

因为他对自己的观点非常坚持。

For he is a mixture of gravity and waggery.

因为他既庄重又诙谐。

For he knows that God is his Saviour.

因为他知道上帝是他的救主。

For without all those for s, this wouldn’t be much of a read. For without all those for s, it would be the ravings of a madman. For with all those for s, it is, at least, the ravings of a mad poet.

如果没有那些“for”，这篇文章就没什么可读的了。如果没有那些“for”，它就只是疯子的呓语。有了那些“for”，它至少是一位疯狂诗人的呓语。

Anaphora gets everywhere. It’s been running through this book. Every chapter, every figure, every writer. Do you remember Dickens’ fog?

反复修辞无处不在。它贯穿了整本书。每一章、每一个人物、每一位作者都运用了反复修辞。你还记得狄更斯笔下的迷雾吗？

Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river […] Fog on the Essex marshes, fog on the Kentish heights. Fog creeping into the cabooses of collier-brigs; fog lying out on the yards and hovering in the rigging of great ships; fog drooping on the gunwales of barges and small boats. Fog in the eyes and throats of ancient Greenwich pensioners, wheezing by the firesides of their wards; fog in the stem and bowl of the afternoon pipe of the wrathful skipper …

到处都是雾。河水上游雾气弥漫，绿树成荫，草地如茵；河水下游也雾气缭绕……埃塞克斯郡的沼泽地雾气弥漫，肯特郡的高地也雾气弥漫。雾气悄悄渗入运煤船的船尾；雾气笼罩着大船的桅杆，盘旋在索具间；雾气垂落在驳船和小船的舷缘。雾气迷蒙了格林威治养老院老人们的眼睛和喉咙，他们在病房的炉火旁喘息；雾气也弥漫在暴躁船长午后烟斗的烟嘴和烟斗碗里……

That was anaphora. Do you remember Blake’s rhetorical questions?

那是首语重复。你还记得布莱克的反问句吗？

What the hammer? what the chain?

锤子是什么？链条是什么？

In what furnace was thy brain?

你的大脑是在怎样的熔炉中淬炼的？

What the anvil? what dread grasp

这是什么铁砧？这可怕的魔爪

Dare its deadly terrors clasp?

它那致命的恐怖胆敢紧握吗？

That was anaphora too. Do you remember the progressio of Ecclesiastes? That was anaphora.

那也是首语叠句。你还记得《传道书》的渐进句吗？那也是首语叠句。

A time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted; A time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up; A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance

生有时，死有时；栽种有时，拔出所栽种的也有时；杀戮有时，医治有时；拆毁有时，建造有时；哭泣有时，欢笑有时；哀恸有时，跳舞有时

And I suppose there is a time to conclude.

我想，总有一天要到结尾了。

1 This is part of a speech Churchill delivered to Parliament on 4 June 1940.

这是丘吉尔于 1940 年 6 月 4 日在议会发表的演讲的一部分。

2 This line was noted down by Hugh Dalton, Minister of Economic Warfare, who also remembered it as: ‘If this long island story of ours is to end at last, let it end only when each of us lies choking in his own blood upon the ground.’

2 经济战部长休·道尔顿记下了这句话，他还回忆说：“如果我们这个漫长的岛屿故事最终要结束，那就让它在我们每个人都倒在地上，被自己的鲜血呛死的时候结束吧。”
